Same operations are available through 4 MCP tools (create_agent_run, complete_agent_run, list_agent_runs, replay_agent_run) and the underlying REST API at /api/v1/projects/{project_id}/agent-runs.

sections.heading: Replay and compare runs
sections.text: To see whether a different prompt or more context changes what a reviewer finds, replay the run instead of re-creating it by hand: NEW=$(sfs agent replay run_abc123 --prompt-file review-prompt.md \ --context-ref docs/threat-model.md --output-id) sfs agent run --run-id "$NEW" --context-file .sessionfs/context.md # ... run your agent, then complete as usual ... sfs agent compare run_abc123 "$NEW" sfs agent replay creates a queued copy of the run. Fields you don't pass (--prompt / --prompt-file, --ticket, --persona, --context-ref) are copied from the original; the ticket must still belong to the same project. The new run records which run it came from, and the command prints the matching sfs agent run --run-id line plus a GitHub Actions / GitLab snippet to run it in CI. A replay is a fresh, manual run: it doesn't copy the original's CI provider, run URL or trigger source. sfs agent run --run-id RUN_ID starts an existing queued run instead of creating one. sfs agent run also accepts --prompt and a repeatable --context-ref to store the prompt and context references on a new run. sfs agent compare A B matches findings by rule or title, file and line, and lists them as added, removed or unchanged, with severity counts for each run (--format json for scripts). Both runs must be in the same project. In the dashboard, open a run and use Replay or Compare.

sections.heading: Agent feedback (outcome records)
sections.text: Beyond the pass/fail AgentRun record, SessionFS lets you attach structured feedback to agent work — a lightweight signal that classifies *what kind* of outcome happened, not just whether it passed: sfs agent feedback add --type route --verdict negative --label wrong_route \ --ticket TK_ID --final-owner sentinel sfs agent feedback list --type route sfs agent feedback summary Each record points at a run, ticket, or comment and carries a fixed vocabulary — route (correct_route/wrong_route), summary (summary_good/summary_bad), actionability (actionable/not_actionable), duplicate (duplicate/new_issue), resolution (false_positive/flaky/resolved_by_fix/resolved_by_test_update). Reassigning an agent-created ticket to a different persona auto-records a route/negative/wrong_route entry, so the router learns from every correction. summary is pure SQL aggregation — no LLM. The same surface is available as 3 MCP tools (record_agent_feedback, list_agent_feedback, get_agent_feedback_summary).

sections.heading: What this does NOT do
sections.text: No transcript / session capture. AgentRun records the *outcome* of a review; the model's transcript is not uploaded. No model orchestration. SessionFS doesn't spawn Claude/Codex/Bedrock. Your script picks the LLM and writes findings. No automatic KB promotion. Findings stay as run data. If you want a finding promoted into the persistent knowledge base, call sfs project entries add (or the MCP add_knowledge tool) explicitly. Scoped service API keys (v0.10.10+). CI runners should use a scoped service key (POST /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/service-keys) restricted to agent_runs:write (and optionally tickets:read, knowledge:write, etc.) — not a personal user bearer token. Service keys are expirable, org-scoped, can be rotated server-side, and write actor_type="service_key" provenance on every AgentRun and resulting audit row. Existing personal bearer tokens still authenticate (back-filled to scopes=["*"]) but are no longer the recommended pattern for CI.

sections.heading: See also
sections.text: External Agent Orchestration — wrap a spawned Codex/Gemini/Claude Code CLI agent in an AgentRun (same record, orchestrator-initiated instead of CI-gated). Cloud Agent Control Plane — same persona / ticket / knowledge surface for Bedrock + Vertex. MCP Server — create_agent_run, complete_agent_run, list_agent_runs in the full tool catalogue. CLI reference — sfs agent group + the new --output-id flag on sfs ticket create.

Cloud Agent Control Plane SessionFS coordinates AI agents across local tools and cloud platforms through one shared control plane: personas, tickets, project knowledge, and rules. This page covers integrating cloud agents — Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex/Gemini, and any custom HTTP-callable agent — directly with the SessionFS REST API. This is a control-plane integration: cloud agents can participate in your team's personas, tickets, knowledge, and rules. Transcript capture as .sfs sessions is not part of this layer — that ships in a future release. Until then, what your cloud agent says inside its own platform stays there; what it *does* against SessionFS (tickets, knowledge contributions) is captured here. This page covers *agent-initiated* runs — the cloud agent itself calls the REST API. If instead a coordination layer (a script, n8n, a GitHub Action, a Claude Code session) *spawns* an external CLI agent (Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Claude Code) to do ticket work, see External Agent Orchestration for the create_agent_run → spawn → complete_agent_run provenance wrapper.

sections.heading: What cloud agents can do today
sections.text: | Capability | Endpoint(s) | Tier | | List + load personas (atlas, prism, scribe, ...) | GET /api/v1/projects/{project_id}/personas[/{name}] | Pro+ | | List, create, start, complete tickets | GET/POST /api/v1/projects/{project_id}/tickets[/{ticket_id}/{start,complete}] | Team+ | | Get the compiled persona + ticket context for a started ticket | Returned by POST /tickets/{ticket_id}/start | Team+ | | Add knowledge entries (decisions, patterns, bugs, ...) | POST /api/v1/projects/{project_id}/entries/add | Paid | | Search knowledge | GET /api/v1/projects/{project_id}/entries?search=... | Paid | | Fetch canonical project rules | GET /api/v1/projects/{project_id}/rules | Paid | | Resolve project + compiled context by git remote | GET /api/v1/projects/{git_remote_normalized} | Paid | All operations require Authorization: Bearer <SessionFS_API_key>. As of v0.10.10, scoped service API keys (created at POST /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/service-keys) are the recommended credential for cloud agents — they are org-scoped, expirable, and restricted to a specific scope set (e.g. tickets:write, knowledge:write, agent_runs:write). Your existing user bearer tokens still work for prototyping.

sections.heading: Why this is not MCP
sections.text: MCP works great for local tools (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, etc.) where the agent runtime can spawn sfs mcp serve as a stdio subprocess. Bedrock, Vertex, and custom cloud agents typically can't. The Cloud Agent Control Plane gives those agents the same operations through plain HTTP, with no client-side daemon, no MCP transport, and no special SDK. If your agent *can* speak MCP, prefer it — you get 115 tools and richer descriptions. If it can't, use this layer.

sections.heading: Amazon Bedrock
sections.text: Bedrock agents call out to AWS Lambdas for every action group operation. SessionFS ships two reference artifacts:

sections.heading: 1. OpenAPI spec — docs/integrations/bedrock-action-group.yaml
sections.text: Import this file when creating a Bedrock Action Group. It declares 10 operations: listPersonas — GET /api/v1/projects/{project_id}/personas getPersona — GET /api/v1/projects/{project_id}/personas/{name} listTickets — GET /api/v1/projects/{project_id}/tickets createTicket — POST /api/v1/projects/{project_id}/tickets startTicket — POST /api/v1/projects/{project_id}/tickets/{ticket_id}/start completeTicket — POST /api/v1/projects/{project_id}/tickets/{ticket_id}/complete addKnowledge — POST /api/v1/projects/{project_id}/entries/add searchKnowledge — GET /api/v1/projects/{project_id}/entries getRules — GET /api/v1/projects/{project_id}/rules getProjectContext — GET /api/v1/projects/{git_remote_normalized}

sections.heading: 2. Lambda reference handler — docs/integrations/bedrock_lambda.py
sections.text: A 220-line Python 3.12 handler that: Parses the Bedrock action-group event (messageVersion, apiPath, httpMethod, parameters, requestBody). Dispatches to the matching SessionFS HTTP endpoint via an internal operation table that mirrors the OpenAPI spec. Reads SESSIONFS_API_URL + SESSIONFS_API_KEY from the Lambda's environment. In production, fetch SESSIONFS_API_KEY from AWS Secrets Manager rather than env directly — the env path is for quick testing. Returns a Bedrock-compatible response envelope. Uses only urllib.request so it runs on the vanilla Lambda Python runtime with no packaging dependencies.

sections.heading: Deploy
sections.text: Create a Lambda from bedrock_lambda.py (Python 3.12 runtime; handler bedrock_lambda.lambda_handler). Grant the Lambda permission to read your SessionFS API key from Secrets Manager. Set SESSIONFS_API_URL (default https://api.sessionfs.dev works for cloud-hosted SessionFS). In the Bedrock agent console: create an action group, point it at the Lambda, and upload bedrock-action-group.yaml as the API schema. Bedrock validates the schema, generates tool descriptions for the agent, and routes function calls through your Lambda.

sections.heading: Google Vertex / Gemini
sections.text: Vertex agents use function calling (google-generativeai ≥ 0.7). SessionFS ships:

sections.heading: docs/integrations/vertex_tools.py
sections.text: This file is two things in one: FUNCTION_DECLARATIONS — a list of 10 function-declaration dicts (name, description, parameters in OpenAPI-subset JSON Schema). Convert them with genai.protos.FunctionDeclaration(**decl) in your agent runtime. call_sessionfs_function(name, args) — a reference handler that maps a Gemini function-call result back into a SessionFS HTTP request. Deploy as a Cloud Function or Cloud Run service that proxies tool calls from your Vertex agent. from google.generativeai import protos from vertex_tools import FUNCTION_DECLARATIONS, call_sessionfs_function tools = [protos.Tool(function_declarations=[ protos.FunctionDeclaration(**d) for d in FUNCTION_DECLARATIONS ])] # In your message loop: response = model.generate_content(prompt, tools=tools) for fc in response.candidates[0].content.parts: if fc.function_call: result = call_sessionfs_function(fc.function_call.name, dict(fc.function_call.args)) # Feed `result` back into the model as a function-response part.

sections.heading: Cloud Function entry point
sections.text: vertex_tools.cloud_function_entrypoint(request) is a Flask-style HTTP handler ready to deploy. Wire your Vertex agent's function-call loop to POST {"name": "...", "args": {...}} to that URL.

sections.heading: Custom HTTP agents
sections.text: If you're rolling your own (LangChain, LlamaIndex, custom agent runtime, internal AI gateway, ...), you don't need either reference handler. Just speak HTTP: curl -X POST "$SESSIONFS_API_URL/api/v1/projects/$PROJECT_ID/tickets/$TICKET_ID/start?tool=generic" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $SESSIONFS_API_KEY" The OpenAPI spec at docs/integrations/bedrock-action-group.yaml doubles as a generic API reference for the control plane — the operationIds are platform-neutral.

sections.heading: Recommended workflow
sections.text: A cloud agent kicking off a piece of work typically does: getProjectContext to load the project's compiled context document. getRules to learn project-wide constraints. listTickets (filtered to its assigned persona) to find work. startTicket on the chosen ticket — the response includes the compiled persona + ticket context as markdown. Feed this back into the model as system prompt / role context. Do the work (writing code, drafting docs, etc.). addKnowledge for any decisions or discoveries surfaced during the work. completeTicket with notes + changed_files when done. The ticket moves to review and propagates completion notes to dependents.

sections.heading: Authentication
sections.text: Scoped service API keys (v0.10.10+, recommended for cloud agents). Create a service key scoped to the capabilities your agent needs: curl -X POST "$SESSIONFS_API_URL/api/v1/orgs/$ORG_ID/service-keys" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "name": "bedrock-atlas-agent", "scopes": ["tickets:write", "knowledge:write", "personas:read", "rules:read", "agent_runs:write"], "expires_at": "2026-12-31T23:59:59Z", "project_ids": ["proj_abc"] }' The response includes the raw key exactly once — copy it into AWS Secrets Manager (Bedrock Lambda) or Google Secret Manager (Vertex). The list endpoint only returns the key_prefix going forward. Service keys are deny-by-default at the route layer: get_current_user rejects them with 403 service_key_not_allowed, and a key only reaches a handler via require_scope("tickets:write") style dependencies. Cross-org access is blocked at the project boundary. Audit rows (HandoffEvent, AgentRun, TicketComment, KnowledgeEntry, RetrievalAuditEvent) record actor_type="service_key" + service_key_id + service_key_name so service-key activity is distinguishable from human activity. As of v0.29.1, knowledge:read also lets an agent read the project context (GET /projects/{id}, GET /projects/{id}/context/sections/{slug}) and wiki pages, and knowledge:write lets it write wiki pages — each scoped to the key's project_ids allowlist. Wiki writes record the service key as the actor (actor_type="service_key" + service_key_id/service_key_name). Structured error codes: api_key_revoked, api_key_expired, service_key_not_allowed, insufficient_scope (with required/current arrays), cross_org_denied. Legacy user bearer tokens still work (their scopes back-fill to ["*"]) but are not recommended for cloud agents. If you ship a personal token to Lambda, treat it like any production secret — load from AWS Secrets Manager or Google Secret Manager, never bake into Lambda/Cloud Function source.

sections.heading: What this does NOT include
sections.text: To keep this release thin and reviewable: No transcript / session capture. Cloud agents don't yet upload .sfs sessions. That ships separately. No new server endpoints. Everything is the v0.10.2 shipped API. Bearer tokens only at the wire layer. Service keys (v0.10.10) and user keys both ride the standard Authorization: Bearer ... header — no new client-side flow. No broad CORS changes. Lambda and Cloud Functions are server-to-server callers; CORS would only matter for browser-hosted cloud agents, which is not in scope. No new ticket fields for platform routing. If you need to know which cloud platform executed a ticket, that's an AgentRun design — open a follow-up.

sections.heading: See also
sections.text: External Agent Orchestration — wrap a spawned Codex/Gemini/Claude Code CLI agent in an AgentRun for ticket-scoped provenance. CI Integration (Agent Runs) — gate a CI build on a persona review's outcome. MCP Server — full MCP tool catalogue, including the 14 persona + ticket tools. MCP integration — preferred path for local tools (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, ...). CLI reference — sfs persona, sfs ticket, sfs project entries — the same operations from a terminal.

Sync a project's wiki pages and context document to Confluence Cloud as real, polished pages. The link is one way: SessionFS creates or updates the Confluence page from the SessionFS source and reads the page's version back for drift detection. Changes made in Confluence never come back. The wiki page and context document stay the source of truth. Available on the Enterprise plan, from the dashboard, the CLI and the API. Added in v0.26.0.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: A member of a project's organization who can edit the project can: Preview a Confluence page built from a wiki page or the project context, without sending anything to Confluence. Publish it. The first publish creates the page; later publishes update its content. Markdown is converted through a strict allowlist to Confluence storage format — never raw markup. Opt into the scheduled sweep, which batch-pushes opted-in wiki pages and, when the mapping allows it, the context tree on a schedule without a model call. A wiki page opts in with its Publish switch, which changes only that flag. Resolve drift (project admins). If Confluence was edited since the last push, the link is marked drifted and must be overwritten or unlinked before publishing again. Each source links to at most one Confluence page, so publishing again updates the same page instead of creating a duplicate. Publishing is safe to retry: Each page gets a sessionfs-… label right after it is created. If a publish times out or its answer is lost once the page may exist, the link is kept as *unconfirmed* (never dropped), and the next publish adopts the page by its id, its label (CQL label = "…"), or its exact title before creating anything. A page is only adopted if it is in the mapped space, was created by the connection's account, is not older than the publish that went missing, and is not already linked to another SessionFS source (409 confluence_title_conflict). If Confluence refuses a create outright (for example a page with that title already exists), nothing is adopted: the publish returns 409 confluence_create_refused and the next publish simply tries to create again. Two wiki pages of one project with the same title get distinct Confluence titles (Title (slug)). Two publishes of the same source at once can't both run: the second gets 409 publish_in_progress, never a false drift. One publish shares a single 60-second deadline across all its Confluence calls. A body over the 1 MiB cap is refused before anything is sent.

sections.heading: Setup
sections.text: Connect the org (org owners and admins): on the Organization page's Integrations tab, choose Connect on the Confluence row, or: sfs org confluence connect \ --site-url https://acme.atlassian.net \ --email docs@acme.com \ --template reference The credentials are checked against Confluence first (the current-user endpoint). You'll be prompted for an Atlassian API token, which is encrypted at rest and never returned. Map projects to a Confluence space and parent page under Manage → Mappings, or with PUT /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/integrations/confluence/mappings/{project_id}. A mapping sets the space key, a parent page (which must be in that space and a real child page, never the space's home page), an optional template override, and two opt-ins: publish the context document (this also shows the context tab's publish button), and include opted-in wiki pages in the scheduled sweep. Both pickers in the Add mapping dialog are searchable against the real Confluence site. Publish pages. On a wiki page or the context tab, Publish to Confluence opens a preview. From the CLI: sfs project confluence publish my-page --preview sfs project confluence publish my-page sfs project confluence publish --context The Confluence row on the Integrations tab shows a one-line summary of any problems. Manage opens Overview (health first: unmapped projects, drifted links, unconfirmed publishes and push failures from the last 24 hours, with in-progress publishes listed for information), Connection (a read-only summary; Edit connection opens the form) and Mappings (sfs org confluence status).

sections.heading: Templates
sections.text: Five built-in templates: Reference (reference), Architecture (architecture), Runbook (runbook), Onboarding (onboarding), and Concept (concept). The org picks a default when connecting, and a project mapping can override it. Each template is a list of sections: Copied word for word from the source: claims by type, session evidence, and backlinks. These never come from a model. Reworded sections are built from the source fields (page body, context sections, claims, evidence, compile metadata) and, when the org or user has an LLM key, reshaped by that model. Every reworded paragraph has to cite a real source field, or it is dropped; a section with nothing left falls back to the plain draft. With no LLM key, every section uses the plain draft. Custom Confluence templates are out of the MVP — only the built-ins exist. Every published page ends with a footer such as Generated by SessionFS · Shaped by 12 active claims (9 current, 2 aging, 1 stale) · last compile <ts> · template Reference. Only active claims count. When the dashboard URL is configured it also links back to the source page. Publishing echoes the template the preview used; if the mapping's or the org's default template changed since, publish is refused with 409 template_changed and you preview again.

sections.heading: Drift, stale links and resolution
sections.text: Before an update SessionFS reads the page's version. If someone edited the page in Confluence since the last publish, the link is marked drifted and publish returns 409 confluence_page_drifted with a short diff of what changed in Confluence. A project admin then chooses Overwrite (the next publish replaces the Confluence edit) or Stop syncing (unlink; the next publish creates a fresh page) in the publish dialog or through the resolve endpoint. Unlink and resolve wait while a publish is in progress. Resolve and unlink are shown to project admins only. A link belongs to the organization and Confluence site it was created on. If the connection moves to another site, or the link came from another organization, the link is *stale*: publish and resolve refuse with 409 confluence_link_stale and touch nothing; the publish dialog shows the stale link so an admin can unlink it. Transferring or merging a project removes its Confluence mapping and page links. If a linked page was deleted in Confluence, the next publish removes the link and returns 409 confluence_page_missing; publishing again by hand creates a fresh page, while the scheduled sweep leaves it alone so automation never resurrects a deleted page. Confluence answers the same way when the page still exists but the connection's account lost permission to see it; restore the permission and unlink and republish. Moving a mapping to another space forgets the links to pages in the old space (they stay in Confluence, and the move is audited) so the next publish and the sweep create them in the new one; the move waits while a publish is in progress. Saving a mapping makes you the admin the sweep publishes as. Drift is detected when you publish; webhook-driven drift and pulling Confluence edits back into SessionFS are planned for later.

sections.heading: Scheduled sweep
sections.text: Operators run POST /api/v1/admin/sweeps/confluence-publish (platform admin, or a platform_sweeps:run service key; optional {"limit": N}, default 100). Each run: rotates through opted-in mappings, least recently attempted first, stamping each one before working it, so a failing or very large mapping can't starve the others; at most 20 publishes per mapping per run, with pages that failed last time tried after the healthy ones; skips a mapping when the org no longer has the Confluence feature or the mapping's creator is no longer an org owner or admin — every publish is attributed to that creator; publishes the context tree (the context page, with one child page per section) when the mapping publishes context, and wiki pages switched to Publish when it auto-publishes pages; skips anything unchanged since its last publish, or changed within the connection's batch window, so several compiles become one publish. Drifted, unlinked and stale pages are left alone. Running the sweep again with nothing changed does nothing and calls Confluence zero times.

sections.heading: Security
sections.text: The Atlassian API token is encrypted at rest and never returned or logged. Site URLs must be https://<name>.atlassian.net. Redirects aren't followed, requests time out after 20 seconds, and responses are capped. Raw HTML and markup are escaped, not injected; links are limited to http(s) and mailto:. Source text is redacted for secrets before any of it reaches a model, even when the org has no DLP policy, and the final page is redacted again with the org's DLP policy before it is sent (the preview shows the redacted text). Org routes check membership and the org's plan; project routes check the project's org, require org membership and edit standing on the project, and reuse the existing knowledge:read / knowledge:write scopes. Service keys can list links but not publish, unlink or resolve.

sections.heading: API
sections.text: | Method | Path | Purpose | | GET / PUT / DELETE | /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/integrations/confluence | Read, save or remove the connection | | POST | /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/integrations/confluence/test | Validate credentials without saving | | GET | /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/integrations/confluence/spaces[/{key}/pages] | List/search spaces and pages | | GET | /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/integrations/confluence/templates | List the built-in templates | | GET / PUT / DELETE | /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/integrations/confluence/mappings[/{project_id}] | Read, save or remove mappings | | GET | /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/integrations/confluence/health | Unmapped projects, failures, drifted links | | POST | /api/v1/projects/{pid}/confluence/preview | Draft a page | | POST | /api/v1/projects/{pid}/confluence/publish | Create or update the page | | GET | /api/v1/projects/{pid}/confluence/links | List the project's page links | | DELETE | /api/v1/projects/{pid}/confluence/links/{link_id} | Unlink (project admin) | | POST | /api/v1/projects/{pid}/confluence/links/{link_id}/resolve | Resolve drift: overwrite or unlink | | PATCH | /api/v1/projects/{pid}/pages/{slug} | Set a wiki page's publish opt-in (flag only) |

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Confluence Cloud is the only documentation provider so far. Failures are reported when you publish; there is no background retry. A failed update of a linked page is listed in the health view until the next successful publish.

External Agent Orchestration You point a coordination layer — a Python script, an n8n flow, a GitHub Action, or even a human-in-the-loop Claude Code session — at an external CLI agent (Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Claude Code) and tell it to do ticket work. The agent edits files, runs tests, and reports back. Without provenance, that run is invisible: nothing ties the external agent's session to the persona it acted as, the ticket it worked, or the outcome it produced. An AgentRun closes that gap. Wrap the spawn in create_agent_run → run the agent → complete_agent_run, and SessionFS records who ran (persona), what they worked (ticket), the result (status + severity + findings), and — when the orchestrator uses a service key — which key minted and completed the run.

sections.heading: Where this fits
sections.text: SessionFS has three agent-integration shapes. Pick by who starts the run: | Pattern | Who starts the run | Doc | | Orchestrator-initiated (this page) | A coordination layer spawns a local/external CLI agent and wraps it | here | | Agent-initiated (cloud) | The cloud agent itself calls the REST control plane | Cloud Agents | | CI gating | A CI job runs a review script and gates the build on the outcome | CI Integration | All three write to the same AgentRun record — the field table, status lifecycle (queued → running → passed / failed / errored / cancelled), and policy semantics are documented in CI Integration. This page is about the orchestrator-spawning flow specifically. SessionFS does not spawn the model. create_agent_run records that a run exists and enforces a fail_on policy at completion; your orchestrator executes the actual agent (codex exec, gemini, claude, …). AgentRun records the *outcome*, not the model transcript.

sections.heading: The reference flow
sections.text: Three steps. Use MCP tools if your orchestrator speaks MCP, the sfs agent CLI if it shells out, or REST if it's a script or webhook — all three hit the same API. Create + start the run. Returns the run id and the compiled persona + ticket context. Spawn the external agent, feeding it that compiled context as its system prompt. Complete the run with status, severity, and structured findings.

sections.heading: Via MCP
sections.text: create_agent_run(persona_name="implementer", ticket_id="tk_xxx", tool="codex-cli", trigger_source="manual", fail_on="high", start_now=true) → returns the run + compiled_context (persona + ticket, as markdown) # ... orchestrator runs the external agent against compiled_context ... complete_agent_run(run_id="run_xxx", status="passed", severity="low", findings=[{...}], session_id="<captured .sfs session, if any>") start_now=true chains create + start in one call. Omit it to create a queued run and start it later (start_agent_run, or POST .../start).

sections.heading: Via the sfs CLI
sections.text: RUN=$(sfs agent run implementer \ --ticket tk_xxx \ --tool codex-cli \ --trigger-source manual \ --fail-on high \ --context-file .sessionfs/context.md \ --output-id) # ... spawn the agent against .sessionfs/context.md ... sfs agent complete "$RUN" \ --summary "Implementer completed tk_xxx via Codex CLI." \ --severity low \ --findings-file .sessionfs/findings.json \ --session-id "<captured session id, if any>"

sections.heading: Worked example — Codex CLI as an implementer on a ticket
sections.text: This shows a common shape: an orchestrator spins up Codex CLI to act as the implementer persona on a ticket — but with the AgentRun wiring that ties the run to the persona, the ticket, and the result. import json import subprocess from sessionfs_client import create_agent_run, complete_agent_run # your wrapper REPO = "/path/to/repo" TICKET = "tk_xxx" # 1. Create + start the run. The start response carries the compiled # persona + ticket context (acceptance criteria, dependencies, # recent comments) as markdown. run = create_agent_run( persona_name="implementer", # lowercase — persona names are case-insensitive-unique ticket_id=TICKET, tool="codex-cli", # token-budget hint; also recorded for audit trigger_source="manual", # manual / ci / webhook / scheduled / mcp / api fail_on="high", # policy: non-zero exit if a >=high finding lands start_now=True, ) run_id = run["run"]["id"] context_md = run["compiled_context"] # 2. Spawn Codex CLI with the compiled context as the system prompt. # Codex's runtime is .git-readonly (see "Sandbox limitation" below), # so we ask it to PRINT a unified diff rather than commit. prompt = ( f"{context_md}\n\n" "Implement this ticket. Run the tests. When done, print a unified " "diff of your changes and a JSON findings array to stdout." ) proc = subprocess.run( ["codex", "exec", "--cd", REPO, prompt], capture_output=True, text=True, ) # 3. The orchestrator owns the commit (the sandboxed agent can't). # Parse the agent's diff/findings, apply + commit, then complete. findings = parse_findings(proc.stdout) # your parser → list[dict] severity = worst_severity(findings) # none/low/medium/high/critical commit_sha = apply_and_commit(proc.stdout, REPO) # orchestrator commits complete_agent_run( run_id=run_id, status="passed" if proc.returncode == 0 else "failed", severity=severity, findings=findings, result_summary=f"Implementer completed {TICKET} via Codex CLI; commit {commit_sha}.", # session_id="<id of the captured .sfs session, if the daemon watches Codex>", ) Notes that keep this accurate: status at completion is passed / failed / errored — not succeeded. The orchestrator sets it from the agent's exit; the server may flip passed → failed if severity trips fail_on. Use errored when the agent itself crashed (so the run reaches a terminal state instead of hanging in running). exit_code is server-derived, not submitted. SessionFS computes it (0 pass / 1 fail) from fail_on + severity and exposes it on the response. complete_agent_run takes no exit_code argument. There's no commit field on AgentRun. Tie the resulting commit into result_summary or a finding; record changed files on the *ticket* via complete_ticket(changed_files=[...]). session_id links provenance. If your daemon captures the Codex/Gemini/Claude session as a .sfs file, pass its id to complete_agent_run so the run points at the transcript.

sections.heading: Sandbox limitation: who commits
sections.text: Codex CLI runs with the working tree writable but .git read-only — the agent can edit files but cannot create commits. Two operational patterns: Agent prints, orchestrator commits (recommended). Instruct the agent to print a unified diff to stdout; the orchestrator applies it (git apply) and commits on the agent's behalf with your bot author. This keeps commit authorship and signing under the orchestrator's control and is what the example above does. Orchestrator commits the dirty tree. Let the agent edit in place, then git add -A && git commit from the orchestrator after the run, reading changed paths from git status --porcelain. Either way, the orchestrator owns the commit — never assume the spawned agent left a commit behind. Gemini CLI and Claude Code have their own sandbox postures; treat "the agent may be unable to commit" as the default and have the orchestrator handle it.

sections.heading: Authentication — scoped service key
sections.text: An orchestrator that polls tickets and writes runs needs both ticket and agent-run scopes. Mint a service key (v0.10.10+) restricted to exactly that: curl -X POST "$SESSIONFS_API_URL/api/v1/orgs/$ORG_ID/service-keys" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "name": "codex-orchestrator", "scopes": ["tickets:read", "tickets:write", "agent_runs:read", "agent_runs:write"], "expires_at": "2026-12-31T23:59:59Z", "project_ids": ["proj_abc"] }' tickets:read / tickets:write went live in v0.10.18, so a Codex/Gemini orchestrator can now poll a ticket, start work, post comments, and complete it — all with a scoped key, no personal bearer token. The raw key is returned exactly once; store it in your secret manager. The same flow over plain REST: # create + start RUN=$(curl -s -X POST "$SESSIONFS_API_URL/api/v1/projects/$PROJECT_ID/agent-runs" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $SERVICE_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"persona_name":"implementer","ticket_id":"tk_xxx","tool":"codex-cli","trigger_source":"manual","fail_on":"high"}' \ | jq -r .id) curl -s -X POST "$SESSIONFS_API_URL/api/v1/projects/$PROJECT_ID/agent-runs/$RUN/start" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $SERVICE_KEY" # ... run the agent ... # complete curl -s -X POST "$SESSIONFS_API_URL/api/v1/projects/$PROJECT_ID/agent-runs/$RUN/complete" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $SERVICE_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"status":"passed","severity":"low","findings":[],"result_summary":"…"}' Service-key runs record actor_type="service_key", service_key_id, and service_key_name on the AgentRun, so an auditor can tell an orchestrated external run from a human one without DB access. See the Cloud Agents auth section for the full service-key model, scope catalogue, and structured error codes.

sections.heading: What this does NOT do
sections.text: It does not spawn the agent. Your orchestrator runs codex exec / gemini / claude; SessionFS records the run. It does not capture the transcript by itself. AgentRun stores the outcome. If you want the agent's .sfs session, run the daemon against that tool and pass the captured session_id to complete_agent_run. It does not commit for you. The orchestrator owns the commit (see Sandbox limitation). It adds no new endpoints. Everything here is the v0.10.2 AgentRun API + v0.10.10 service keys + v0.10.18 ticket scopes.

sections.heading: See also
sections.text: CI Integration (Agent Runs) — the AgentRun field table, lifecycle, policy evaluation, and crash-safety patterns. Cloud Agent Control Plane — agent-initiated cloud agents (Bedrock, Vertex) + the full service-key model. MCP Server — create_agent_run, complete_agent_run, list_agent_runs in the tool catalogue. CLI reference — the sfs agent group.

Promote a SessionFS ticket to a Jira Cloud issue. Promotion itself is one way: SessionFS creates or updates the Jira issue from the ticket and reads its status on demand, never touching status or assignee. Since v0.28.0 a publish can also place the issue in a sprint you pick, set its parent from the ticket's parent, and carry the ticket's due date and estimate. With two-way sync enabled (see below), a linked ticket can also mirror changes in both directions: status transitions, field edits and comments can flow back into SessionFS through a signed inbound webhook, and SessionFS status changes, opted-in comments and completion evidence can be pushed to Jira. The ticket stays the source of truth — inbound transitions go through the same ticket FSM as any other status change and are never forced past a legal step. Available on the Enterprise plan, from the dashboard, the CLI and the API. Added in v0.23.0.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Anyone who can write to a ticket can: Preview a Jira story built from the ticket, without sending anything to Jira. The preview is editable. Publish it. The first publish creates the issue; later publishes update its summary and description. Check status: the linked issue key, URL and current Jira status (cached for 60 seconds). Unlink it (project admins). The Jira issue itself is left alone. Anyone who can edit a ticket can also: Link an existing issue instead of creating one (v0.27.0). See Link an existing issue. Update from Jira: replace a linked ticket's title and description with the issue's. A ticket links to at most one Jira issue, so publishing again updates the same issue instead of creating a duplicate. Publishing is safe to retry: each issue carries a sessionfs-<ticket_id> label, and whenever a create's outcome is unknown (Jira didn't answer in time, the connection dropped, or the publish was interrupted) the next publish finds and adopts the issue by that label instead of creating a second one. It also creates into the same Jira project the interrupted publish chose, even if the mapping changed in between. Two publishes of the same ticket at once can't both create an issue, and a description over Jira's 32,000-character limit is refused before anything is sent.

sections.heading: Setup
sections.text: Connect the org (org owners and admins): on the Organization page's Integrations tab, choose Connect on the Jira row, or: sfs org jira connect \ --site-url https://acme.atlassian.net \ --email jira@acme.com \ --template agile The credentials are checked against Jira first. You'll be prompted for an Atlassian API token, which is encrypted at rest and never returned. Map projects to Jira projects under Manage → Mappings, or with PUT /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/integrations/jira/mappings/{project_id}. A mapping sets the Jira project key, issue type (default Story), an optional template override and an optional "done" status name. Both pickers in the Add mapping dialog are searchable; typing part of a Jira project key or name searches the whole Jira site. Promote tickets. On a ticket, Promote to Jira opens the preview; a linked ticket shows its issue key and an Update Jira button. From the CLI: sfs ticket jira preview tk_abc123 --out preview.json sfs ticket jira publish tk_abc123 --from preview.json sfs ticket jira status tk_abc123 sfs ticket jira unlink tk_abc123 --confirm The Integrations tab also shows health (sfs org jira health); see In the dashboard.

sections.heading: Link an existing issue
sections.text: When the work is already tracked in Jira, link the ticket to that issue instead of publishing a new one. On a ticket, Link existing issue takes an issue key such as PAY-142, or call POST /api/v1/projects/{pid}/tickets/{tid}/jira/link with {"issue_key": "PAY-142"}. Linking needs edit rights on the ticket. SessionFS reads the issue to check that it exists, belongs to the Jira project mapped to this project and isn't already linked to another ticket, then records the link. Nothing is sent to Jira. A linked issue that has never been published from SessionFS can differ from the ticket, so you choose which side wins: Overwrite KEY in Jira publishes the ticket over the issue, replacing its summary and description. Publishing such an issue is refused with 409 jira_overwrite_required until you confirm the overwrite: the dashboard asks first, the CLI takes --overwrite-existing, and the API takes "overwrite_existing": true on publish. After that first publish, later publishes update the issue as usual. Update from Jira replaces the ticket's title and description with the issue's summary and description (sfs ticket jira pull, or POST /api/v1/projects/{pid}/tickets/{tid}/jira/pull with {"confirm": true}). An empty Jira summary or description leaves that ticket field unchanged, the pulled text goes through your org's DLP policy, and nothing is pushed back to Jira. Pulling needs a user key and edit rights on the ticket; the change is recorded in the ticket's edit history like any other edit. sfs ticket jira publish tk_abc123 --from preview.json --overwrite-existing sfs ticket jira pull tk_abc123 The session helper can propose the same link and either overwrite for you to confirm.

sections.heading: Sprints, parents and scheduling
sections.text: Added in v0.28.0.

sections.heading: Agile fields
sections.text: Jira Cloud stores sprints and, on older projects, epic links in custom fields whose ids differ from site to site. SessionFS detects both when an org first connects, so most orgs never have to look them up. An org owner or admin can see and change them under Manage → Connection → Agile fields: Detect fields asks the site again and fills in what it finds for you to review and save, or you can enter an id like customfield_10020 by hand. A connection made before v0.28.0 has no agile fields yet: run Detect fields once and save. The same overrides can be set with sprint_field_id and epic_link_field_id on PATCH /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/integrations/jira/sync. The API token isn't needed. A field you leave out keeps its value and an explicit null clears it. A manual override survives re-saving the connection. Reconnecting to a different Jira site resets both fields to what that site reports, since ids from the old site may not exist there. POST /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/jira/fields/detect runs detection again and shows the result without saving it.

sections.heading: Pick a sprint
sections.text: The publish dialog lists the mapped Jira project's active and future sprints, active first, with their dates in your own time zone (GET /api/v1/projects/{pid}/jira/sprints, up to 100). Choose one to place the issue in it: a new issue gets the sprint on create, and an existing issue is moved into it. When the site has no sprint field, or Jira Software isn't enabled, the dialog says so and publishes without a sprint. The API takes sprint_id on publish.

sections.heading: Parent issue
sections.text: When a ticket has a parent (an Issue it rolls up to) and that parent is linked to a Jira issue, publishing sets the Jira parent, falling back to the epic-link field on projects that still use one. If the parent isn't linked to Jira yet, the issue is published without a parent and a warning tells you to publish or link the parent first. A linked ticket shows its Jira sprint and parent next to the issue key.

sections.heading: Due date and estimate
sections.text: A ticket's due date and estimate (see Project Detail) go to Jira as the issue's due date and original estimate. Update from Jira brings them back when Jira has them. With two-way status sync on, a due date changed in Jira updates the ticket too, recorded in its history as a change made by Jira.

sections.heading: Publish warnings
sections.text: A publish never fails because Jira refused an optional field. Jira leaves the field out, the issue is published, and the dialog explains what happened in plain language, for example "The due date wasn't set: the field isn't on this issue type's screen in Jira" or "The issue was published, but Jira didn't move it into the chosen sprint." The API returns the same as warnings codes such as jira_sprint_not_set:move_failed, jira_parent_not_linked or jira_field_not_on_screen:duedate.

sections.heading: In the dashboard
sections.text: Once connected, the Jira row on the Integrations tab shows the site and a one-line health summary that only names problems (for example "1 unmapped project · 1 push failure"). Manage opens the Jira settings in sections: Overview (health first, then sync and mapping status at a glance), Connection, Mappings, Templates, Sync and Activity. Each health problem links to the section that fixes it, and a healthy integration shows a single "All good" line. The Connection section is a read-only summary (site, account, last four characters of the token, verified date, default template). Edit connection opens the form, which always asks for the API token again so it can be re-encrypted.

sections.heading: Two-way sync
sections.text: Two-way sync is off by default. An org owner or admin turns it on under Manage → Sync in the Jira settings, or with PATCH /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/integrations/jira/sync and any of sync_status, sync_comments (off, inbound, outbound or both) and status_map. The PATCH merges: fields you leave out keep their value, and you don't re-enter the API token. The connection PUT merges the same way, so reconnecting or rotating the token never resets sync. Every sync action is recorded in the tracker_sync_events ledger. The health response reports last_inbound_at, last_synced_at, pending_sync_events, failed_sync_events_24h (failed or refused events, in either direction) and webhook_auth_failures_24h. The dashboard lists recent events under Manage → Activity. In the Sync section the status map is a two-column table: each SessionFS status and the Jira transition it pushes (blank means "Not synced"), next to each Jira status category and what it does to the ticket. You can edit and save the map while two-way status sync is off; it applies once sync is on.

sections.heading: Inbound webhook
sections.text: In Jira Cloud, create an admin webhook for the jira:issue_updated and comment_created events, pointing at: POST /api/v1/webhooks/jira/{org_id} The Sync section shows the full URL for your org, with a Copy button. The webhook lives under /api/v1 so the same URL works on the hosted service and on a Helm install, whose dashboard proxy forwards only /api, /mcp and /health. Generate a secret in the Sync section, or with POST /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/integrations/jira/webhook-secret. The secret is returned once. The server stores it encrypted, because it has to recompute each delivery's signature; only its last 4 characters are ever shown again. The dashboard shows it once, with a Copy button. Paste it into Jira's webhook settings. Jira signs each delivery with X-Hub-Signature: sha256=<hex> over the raw body, and SessionFS checks it in constant time. It fails closed: the org has no Jira connection → 404; no secret has been generated → 503; the signature is missing or wrong → 401. Rejected deliveries are counted in a rolling 24-hour window on the connection, and at most one audit row per org per hour records them. The body is read as a stream and refused with 413 once it passes 1 MiB, with or without a Content-Length. A delivery for an issue with no SessionFS link on the connection's site is ignored with 200. If the org's plan no longer includes the Jira integration, the delivery is ignored and an error event is recorded. Idempotency. Jira's X-Atlassian-Webhook-Identifier header is the delivery key, so a retry is answered {"status": "duplicate"}. Without that header the key falls back to Jira's comment or changelog id, prefixed with the event type. That way a comment_created delivery is never mistaken for the jira:issue_updated delivery Jira sends for the same comment. Status. Only an issue_updated delivery whose changelog contains a status change can move a ticket. Every delivery carries the issue's current status, but an edit that doesn't change it never re-applies it. With sync_status on, the new status category is looked up in the status map and the action goes through the same ticket transitions as the ticket routes. Those keep the FSM checks, resolved_at, dependent unblocking and enrichment, and watcher notifications. The org's admin configured the map, so an inbound transition acts on the org's behalf, attributed to "jira". It still can't do anything the FSM forbids: only Tasks in review resolve to done, only Issues in progress close. A refused transition is recorded as an error event and counted in health; it is never forced. Echoes. A delivery is dropped as an echo only when it matches something SessionFS actually pushed. A status change is an echo when SessionFS pushed a transition of the same name, for the same target status, in the last 5 minutes. A comment is an echo when its Jira id was recorded when SessionFS posted it. As a fallback, for a post whose id was never recorded, it is also an echo when it ends with the outbox reference SessionFS adds to every comment it posts, and it comes from the connection's own account (or that account isn't known yet). A reply that quotes or pastes a reference is still mirrored. SessionFS never pushes field edits, so those always apply. The connection's own Atlassian accountId is only a hint: it can rule an echo out (a different user made the change), never in. A dedicated Jira integration account is recommended for the connection, so SessionFS's own changes are easy to tell apart in Jira. A personal account works too: your own transitions, edits and comments in Jira still sync back. Field edits. A change to summary, description or priority posts a system comment on the ticket: Edited in Jira by <name>: <field> changed. It includes at most a 500-character excerpt, which is DLP-redacted *before* it is cut so a secret can't survive truncation. Only the redacted excerpt is stored. Changes to other fields are ignored. Comments. When sync_comments is inbound or both, a comment_created delivery becomes a ticket comment with source=jira, and it is never trusted. The text is DLP-redacted and capped at 10,000 characters. The author is shown as <name> (Jira), with the name DLP-redacted and shortened to fit.

sections.heading: Outbound pushes
sections.text: A status change on a linked ticket queues an outbound push. A queued push becomes a pending row in the sync ledger, written in the same transaction as the ticket change. After the request commits, a background task delivers it, so a Jira call never runs inside the ticket request and a Jira outage never fails it. If the task is lost (for example an instance shutdown), the sweep delivers the row later. Only an actor with edit standing on the project, or a service key within its org and project allowlist, drives Jira. A reader's lifecycle moves on tickets they created stay inside SessionFS. Each Jira call has a 30-second timeout and one retry after a timeout. A failed delivery is retried with exponential backoff (1, 4, 16 and 64 minutes) through next_attempt_at. After 5 attempts the row is marked exhausted. A row is skipped with a reason when it no longer applies: the ticket was unlinked, sync was turned off, the status is unmapped, the row was superseded by a newer status, or the plan lost the integration. Comments go to Jira only when the org's sync_comments is outbound or both: Send to Jira on a comment is honoured for editors. A reader's flag is ignored. When an editor ticks it but the ticket is not linked or outbound comment sync is off, the comment is refused with 409 jira_comment_sync_off and nothing is written. A trusted reviewer's verdict is forwarded only when it is VERIFIED-CLEAN, as read by the review-state parser. CHANGES-REQUESTED and plain comments are never forwarded. Outbound comments carry a "via SessionFS —" prefix, are DLP-redacted and are cut to fit the ADF budget. Every comment SessionFS posts (including completion evidence) ends with a [SessionFS ref tse_…] line naming its outbox row. Before posting, SessionFS looks for that reference among the issue's 20 newest comments. A post that landed before a client timeout, or before a lost commit, is therefore never posted twice. If the lookup itself fails, SessionFS posts anyway rather than fail the delivery. Transitions are idempotent in the same way. The target status comes from the transition itself, because Jira reports which status each transition leads to. That works even when the names differ, such as "Resolve" leading to "Resolved". SessionFS records the target before posting. If Jira no longer offers the transition, or a request timed out, SessionFS re-reads the issue. When the issue is already at the target status, the push counts as delivered instead of failing with "no transition named …".

sections.heading: Sweep
sections.text: POST /api/v1/admin/sweeps/jira-sync needs a platform-admin user key or a platform_sweeps:run service key. It does two things: It delivers due rows: pending, fewer than 5 attempts, next_attempt_at reached. Terminal rows never block new failures. It deletes finished ledger rows older than 90 days. Each row is claimed, delivered and committed on its own, and an exception on one row is recorded on that row. Run it every few minutes. The optional body {"limit": 1-1000, "budget_seconds": 1-120} bounds a run (defaults 100 and 50).

sections.heading: Status map
sections.text: status_map maps both directions: transitions: SessionFS status → Jira transition name (outbound). The keys are open, in_progress, blocked, review, done, cancelled and closed. categories: Jira status category (new, indeterminate, done) → SessionFS action (inbound): resolve, start, reopen or none. "none", an empty string or null means "not synced". The defaults cover only what a stock Jira workflow has. Outbound, open → "To Do", in_progress → "In Progress", and done and closed → "Done"; blocked, review and cancelled are not synced. Inbound, only Done acts (resolve). Moving an issue back to To Do or In Progress in Jira never rewinds SessionFS unless you map it. Unknown statuses, categories or actions are rejected with 422. A transition your Jira workflow doesn't offer is recorded as a failed event.

sections.heading: Completion evidence
sections.text: When a linked ticket reaches its completed status (done for a Task, closed for an Issue) with status sync on, SessionFS posts one evidence comment to the Jira issue. It contains: the latest agent-run verdict, the persona and a trusted-reviewer badge; per-file line counts from the sessions the ticket links (its resolver session and related sessions, in the ticket's own project and not deleted), capped at 20 files; the knowledge claims the ticket records (count plus up to 5 titles; live claims of the ticket's project only); links to the ticket and sessions when SFS_DASHBOARD_URL is set. The comment is DLP-redacted and fits the ADF budget. It posts once per completion: the evidence row is claimed under a unique key on the link and the completion time before anything is sent. Concurrent jobs can't double-post, and reopening and re-resolving a ticket posts new evidence. Evidence is its own outbox row, so a failure building it can't undo the status push. The failure is recorded and retried.

sections.heading: Templates
sections.text: Five built-in templates: Agile (agile), Compliance (compliance), SRE (sre), Bug report (bug) and Design/UX (design). The org picks a default when connecting, and a project mapping can override it. Each template is a list of sections: Copied word for word from the ticket: acceptance criteria, completion notes and linked sessions. These never come from a model. Reworded sections are built from the ticket's fields and, when the org or user has an LLM key, reshaped by that model. Reworded sections can carry a guidance string that is passed to the model alongside the source fields. Org admins can also create custom templates (up to 50 active per org) under Manage → Templates, each with a unique slug and up to 12 sections. Copied-word-for-word sections can use acceptance criteria, completion notes or linked sessions; reworded sections can use any field (title, description, acceptance_criteria, priority, kind, persona, completion_notes, linked_sessions). Reworded sections can carry guidance: a hint to the model about tone or emphasis, not a source. It can't add content, because every reworded paragraph still has to cite the ticket. The editor previews a draft against a real ticket from a mapped project before you save, in a side pane next to the sections. Since v0.28.0 every mode and source field has a tooltip explaining it, Copy from… starts a new template from a built-in or an existing custom one, and the project picker for the preview is searchable. Editing a custom template creates a new version; if another admin saved in the meantime you're asked to reload instead of overwriting their change. Archiving stops a template being picked as a new choice, but mappings, the org default and published tickets already using it keep working, and the health panel lists them. You can unarchive it later. Archived templates keep their slug reserved, so a new template can't reuse it. The template for a ticket comes from the choice in the promotion dialog, then the project mapping, then the connection default. The dialog starts on the template the ticket was last published with. A published ticket keeps that template even after it is archived; other tickets can't pick it. Publishing uses exactly the template version you previewed: if the template changed in between, you're asked to preview again. Each published link records the slug and version it used. Every published story ends with a footer such as Generated by SessionFS · template: Design Lite v3. When the dashboard URL is configured it also links back to the source ticket. Every reworded paragraph has to cite a real part of the ticket (a description line range, an acceptance-criteria entry, or a field such as title or priority). A paragraph whose citation doesn't resolve is dropped, and a section with nothing left falls back to the plain draft. With no LLM key, every section uses the plain draft.

sections.heading: Security
sections.text: The Atlassian API token is encrypted at rest and never returned or logged. Site URLs must be https://<name>.atlassian.net. Redirects aren't followed, requests time out after 20 seconds, and responses are capped at 2 MiB. Ticket text is redacted for secrets before any of it reaches a model, even when the org has no DLP policy. Org routes check membership and the org's plan; ticket routes check the project's org and use the existing tickets:read / tickets:write scopes. If the org reconnects to a different Jira site, existing links are reported as stale (409 jira_link_stale) and must be unlinked before publishing again.

sections.heading: API
sections.text: | Method | Path | Purpose | | GET / PUT / DELETE | /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/integrations/jira | Read, save or remove the connection | | GET | /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/integrations/jira/projects | Jira projects (?q= to search, ?limit= up to 100) | | GET / PUT / DELETE | /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/integrations/jira/mappings[/{project_id}] | Read, save or remove mappings | | GET | /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/integrations/jira/health | Unmapped projects, failures, stale links | | PATCH | /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/integrations/jira/sync | Change two-way sync settings and the sprint/epic-link field overrides (merge; no token needed) | | POST | /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/integrations/jira/webhook-secret | Generate/rotate the inbound webhook secret (returned once; stored encrypted, only the last 4 characters are shown again) | | GET | /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/integrations/jira/sync-events | Recent two-way sync events (admin). ?direction=inbound\|outbound, ?limit= up to 200 | | POST | /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/jira/fields/detect | Detect the site's sprint and epic-link field ids without saving them (v0.28.0) | | GET | /api/v1/projects/{pid}/jira/sprints | Active and future sprints of the mapped Jira project (v0.28.0) | | POST | /api/v1/projects/{pid}/tickets/{tid}/jira/preview | Draft the story | | POST | /api/v1/projects/{pid}/tickets/{tid}/jira/publish | Create or update the issue (optional sprint_id; response warnings) | | GET | /api/v1/projects/{pid}/tickets/{tid}/jira | Linked issue and cached status | | DELETE | /api/v1/projects/{pid}/tickets/{tid}/jira | Unlink (project admin) | | POST | /api/v1/projects/{pid}/tickets/{tid}/jira/link | Link the ticket to an existing Jira issue (issue_key; v0.27.0) | | POST | /api/v1/projects/{pid}/tickets/{tid}/jira/pull | Overwrite the ticket's title and description from the linked issue (confirm: true; user keys only; v0.27.0) | | POST | /api/v1/webhooks/jira/{org_id} | Jira Cloud inbound webhook (HMAC-signed) for two-way sync | | POST | /api/v1/admin/sweeps/jira-sync | Deliver due outbound sync events and expire old ones (platform_sweeps:run) | | GET | /api/v1/projects/{pid}/tickets/{tid}/jira-sync-events | Sync events for a linked ticket | GET /api/v1/projects/{pid}/tickets/{tid} and the get_ticket MCP tool include a jira object when the ticket has been promoted.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Jira Cloud is the only tracker so far. Promotion failures are reported when you publish; there is no retry for a failed publish/update of a linked issue — it is listed in the health view until the next successful publish. Two-way outbound sync, by contrast, is queued durably and retried by the admin sweep (up to 5 attempts with exponential backoff). Two-way sync is a SessionFS-side mirror, not a Jira plugin: status changes made in Jira arrive via webhook, so a Jira outage or misconfigured secret means inbound events are missed rather than queued for later replay. Events older than 90 days are expired from the sync ledger.
The LLM Judge cross-references every AI claim against actual tool outputs. When the AI says "the test passes" but the exit code was 1, that's a critical contradiction flagged with full evidence.

sections.heading: Quick start
sections.text: sfs audit ses_abc --model gpt-4o

sections.heading: Severity classification
sections.text: Findings are auto-classified by category: | Severity | Categories | Example | | CRITICAL | test_result, command_output, dependency | "Test passes" but exit code 1 | | HIGH | file_existence, data_misread, code_claim | "Created file" but no Write call | | LOW | other | Ambiguous claims |

sections.heading: Custom LLM endpoint
sections.text: Works with any OpenAI-compatible endpoint: # LiteLLM sfs audit ses_abc --base-url https://litellm.internal/v1 --model gpt-4o # Ollama (no API key needed) sfs audit ses_abc --base-url http://localhost:11434/v1 --model llama3 # vLLM sfs audit ses_abc --base-url http://gpu-server:8000/v1 --model my-model

sections.heading: Test connection and Base URL
sections.text: Settings → Data protection → Security review model has a Test connection button. It sends one tiny chat request ("ping", a few output tokens) with the values in the form, through the same code path audits and the session helper use, and shows the endpoint, model and latency, or a readable reason it failed. If the key field is empty, the saved key is used, but only for the exact provider and Base URL it was saved with; testing a different provider or address asks you to enter the key. Leave Base URL empty for a listed provider: requests then go to that provider's own API (the field's placeholder shows it). Set it only for LiteLLM, vLLM, Ollama, or another OpenAI-compatible gateway. A Base URL must be the API address, not the provider's website or console: | Wrong (console / website) | Right | | https://platform.deepseek.com | https://api.deepseek.com (or leave empty) | | https://platform.openai.com | https://api.openai.com/v1 (or leave empty) | | https://openrouter.ai/settings/keys | https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 (or leave empty) | | https://console.anthropic.com, https://aistudio.google.com | leave empty | Saving a new Base URL (or a new key with one) runs the same test first. A rejected key (401) or a blocked address is refused with a message on the field, and so is a new Base URL that clearly isn't a chat API (it answers 405, returns a web page, or is a provider's console). Anything else still saves and shows a warning: a timeout, rate limit, provider outage (including a proxy's 502/503 page), or a plain 404. Changing only the key on an unchanged Base URL is never blocked by an endpoint failure. Failure reasons: endpoint_not_api, invalid_key, access_denied (a 403 about region or model permissions; it never blocks a save), model_not_found, rate_limited, insufficient_balance, endpoint_blocked, timeout, unreachable, provider_error.

sections.heading: Auto-audit
sections.text: Configure automatic auditing in the dashboard Settings or via CLI: sfs config set audit.trigger on_sync # Audit after every push sfs config set audit.trigger on_pr # Audit when PR/MR is opened sfs config set audit.trigger manual # Only when you run sfs audit

sections.heading: Consensus mode
sections.text: Run 3 passes and only report findings where 2+ agree: sfs audit ses_abc --consensus # 3x cost, higher confidence

sections.heading: Export
sections.text: sfs audit ses_abc --format json # JSON sfs audit ses_abc --format markdown # Markdown report sfs audit ses_abc --format csv # CSV table

Every AI coding session generates insights — architecture decisions, bug workarounds, dependency quirks — that get lost when the session ends. The Living Knowledge Base captures these into structured entries, compiles them into a project wiki, and feeds them back into future sessions.

sections.heading: The Knowledge Loop
sections.text: Sessions → Extract (evidence) → Promote (claim) → Compile → Wiki → Agents read & write back AI agents discover facts during coding sessions Facts are saved as knowledge entries (via MCP tools or CLI) Each entry is classified as evidence (raw, from sync), claim (promoted active truth), or note (rejected/dismissed) Compilation auto-promotes qualifying evidence to claim, merges active claims into the project context document Section pages and concept articles are auto-generated from active claims only Future agents read the wiki via get_project_context and contribute back The loop is self-reinforcing: the more sessions you run, the richer the knowledge base becomes.

sections.heading: The Claim Model (v0.9.8.6+)
sections.text: Every knowledge entry has a claim_class that controls its lifecycle: | Class | Meaning | When | | evidence | Raw fact extracted from a session or submitted by an agent that didn't meet promotion gates | Default for sync-extracted entries and agent add_knowledge calls | | claim | Promoted active truth | Evidence auto-promoted at compile (confidence ≥ 0.5, content ≥ 30 chars), or agent entries that pass specificity + dedup + rate-limit gates | | note | Rejected or dismissed — audit-visible but excluded from compile | Manual dismiss, or agent submissions that failed all gates | Freshness decay. Each type has its own decay window applied from last_relevant_at: | Type | Window before stale | | bug | 30 days | | dependency | 60 days | | pattern, discovery | 90 days | | convention | 180 days | | decision | 365 days | Past the window, freshness_class moves current → stale → archived. Stale entries are surfaced in the dashboard review queue; only current active claims feed compile by default. Confidence decay. Claims nobody has referenced for 90 days lose confidence (×0.8), at most once every 30 days. Since v0.23.0 this depends on elapsed time only; before, it was applied on every compile, so frequently compiled projects aged their claims much faster. Supersession. Retire an old claim in favor of a new one with PUT /api/v1/projects/{id}/entries/{entry_id}/supersede. The old entry remains readable for audit but is excluded from compile. Refresh. Extend an entry's validity window with PUT /api/v1/projects/{id}/entries/{entry_id}/refresh — updates last_relevant_at and resets freshness_class to current. Rebuild. POST /api/v1/projects/{id}/rebuild (or sfs project rebuild) resets compiled_at=NULL on all active claims and clears context_document, forcing a full re-compile on settled projects.

sections.heading: Getting Started
sections.text: # Initialize a project (auto-detects git remote) sfs project init # Add initial context in your editor sfs project edit # Enable auto-narrative (generates summaries on sync) sfs project set --auto-narrative # Run your first compilation sfs project compile After init, the project is linked to your git remote. Every team member with access sees the same knowledge base.

sections.heading: Knowledge Entries
sections.text: Each entry has a type, content, confidence score (0.0-1.0), and an optional link to the session that created it.

sections.heading: Entry Types
sections.text: | Type | Use For | Example | | decision | Architecture and design choices | "WebSockets rejected in favor of HTTP + ETags" | | pattern | Code patterns and conventions | "All converters follow parse → canonical → write" | | bug | Known issues and workarounds | "SQLite WAL mode can corrupt on power loss" | | convention | Coding standards | "All API routes use async handlers" | | dependency | External library notes | "react-markdown renders project context, not a custom parser" | | discovery | General findings | "The auth middleware resolves tier from org, not user" |

sections.heading: Entry Lifecycle
sections.text: Entries start as pending. After compilation, they become compiled. Irrelevant entries can be dismissed: # List all entries sfs project entries # Filter by type or status sfs project entries --type decision sfs project entries --pending # Dismiss a noisy entry sfs project dismiss 42 Entries with confidence below 0.5 are marked as *(unverified)* in the compiled output.

sections.heading: Compilation
sections.text: Compilation merges pending entries into the project context document and generates section wiki pages. Pending claims sit in the queue until a compile runs, either on the project's schedule or by hand. Scheduled compile (v0.23.0). Each project can compile on a schedule: nightly, weekly or off, optionally also once a number of claims are waiting. Set it under the project's Settings → Scheduled KB compile or with sfs project compile-schedule weekly --after-claims 20. Scheduled compiles use the deterministic compiler, never an LLM. New projects start at nightly when their plan includes project context; projects created before v0.23.0 start at off. On self-hosted servers the schedule takes effect only once the operator runs the compile sweep. The compile history marks which compiles were manual and which were scheduled. To compile by hand: Dashboard. The project Overview shows when the context was last compiled and how many claims are waiting, with a one-click compile when it is out of date, plus the buttons on the Entries and Context tabs. Agent (MCP). Agents are instructed to check get_knowledge_health after writing knowledge, surface the pending count to the user, and call compile_knowledge_base only on explicit consent. CLI. sfs project compile from your terminal. Concurrent compile callers serialize on a project-row lock — duplicate context documents and duplicate concept pages can't be created by races.

sections.heading: Deterministic Compile (Default)
sections.text: When no LLM API key is provided, compilation uses a rule-based approach: Groups entries by type under structured section headings (## Key Decisions, ## Patterns & Conventions, etc.) Appends new entries to the appropriate section Marks low-confidence entries as unverified Adds a ## Recent Changes section from the current batch

sections.heading: LLM Compile
sections.text: When an LLM API key is available, the compiler sends the current context plus grouped entries to the model. The LLM deduplicates, reorganizes, and produces a cleaner merged document. Falls back to deterministic compile on failure.

sections.heading: What Happens During Compilation
sections.text: Fetches all pending (not dismissed, not yet compiled) entries Groups them by entry type Merges into the existing context document Marks all processed entries as compiled Saves a before/after snapshot in the compilation history Creates or updates section pages in the wiki (one per entry type) Auto-generates concept articles for recurring topics sfs project compile # Compiling pending entries... # Project context updated. 12 entries compiled.

sections.heading: Section Pages
sections.text: Each entry type gets its own wiki page, auto-generated from all non-dismissed entries of that type: | Entry Type | Wiki Page Slug | | decision | key-decisions | | pattern | patterns | | convention | coding-conventions | | bug | known-issues | | dependency | dependencies | | discovery | discoveries |

sections.heading: Wiki Pages
sections.text: The wiki is a collection of markdown pages organized by slug. Pages can be manually written or auto-generated from knowledge entries.

sections.heading: Browsing
sections.text: # List all wiki pages sfs project pages # Slug Title Type Words Entries Auto # key-decisions Key Decisions section 340 18 yes # patterns Patterns section 210 12 yes # architecture Architecture Overview section 890 0 no # Read a specific page sfs project page key-decisions

sections.heading: Concept Auto-Generation
sections.text: After compilation, the system identifies recurring topics across entries and generates concept articles. These are standalone wiki pages that synthesize related entries into a coherent narrative.

sections.heading: Regeneration
sections.text: Auto-generated pages can be regenerated from the latest entries: sfs project regenerate key-decisions # Article regenerated (340 words from 18 entries). Only auto-generated pages support regeneration. Manually written pages are left untouched.

sections.heading: Backlinks
sections.text: Pages track which entries and other pages reference them. View backlinks at the bottom of any page: sfs project page architecture # [content rendered in panel] # # Backlinks: # entry:42 (references) # entry:67 (references)

sections.heading: CLI Commands
sections.text: | Command | Description | | sfs project init | Initialize project context for the current repo | | sfs project compile | Compile pending entries into the context document | | sfs project rebuild | Force a full re-compile (reset compiled_at=NULL + clear context document) | | sfs project entries | List knowledge entries (supports --pending, --type, --limit) | | sfs project ask "question" | Search the knowledge base and show matching entries | | sfs project pages | List all wiki pages | | sfs project page <slug> | View a wiki page with backlinks | | sfs project health | Run health checks — pending count, staleness, score | | sfs project regenerate <slug> | Regenerate an auto-generated concept page | | sfs project set --auto-narrative | Enable auto-narrative summaries on sync | | sfs project dismiss <id> | Dismiss an irrelevant entry | | sfs project edit | Edit the context document in $EDITOR | | sfs project show | Display the current context document |

sections.heading: Health Checks
sections.text: The health command scores your knowledge base and flags issues: sfs project health # Project Health: my-project # # ✓ Context document exists (1200 words, 8 sections) # ✓ 45 knowledge entries (38 compiled, 2 dismissed) # ⚠ 5 entries pending compilation # ✓ Last compiled: 2026-04-01 # ✓ Context appears up to date # # Health Score: 90%

sections.heading: MCP Integration
sections.text: The SessionFS MCP server exposes five knowledge-related tools that AI agents call during sessions.

sections.heading: Write Tools
sections.text: | Tool | Description | | add_knowledge(content, entry_type) | Add a knowledge entry. Optional: session_id, confidence (0.0-1.0) | | update_wiki_page(slug, content) | Create or update a wiki page. Optional: title | | list_wiki_pages() | List all wiki pages with slugs, titles, and word counts |

sections.heading: Read Tools
sections.text: | Tool | Description | | search_project_knowledge(query) | Search entries by content. Optional: entry_type, limit | | ask_project(question) | Research a question across context, entries, and local sessions |

sections.heading: How Agents Contribute
sections.text: When an agent calls get_project_context, the response includes contribution instructions. Agents are expected to call add_knowledge() when they discover something significant: # Example: agent discovers a pattern during a session add_knowledge("All CLI commands use the @handle_errors decorator for consistent error handling", "pattern") The entry is stored as pending until the next compilation cycle.

sections.heading: API Endpoints
sections.text: All endpoints are under /api/v1/projects/{project_id} and require authentication. | Method | Path | Description | | GET | /entries | List entries. Query params: type, pending, search, limit | | GET | /entries/search | Search active claims by default. Pass include_stale=true to include evidence, notes, and superseded entries | | POST | /entries/add | Add a single entry. Body: content, entry_type, confidence, session_id, entity_ref, upsert (default: false), claim_class (default: note). When upsert=true AND entity_ref is set, the write is a state-cache roll-forward: similarity dedup is skipped, the new row commits, and any active prior entry sharing the same entity_ref in this project is auto-dismissed with superseded_by=<new_id> + supersession_reason="entity_ref upsert". Response includes upserted_from: [prior_ids] so callers can audit. upsert=true without entity_ref returns 422. Default upsert=false preserves the existing entity_ref semantic where multiple distinct claims about the same entity coexist (compile-time _auto_supersede reasons about them). Cross-project isolation: the upsert query is scoped by project_id, so writing the same entity_ref from another tenant is invisible. | | PUT | /entries/{entry_id} | Dismiss or un-dismiss an entry | | PUT | /entries/{entry_id}/refresh | Reset last_relevant_at and freshness_class=current. Replaces the old "Still valid" no-op | | PUT | /entries/{entry_id}/supersede | Retire an old claim and link it to a superseding entry. Body: superseded_by_id, reason | | POST | /entries/dismiss-stale | Bulk-dismiss low-confidence stale entries (confidence < 0.5 + > 90 days unreferenced) | | POST | /compile | Compile pending entries. Auto-promotes evidence ≥ 0.5 confidence to claim before merging | | POST | /rebuild | Reset compiled_at=NULL on all active claims and clear context_document to force a full re-compile | | GET | /compilations | List compilation history (each marked manual or scheduled) | | GET | /compile-status | Last compile, claims waiting, and whether a compile is recommended (v0.23.0) | | GET | /health | Health status: entry counts, staleness, word count, score inputs, stale review queue | | GET | /pages | List wiki pages | | GET | /pages/{slug} | Get page content with backlinks | | PUT | /pages/{slug} | Create or update a page. Body: content, title | | DELETE | /pages/{slug} | Delete a wiki page | | POST | /pages/{slug}/regenerate | Regenerate an auto-generated page | | PUT | /settings | Update project settings (e.g., auto_narrative, kb_max_context_words — default 2000) |

sections.heading: Best Practices
sections.text: When to compile. Run sfs project compile after batches of sessions, not after every single entry. A good cadence is weekly or after a feature sprint. The health command tells you when pending entries are piling up. Seed the knowledge base early. Before your first AI session, add a few decision and convention entries manually via the API or MCP tools.
