This gives agents immediate context and sets the tone for the kind of knowledge you want captured. Dismiss noise aggressively. Not every discovery is worth keeping. Dismiss trivial entries (sfs project dismiss <id>) so they don't clutter compiled output. The confidence score helps — entries below 0.5 are flagged as unverified. Use upsert=true + entity_ref for state caches. When an autonomous agent needs durable append-only state (e.g. an LRU map of "signals already classified"), pass upsert=true alongside a stable entity_ref like signal-state:decisions. The server skips the similarity-dedup gate, commits the new entry, and auto-dismisses any prior active row sharing that entity_ref (superseded_by=<new_id>). The response surfaces upserted_from: [prior_ids] so the caller can confirm the roll-forward. Default upsert=false preserves the normal entity_ref semantic — multiple distinct claims about the same entity coexist, and compile-time _auto_supersede reasons about them. Use upsert ONLY for state-cache slots, never for natural KB entries. Use wiki pages for depth. Knowledge entries are single facts. For topics that need explanation — architecture, deployment, onboarding — create wiki pages via update_wiki_page() or the dashboard editor. Monitor health regularly. A healthy project has a score above 80%, no stale context, and fewer than 10 pending entries. Run sfs project health in CI or as a periodic check. Let auto-narrative do its job. With --auto-narrative enabled, session summaries are extracted on sync and stored as entries automatically. This is the lowest-effort way to build the knowledge base — just use your AI tools normally.

The SessionFS MCP server gives AI coding agents access to your session history and project knowledge base during conversations. Agents can search past sessions, read project context, and contribute knowledge back — building a shared memory that persists across tools and teammates. Transports: stdio for local use (agent launches sfs mcp serve as a subprocess). Remote use over HTTP/SSE is not currently supported (see Remote MCP).

sections.heading: Installation
sections.text: Run sfs mcp install --for <tool> to register the MCP server with your AI tool. This registers the server in the tool's MCP configuration and injects knowledge-contribution instructions into the tool's project config file (e.g., CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules). Supported tools: sfs mcp install --for claude-code # ~/.claude.json sfs mcp install --for cursor # ~/.cursor/mcp.json sfs mcp install --for codex # via codex mcp add sfs mcp install --for gemini # via gemini mcp add sfs mcp install --for copilot # ~/.copilot/config.json sfs mcp install --for amp # ~/.amp/config.json sfs mcp install --for cline # VS Code globalStorage sfs mcp install --for roo-code # VS Code globalStorage sfs mcp install --for kilo-code # VS Code globalStorage sfs mcp install --for antigravity # ~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json (+ legacy ~/.gemini/antigravity/mcp_config.json) To skip the instruction injection (server registration only): sfs mcp install --for claude-code --skip-instructions

sections.heading: Tools
sections.text: The MCP server exposes 115 tools in fifteen categories: Session, Knowledge Read, Knowledge Write, Rules, Personas (Pro+), Tickets (Team+), AgentRun (Team+), Agent Feedback (Team+), Review Checklist (Team+), Handoffs (Pro+ for direct, Team+ for team handoffs), Work Queues, Review Loops, Skills Marketplace, Project Groups (Team+), and Meetings. The git_remote parameter. Project-scoped tools take an optional git_remote that picks the project. Pass a remote URL such as github.com/org/repo, or a local folder: a value starting with /, ~, ./ or ../ (or . / ..) is resolved through that repository's origin remote, git worktrees included. A folder that isn't a git repository with an origin returns an error rather than acting on another project. Omit git_remote to use the current workspace.

Filter: claim_class='claim' AND compiled_at IS NULL AND not dismissed AND freshness_class IN ('current', 'aging') AND superseded_by IS NULL. auto_promotable_evidence (v0.10.17+) — evidence rows the compiler's auto-promotion phase will promote AND that survive the post-promotion claim filter. Filter: claim_class='evidence' AND confidence >= 0.5 AND length(content) >= 30 AND not dismissed AND compiled_at IS NULL AND current/aging AND no superseder. uncompiled_notes (v0.10.17+) — notes that need a bulk_promote call before they can compile. compiled_entries, dismissed_entries, total_entries — straightforward counts. stale_entries, low_confidence_entries, potentially_stale — review surfaces. potentially_stale uses the same compile-eligible predicate as pending_entries (notes / superseded claims with novel terms can't trigger a false-positive "Context may be stale" warning). word_count — current compiled context size. recommendations — strings driven by compile_work_total = pending_entries + auto_promotable_evidence. Notes-only fresh projects get "No compile-eligible entries yet — add claims (or promote evidence) before running compile" instead of a "compile to build context" pointer. Returns the assembled markdown plus a typed sources_cited list — [{type: "kb"|"session", id}] — resolved from a structured re-fetch of KB IDs and the local session search index, never regex-extracted from prose. | Parameter | Type | Required | Description | | question | string | yes | A question about the project |

sections.heading: Personas (Pro+)
sections.text: Tier-gated by the agent_personas feature flag. Personas are portable AI roles — each persona has a name (^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,50}$) and markdown content, and belongs to one project or to one organization. Org-level personas are usable from every project in the org. Inside a project, a name resolves to the project's own persona first, then the org's, so a project persona with the same name overrides the org one. get_persona, assign_persona, start_ticket, and agent runs all resolve this way. Names match case-insensitively. Org personas are visible only to current members of the project's current org (and that org's service keys); other callers with project access see project personas only. list_personas List the personas usable in the current project. Each row carries scope (project or org); an org persona overridden by a project persona of the same name is left out. | Parameter | Type | Required | Description | | include_org | boolean | no | Include the org's personas (default true) | | git_remote | string | no | Git remote URL (auto-detected if omitted) | get_persona Return a single persona's full content. | Parameter | Type | Required | Description | | name | string | yes | Persona name | | git_remote | string | no | Git remote URL (auto-detected if omitted) | | audit_session_id | string | no | Current session id to append this retrieval to its audit log | create_persona Define a new persona for the project, or for an organization when org_id is passed. sections.heading: Session checkpoint + fork
sections.text: Local-only tools that operate on ~/.sessionfs. Use these to branch a session for "what-if" exploration or to mark a known-good state before risky changes. Neither tool uploads anything — call sfs push <new_id> afterwards if the fork should sync. checkpoint_session Create a named snapshot of a session's current manifest + messages under ~/.sessionfs/sessions/<id>.sfs/checkpoints/<name>/. Snapshot names must start with alphanumeric and use only [A-Za-z0-9._-] (1–100 chars). Re-using a name returns an error. | Parameter | Type | Required | Description | | session_id | string | yes | Full session id or unique prefix | | name | string | yes | Checkpoint name | list_checkpoints List checkpoints for a session, oldest first. Each entry returns name, created_at, message_count, and the on-disk path. Returns an empty list if there are no checkpoints. | Parameter | Type | Required | Description | | session_id | string | yes | Full session id or unique prefix | fork_session Fork a session (or one of its checkpoints) into a new independent session. The new manifest records parent_session_id and — when from_checkpoint is supplied — forked_from_checkpoint, so lineage is introspectable. | Parameter | Type | Required | Description | | session_id | string | yes | Source session id or unique prefix | | name | string | yes | Title for the forked session | | from_checkpoint | string | no | Fork from this snapshot instead of the live head |

sections.heading: Handoffs
sections.text: Handoffs are first-class coordination primitives. A handoff carries a session blob plus optional provenance (ticket_id + persona_name) and curated attachments (KB entries, wiki pages, ticket refs). On claim, the recipient's CLI persists an active_ticket_payload so the next captured session is automatically tagged with the handed-off context. Three recipient kinds, exactly one per handoff: recipient_email (any user by email), recipient_user_id (direct account match), or recipient_team_id (Team+ tier; any team member can claim with atomic race protection). Non-parties get 404 (not 403) on all handoff routes — existence-hiding so recipients can't distinguish pending vs claimed vs revoked. Pending handoffs past expires_at flip to expired on read; per-tier clamping is 720h (30d) on Free/Pro/Team, 2160h (90d) on Enterprise. create_handoff Create a handoff for a session. Sender provides exactly one recipient field plus optional ticket/persona provenance, expiry, and attachments. | Parameter | Type | Required | Description | | session_id | string | yes | Session being handed off | | recipient_email | string | no | Recipient email (one-of) | | recipient_user_id | string | no | Recipient user id (one-of) | | recipient_team_id | string | no | Recipient team id (one-of, Team+ tier) | | message | string | no | Optional sender note | | ticket_id | string | no | Attach an active ticket for provenance carry-through | | persona_name | string | no | Attach a persona for provenance carry-through | | expires_in_hours | integer | no | Clamped per tier (720h Free/Pro/Team, 2160h Enterprise) | | attachments | array | no | List of {kind: "kb_entry"\|"wiki_page"\|"ticket", ref_id} | claim_handoff Atomic claim. UPDATE Handoff WHERE id=X AND status='pending' runs first; race losers never write blobs. Returns the new session_id, active_ticket_payload (if attached), and dropped_attachments for refs the recipient can't access. | Parameter | Type | Required | Description | | handoff_id | string | yes | Handoff ID | get_handoff Fetch one handoff. Non-parties get 404. First non-sender read stamps viewed_at and emits a viewed event. | Parameter | Type | Required | Description | | handoff_id | string | yes | Handoff ID | list_inbox_handoffs List handoffs addressed to the caller (by email, user_id, or team membership). Optional status filter. | Parameter | Type | Required | Description | | status | string | no | pending, claimed, revoked, declined, expired | | limit | number | no | Page size | list_sent_handoffs List handoffs created by the caller. Optional status filter. | Parameter | Type | Required | Description | | status | string | no | Status filter | | limit | number | no | Page size | revoke_handoff Sender-only. Atomic revoke with a required reason. Emits revoked audit event and sends send_handoff_revoked email to the recipient. | Parameter | Type | Required | Description | | handoff_id | string | yes | Handoff ID | | reason | string | yes | Required revoke reason | decline_handoff Recipient-only. Atomic decline with an optional reason. sections.heading: Ticket comments listing
sections.text: list_ticket_comments Paginated read of the existing GET /api/v1/projects/{id}/tickets/{id}/comments endpoint. Returns markdown body, author, persona, and timestamps so MCP clients don't have to compose ticket-detail responses to inspect a comment thread. | Parameter | Type | Required | Description | | ticket_id | string | yes | Ticket ID | | limit | number | no | Page size (default: 50) | | cursor | string | no | Opaque pagination cursor | get_ticket_review_state A compact summary of a review ticket: open and closed findings, the last verdict, and open-finding counts by severity, derived from the comment thread. Cheaper than reading a long thread with list_ticket_comments. Returns review_state: null for tickets with no review comments. last_verdict_is_strict_verified_clean is true only when the last trusted verdict is a literal VERIFIED-CLEAN. "Last" means most recently posted: round numbers are labels, so a later changes-requested verdict reopens the review even if it carries a lower round number. Verdict headers take any reviewer name, in the form <Reviewer> R<n> review on <ticket>: <VERDICT>; see Worker Review Loop. | Parameter | Type | Required | Description | | ticket_id | string | yes | Ticket ID | check_merge_readiness Whether a ticket's work is safe to merge at a specific head commit. Returns {ready, reasons, verdict}. ready is true only when a trusted strict VERIFIED-CLEAN verdict exists, its reviewed_commit equals sha exactly, the reviewer's identity differs from every implementer identity recorded for the ticket (with no implementer identity recorded, the answer is not ready), and no open finding is harmful. A finding tagged harm: none is harmless; an untagged finding of medium severity or higher counts as harmful. Pure read: a person still does the merge. CLI: sfs loop ready. See Worker Review Loop. | Parameter | Type | Required | Description | | ticket_id | string | yes | Ticket ID | | sha | string | yes | Head commit id (full 40- or 64-character lowercase hex) | | git_remote | string | no | Project selector (see above) |

sections.heading: Work Queues
sections.text: Point an agent at a queue of tickets and wake it repeatedly — via /loop, cron, or CI — to service, review, and close them with SessionFS as the source of truth. The server holds all loop state, so the agent resumes correctly with no chat memory: each wake returns one bounded directive, and a crash between steps re-emits the same directive rather than losing or repeating work. Modes: review_until_clean (auto-finishes an item only on a server-verified, trusted, literal VERIFIED-CLEAN), implement_until_done, and triage. A built-in safety envelope (per-item attempt cap with 2m → 5m → 15m → 60m backoff that parks a stuck item for human reset, a per-wake ticket cap, a cadence floor, and a step rate limit) keeps an unattended loop bounded. These tools require the work_queues:read / work_queues:write scopes; acting on items also requires the relevant tickets / agent_runs write scopes. Available on all tiers. MCP / API only — there is no dashboard UI or CLI for work queues yet. create_work_queue Create a queue over a ticket filter or explicit ticket list, with a mode, a cadence, and per-run / per-item budgets. get_work_queue Return a queue's configuration and progress. list_work_queues List the work queues for a project. set_work_queue_status Pause, resume, or archive a queue. run_work_queue_step Heartbeat: return one bounded directive (a single intent plus a small comment delta) for the agent to act on. Call this on each wake. complete_work_queue_step Report the result of the directive returned by run_work_queue_step. This is the only call that durably advances the queue. In review_until_clean mode the reviewer passes its verdict as verdict_content, and the server writes the trusted verdict comment itself. The first line must be a verdict header such as Claude R2 review on <ticket_id>: VERIFIED-CLEAN, with any reviewer name; a header that can't be parsed is refused with 422 verdict_header_unparseable before anything is written (v0.27.0). The reviewer can also pass reviewed_commit, the full commit id (40 or 64 lowercase hex characters) of the head it read, which is stored with the verdict so check_merge_readiness can require the clean verdict to be on the current head (v0.29.1). In implement_until_done mode the implementer reporting done no longer finishes an item on its own: the item finishes only once a trusted strict VERIFIED-CLEAN verdict comes from an identity other than the implementer's.

Each record points at least one target (agent_run_id, ticket_id, or comment_id) — all of which must belong to the same project — and classifies the signal with a feedback_type × verdict × optional label. sections.heading: Skills Marketplace
sections.text: Marketplace tools separate discovery from authority. Search and preview return metadata or visibly untrusted text. load_marketplace_skill returns instruction text only after an exact-version project approval or organization assignment; it never installs files or activates scripts, hooks, executable extensions, or local MCP processes. Every preview and load response carries untrusted: true plus a fixed untrusted_preamble telling the model the content is third-party data, not instructions from the user. Approval is never brokered over MCP. A project owner/admin approves from the dashboard or API, confirming each elevated capability (scripts, hooks, MCP, assets) explicitly. If the approver is the same principal that filed the request, the server additionally requires a single-use confirmation code emailed to that account (POST .../challenge); requested_via is recorded for display only. This closes the preview → request → approve → load self-approval loop. | Tool | Purpose | | search_skill_marketplace | Search public, personal, and authorized organization listings; optionally filter by target tool, category, publisher, verified publisher, trusted-publishing provenance, license, max scan severity, capability, works-in tool, updated within N days and deprecation, sorted by relevance or recent | | get_marketplace_package | Inspect immutable hash, provenance, license, verification, risk, compatibility, and the install disclosure (files per tool, hooks, scripts, MCP servers, network endpoints, shell commands, hidden characters). Display only | | diff_marketplace_versions | Compare two versions of one package: files, capability changes, and the update class (text, code, or widening). Read-only | | get_skill_policy | The org skills policies that apply to you and, per tool, what the tool enforces, what only SessionFS checks, and what nothing checks. Use it to explain a refusal. Read-only (Enterprise) | | preview_marketplace_skill | Read a bounded, untrusted instruction preview without granting consent | | load_marketplace_skill | Load approved instruction-only context for one project/tool/device boundary | | request_skill_install | Request an exact hash for project, user, or device scope | | get_skill_install_request | Inspect one request | | list_skill_install_requests | List project requests, optionally filtered by status | | cancel_skill_install_request | Cancel a pending request as requester or project admin | Use the Skills Marketplace guide for the four consumption modes and their security boundaries.

sections.heading: Meetings
sections.text: Stored meeting transcripts for a project (git_remote or the workspace) or a project group (group_id, user keys only). With extract=true it also runs one extraction call using your own LLM key (your key, else your org's; never a SessionFS key); without a key the transcript is still stored | | list_meeting_transcripts | Meetings, newest first (q, limit 1–200, before cursor); summaries only | | get_meeting_transcript | One meeting by id: text, participants and extracted items | | extract_meeting_action_items | Extract participants, action items and decisions with your own LLM key. The preview returns the ticket draft; with confirm=true it creates the ticket, using any edited title, description, priority, kind, assigned_to, assigned_user_id, due_date, target_project_id you pass, and marks the item promoted. publish_to_jira=true also publishes it to Jira | | search_meetings | Search meeting titles and transcript text (q, limit) |

sections.heading: Agent Knowledge Contribution
sections.text: When sfs mcp install runs, it injects a MANDATORY instructions block into the tool's project config file (e.g., CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules). These instructions tell the agent it must call add_knowledge() when discovering architecture decisions, code patterns, bugs, dependencies, or conventions — and must not end a session without contributing if it learned something new. This creates a knowledge loop: each session reads project context at the start and writes back discoveries at the end. Tools that support project-level instructions: Claude Code (CLAUDE.md), Codex (codex.md), Gemini (GEMINI.md), Cursor (.cursorrules). For other tools, instructions are served at runtime via get_project_context.

sections.heading: Remote MCP (HTTP/SSE)
sections.text: Remote MCP over HTTP/SSE, for agents that cannot launch local processes (e.g., claude.ai), is not currently supported — neither as a hosted endpoint nor self-hosted. Use the local server above.

sections.heading: Configuration
sections.text: | Variable | Description | | SFS_API_URL | SessionFS cloud API URL (for knowledge tools) | | SFS_API_KEY | API key for cloud authentication | sfs mcp serve Runs the MCP server on stdio transport. Connect from any MCP-compatible client. Rebuild the search index: sfs mcp index Re-indexes all local sessions into the full-text search database. Uninstall: sfs mcp uninstall --for claude-code Removes the MCP server registration and cleans up injected knowledge instructions from the project config file. Supported tools are the same as for install.

Meetings let a project or group capture a meeting transcript and store it server-side. The stored copy is DLP-redacted under the strictest of the caller's org policies, participants can be resolved to org members or personas, transcripts can be extracted into action items and decisions, and those action items can be promoted to tickets. Transcripts age out under an org-level retention window. The meetings feature is available on every tier. Group-scoped meetings additionally require the project_groups feature (Team+), and promoting an action item to a ticket requires agent_tickets (Team+).

sections.heading: Scope
sections.text: Every meeting belongs to exactly one of: a project (project_id), or a group (group_id). That is the meeting's scope. Its owning org is taken from the scope; a personal project has none. Access follows the scope's normal standing: | Action | Project meeting | Group meeting | | List / get | project read (or a service key with meetings:read + project allowlist) | group reader (user key) | | Upload | project edit (or a service key with meetings:write + project allowlist) | group editor or admin | | Delete | uploader or project admin (a service key's backing user must be one of these) | uploader or group admin | | Override participant | project editor | group editor or admin | Group meetings always require a user key. There are no org-wide meetings.

sections.heading: Upload and DLP
sections.text: POST uploads a meeting with a title (1–200 chars), content (the transcript text), an optional meeting_at / duration_minutes, and a source (manual_paste or file_upload). Set extract: true to run action-item extraction in the same request. The request body is streamed with a hard cap of 1 MiB; the normalised content is capped at 512 KiB and 10 000 lines. Over the cap the upload is refused with 413 meeting_too_large. Before storage the title and content are normalised (newlines collapsed in the title, CRLF → LF, NULs and lone surrogates stripped, trailing whitespace trimmed per line) and scanned under the strictest union of every org the caller is an active member of, plus the scope org. Secrets are always scanned. A block-mode finding refuses the upload with 422 dlp_blocked (counts by finding type). In every other mode — redact, warn, or no policy at all — secrets are redacted before storage and counted in dlp_findings. The stored title and content are the only copy kept — the raw text is never persisted. Re-uploading identical content still stores a new meeting, with warnings: ["duplicate_of: meet_…"] pointing at the earlier one.

sections.heading: Participant resolution
sections.text: Each named participant in the transcript is resolved over the meeting's scope (its org), in order: an exact email matching an active org member, an exact persona name (project personas first, then the org's personas the caller can see), a display name matching exactly one active member, otherwise the participant stays unresolved. A persona that represents a member fills both persona_name and user_id. Personal meetings have no org, so only a project persona resolves; otherwise participants stay unresolved until overridden. A project or group editor can override any participant manually with exactly one of user_id or persona_name, which sets the resolution method to manual and records who made the override.

sections.heading: Action-item extraction
sections.text: Extraction turns a stored transcript into a list of participants and items (each an action or decision) with one LLM call. Run it on upload with extract: true, or later with POST /api/v1/meetings/{meeting_id}/extract. The model is asked for names, owners, due dates and 1-based line citations, but everything it returns is validated against the stored text before it is persisted: participants are resolved server-side (same order as participant resolution), and each item must cite a valid line range (at most 40 lines apart). An item whose owner matches no resolved participant is dropped and counted in the response's dropped_items. Extraction uses the same LLM key resolution and monthly token budget as the session helper. With no key configured it returns 409 llm_key_required; an exhausted org budget returns 429 helper_budget_exceeded. AI usage is recorded as meeting_extract, separately from helper chats, and counts against the same org budget. A provider failure or an unparseable response marks the meeting extraction_status: "failed" with a classified extraction_error and leaves existing items untouched. Re-running replaces pending items and every non-manual participant; promoted / dismissed items and manually overridden participants are kept, so a re-extract never undoes a promotion or a dismissal.

sections.heading: Promote to a ticket
sections.text: A pending action item (never a decision) can be promoted to a ticket. First build a confirmable draft with POST /api/v1/meetings/{meeting_id}/action-items/{item_id}/promote/preview, then confirm with POST .../promote (body: title ≤ 200, description, priority, kind, optional assigned_to / assigned_user_id / due_date, and for a group meeting target_project_id). The preview also returns jira_publish_available (true only when the plan includes Jira, you can edit the target project, the org has an enabled Jira connection and the project is mapped; computed from the database, never by calling Atlassian). For a group meeting it is judged for the project passed as ?target_project_id= and is false without one. The draft title is the item's first sentence; the description carries the item text plus a From meeting … provenance header and the quoted source lines. The target project is the meeting's own project for a project meeting, or an editable project the caller chooses from the group for a group meeting (omitting it returns 422 target_project_required). Confirming creates the ticket, flips the item to promoted with promoted_ticket_id, and — with publish_to_jira: true — publishes it to Jira. A concurrent promote is refused with 409 item_not_pending. Dismiss a pending item with POST .../dismiss (a second dismiss returns 409 item_not_pending) and bring it back with POST .../restore (409 item_not_dismissed if it was not dismissed).

sections.heading: CLI
sections.text: sfs meeting is a thin client of the REST routes below; the server enforces every access rule. Without --project or --group it uses the project of the current repository. sfs meeting upload standup.vtt --title "Standup" --date 2026-10-29 --extract sfs meeting upload --stdin --title "Planning" --group pg_abc123 < notes.txt sfs meeting list --query roadmap sfs meeting show meet_0123456789abcdef # numbered transcript, participants, items sfs meeting resolve-participant meet_… mp_… --persona atlas sfs meeting promote meet_… mi_… --assignee atlas --due 2026-11-05 # shows the draft, asks to confirm sfs meeting promote meet_… mi_… --target-project proj_… --yes # group meeting, no prompt A file upload is stored with source=file_upload (.vtt and .srt cue timing is stripped server-side); --stdin uses manual_paste. promote always prints the ticket draft first and asks before creating it unless --yes is given. See the CLI reference for every command.

sections.heading: MCP tools
sections.text: Six tools cover the same flows for agents: upload_meeting_transcript, list_meeting_transcripts, get_meeting_transcript, extract_meeting_action_items, promote_meeting_action_item and search_meetings. A project is picked by git_remote or the workspace, a group by group_id (user keys only). promote_meeting_action_item is preview only unless confirm=true. Extraction (extract_meeting_action_items, or extract=true on upload) uses your own LLM key. See MCP Server.

sections.heading: Session helper
sections.text: The session helper can read meetings you have access to: search_meetings, list_recent_meetings, get_meeting (numbered lines) and list_my_meeting_actions (pending action items owned by you or by a persona that represents you). It is read-only, honours the conversation's scope, and cites passages as [meeting:<id> L<first>-<last>], which are checked against the meeting's real line count before the answer is shown.

sections.heading: Retention and deletion
sections.text: DELETE soft-deletes a meeting. A scheduled retention sweep hard-deletes: live meetings older than their org's general.meeting_retention_days (default 180 days, configurable 1–3650), and soft-deleted meetings older than 30 days. Participants and action items are deleted with the meeting. Uploads, deletes and manual overrides are recorded in the org audit trail (ids and counts only — never transcript text); personal meetings are audited too, with a null org_id.

sections.heading: REST API
sections.text: | Method | Path | Auth | Description | | POST | /api/v1/projects/{project_id}/meetings | meetings:write | Upload a project meeting | | GET | /api/v1/projects/{project_id}/meetings | meetings:read | List project meetings, newest first (?q= substring search); each entry carries extraction_status, extraction_error, pending_action_count and decision_count | | POST | /api/v1/groups/{group_id}/meetings | user key, group editor/admin | Upload a group meeting | | GET | /api/v1/groups/{group_id}/meetings | user key, group reader+ | List group meetings, newest first (?q=); same entry fields as the project list | | GET | /api/v1/meetings/{meeting_id} | meetings:read | Get a meeting with content, participants and action items | | DELETE | /api/v1/meetings/{meeting_id} | meetings:write | Soft-delete a meeting | | PUT | /api/v1/meetings/{meeting_id}/participants/{participant_id} | user key | Manually override a participant | | POST | /api/v1/meetings/{meeting_id}/extract | meetings:write | Extract participants and action items (returns dropped_items) | | POST | /api/v1/meetings/{meeting_id}/action-items/{item_id}/promote/preview | meetings:write | Draft a ticket from an action item | | POST | /api/v1/meetings/{meeting_id}/action-items/{item_id}/promote | meetings:write | Promote an action item to a ticket (agent_tickets) | | POST | /api/v1/meetings/{meeting_id}/action-items/{item_id}/dismiss | meetings:write | Dismiss a pending action item | | POST | /api/v1/meetings/{meeting_id}/action-items/{item_id}/restore | meetings:write | Restore a dismissed action item |

sections.heading: Org setting
sections.text: GET /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/settings # includes meeting_retention_days (null = platform default 180) PUT /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/settings # {"meeting_retention_days": 365}
Organizations group team members under a shared billing account with centralized administration. Each member inherits the organization's tier, storage pool, and feature set.

sections.heading: What is an organization?
sections.text: An organization is a billing and access boundary. When you create one, your personal subscription transfers to the org level. Members you invite share the org's tier — they do not need individual subscriptions. Organizations are available on the Team ($14.99/user/month) and Enterprise (contact sales) tiers.

sections.heading: Creating an organization
sections.text: You need a Team or Enterprise subscription before creating an org. POST /api/v1/org { "name": "Acme Engineering", "slug": "acme-eng" } Slugs must be lowercase alphanumeric with hyphens, at least 3 characters, and unique across all orgs. The creator automatically becomes the owner. When the org is created, billing moves to the organization so seats, storage, and tier access are managed centrally. Seat count is derived from the organization's subscription. Defaults: 5 seats for Team, 25 for Enterprise. A user can only belong to one organization at a time.

sections.heading: Roles
sections.text: Organizations have these roles: | Role | Capabilities | | owner | Everything an admin can do, plus transfer ownership of the organization. Every org has exactly one owner. | | admin | Invite/remove members, change roles, manage billing, activate a license, view all org settings | | member | Use all features included in the org tier, view org info | Admins cannot change their own role. This prevents accidental last-admin lockout. An organization can never be left without an owner — the last owner cannot be removed or deactivated without first transferring ownership (see Ownership transfer).

sections.heading: Inviting members
sections.text: Only admins can send invites. POST /api/v1/org/invite { "email": "dev@company.com", "role": "member" } Invites expire after 7 days. The server checks seat capacity at invite time and again at acceptance time. If all seats are in use, the invite or acceptance is rejected with a seat_limit error. You cannot invite someone who is already a member, and duplicate pending invites to the same email are blocked. Starting in v0.10.22, both invite endpoints (/api/v1/org/invite and the multi-org /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/members/invite) automatically send a notification email to the invitee through the configured email provider. Email dispatch is best-effort — the invite is created even if email delivery fails, and admins can use the resend endpoint below to retry delivery.

sections.heading: Listing and revoking invites
sections.text: GET /api/v1/org/invites # List pending invites (admin only) GET /api/v1/org/invites/me # List pending invites addressed to me (v0.10.22) DELETE /api/v1/org/invites/{id} # Revoke a pending invite (admin only) POST /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/invites/{id}/resend # Resend the invite email (admin only, v0.10.22) The new /invites/me endpoint powers the dashboard /invites page where invitees see every org currently waiting on their decision.

sections.heading: Accepting or declining an invite
sections.text: POST /api/v1/org/invite/{invite_id}/accept POST /api/v1/org/invite/{invite_id}/decline # v0.10.22 — optional body: {"decline_reason": "..."} The authenticated user's email must match the invite email. Users already in an organization cannot accept a new invite — they must leave their current org first. Seat capacity is rechecked at acceptance time. If the org filled up between invite and acceptance, the request is rejected. Both accept and decline are protected by atomic rowcount-1 FSM transitions, so two browser tabs can't both succeed on the same invite. Declining records declined_at and the optional decline_reason so admins can see why an invite was turned down.

sections.heading: Managing members
sections.text: Admins can change roles and remove members: PUT /api/v1/org/members/{user_id}/role # Change role (admin only) DELETE /api/v1/org/members/{user_id} # Remove member (admin only) Role must be admin or member. Admins cannot change their own role or remove themselves, and ownership transfer is a separate flow (POST /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/owner/transfer) — owner is never assignable via the role endpoint. The CLI accepts a user ID or email for both operations, and supports bulk removal: sfs org set-role alice@example.com admin sfs org remove bob@example.com sfs org remove --bulk members.txt --yes # one user ID/email per line

sections.heading: Auto-join by verified domain (v0.17.0)
sections.text: Organizations can automatically add users as members when their email is verified against a domain the org has already verified. This is managed via the org settings surface: GET /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/settings # includes auto_join_domains PUT /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/settings # {"auto_join_domains": ["example.com"]} Each domain must already be verified by this org (via SSO domain verification). Submitting an unverified domain is rejected with a 422. Auto-join requires a paid plan (the oidc_sso feature). If the org loses that entitlement, auto-join stops at join time. When a user verifies their email address (by clicking the verification email, or when an administrator verifies them) and they are not yet a member of any org, and exactly one org lists their email domain for auto-join, they are added as a member (never admin or owner). Auto-join needs email verification switched on, because it relies on users proving they own their address. On deployments that skip email verification (SFS_REQUIRE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION=false), auto-join never runs; use SSO sign-in, which provisions members automatically, instead. Self-hosted: auto-join also requires SFS_VERIFICATION_SECRET to be set to a random value of at least 32 characters (the Helm chart generates one for you). With the built-in default secret, verification links could be forged, so auto-join stays off. Auto-join applies when a user verifies their email. Accounts that were already verified before you enabled it are not added retroactively; invite them instead. Seat limits still apply — a full org skips the join and records an auto_join_skipped_seat_cap audit event rather than failing the user's sign-in or verification. Users who were previously removed, or who already have an invite to the organization (accepted, declined or pending), are never added by auto-join. The dashboard exposes a checkbox per verified domain under Organization → Policies, and the CLI mirrors it: sfs org auto-join list sfs org auto-join add example.com sfs org auto-join remove example.com

sections.heading: Viewing org info
sections.text: GET /api/v1/org Returns the org details, full member list, and the current user's role. Non-org users get an empty response. The response includes: Org name, slug, tier Seat usage (used vs. limit) Storage usage (used bytes vs. limit) Each member's email, display name, role, and join date

sections.heading: Org billing
sections.text: The organization owns the subscription for all members. Admins manage seats, payment, invoices, upgrades, downgrades, and cancellation from the dashboard billing page. Admins access the subscription page to manage the org subscription. Members cannot purchase individual plans while in an org. Their tier is determined entirely by the org. If a member had a personal subscription before joining, it remains separate from the organization subscription and can be managed from the subscription page.

sections.heading: Storage
sections.text: | Tier | Storage | | Team | 1 GB per seat (e.g., 5 seats = 5 GB pool) | | Enterprise | Unlimited | Storage is pooled across all org members. The GET /api/v1/org response includes storage_used_bytes and storage_limit_bytes so admins can monitor usage.

sections.heading: Dashboard
sections.text: Open Organization (under Manage in the sidebar) in the web dashboard. Its tabs are Members (view members, change roles, send invites), Personas (org-wide agent personas), Policies (organization defaults, domain auto-join, notifications and, on Enterprise, the session helper AI key), Integrations (Jira Cloud and Confluence Cloud, Enterprise) and, for admins, Security (single sign-on). Subscription management is under Billing. Members see the org info and their role but cannot modify settings.

sections.heading: Multi-org membership (v0.10.0)
sections.text: Starting in v0.10.0, a user can belong to more than one organization. The new multi-org API lives at /api/v1/orgs/... and is the canonical surface for member and project management: GET /api/v1/orgs — list the caller's memberships with role. GET/POST/PUT/DELETE /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/members[/...] — list, invite, promote/demote, and remove members in a specific org. GET/PUT /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/settings — read/write the org's knowledge base creation defaults (kb_retention_days, kb_max_context_words, kb_section_page_limit), verified-domain auto-join (auto_join_domains) session helper retention (helper_retention_days) and meeting retention (meeting_retention_days, default 180 days). New org-scoped projects inherit these defaults at create time. Since v0.23.0 a save merges: general settings you leave out are kept, and an explicit null returns a setting to its default. GET /api/v1/auth/me includes default_org_id; PUT /api/v1/auth/me/default-org sets it (membership validated). Removal preserves all member-authored data — sessions stay user-owned, org-scoped projects auto-transfer to the removing admin (with a ProjectTransfer audit row), KB entries keep their authorship, and pending transfers tied to the removed user's standing are cancelled. The legacy /api/v1/org/members/... routes still work and delegate to the same services as the multi-org routes, so both URL surfaces enforce the same invariants.

sections.heading: Project transfers (v0.10.0)
sections.text: Projects carry an explicit org scope (projects.org_id, nullable). Transfers move a project between scopes (personal ↔ org, or org ↔ org) through a durable state machine: POST /api/v1/projects/{id}/transfer initiates a transfer. POST /api/v1/transfers/{xfer_id}/accept | reject | cancel mutates state. Atomic UPDATE ... WHERE state='pending' prevents double-accept. GET /api/v1/transfers?direction=&state= lists incoming and outgoing transfers. Auto-accept fires when the initiator and target are the same user/org (e.g. moving a personal project into your own org). Standing is re-validated at accept/reject — a member demoted between initiate and accept loses the right to act on the transfer. Admin-proposed transfers (v0.23.0). An owner or admin of an organization can ask the owner of a personal project to move it into that org, with a reason (POST /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/projects/{project_id}/propose-transfer). The project owner must already be an active member of the org. The owner sees the proposal in their transfer inbox, labelled with the proposer, org, reason and expiry, and by email; nothing moves until they accept. The proposer can cancel it before then. Proposals expire after 7 days, a declined proposal can't be repeated for 7 days (24 hours after a cancel), and an org can have at most 10 pending. The CLI surface mirrors the API: sfs project transfer --to | --accept | --reject | --cancel, sfs project transfers --direction --state, and sfs config default-org [<id>|--clear]. See the CLI reference for full options.

sections.heading: Session-to-project routing (v0.10.0)
sections.text: Sessions carry an explicit project_id (sessions.project_id, nullable). On every upload (POST /sessions and PUT /sessions/{id}/sync) the server resolves the linkage from the workspace's git remote inside the write transaction. Re-sync re-evaluates: pre-v0.10.0 sessions retroactively pick up a project_id when the matching project is created later; stale linkages clear when access is revoked.

sections.heading: Entitlements (v0.11.0)
sections.text: As of v0.11.0, an organization's plan tier, seat count, and storage allowance are resolved from a single authoritative entitlement record per organization. This replaced the older arrangement where plan signals were spread across user rows and license tables, which could leave enterprise admins unable to fully see or administer their own orgs. The entitlement has its own lifecycle (active / canceled / expired / revoked), tracked separately from billing health (current / past_due). Effective tier is resolved entitlement-first across the server, with a safe fall-back to the legacy columns for any record not yet migrated. Existing organizations were backfilled deterministically from their strongest existing signal (license, then subscription, then manual grant), so no plan changed for anyone during the upgrade. This is an internal model change — there is nothing to configure. It is the foundation that makes self-service license activation and ownership transfer possible.

sections.heading: Self-service license activation
sections.text: A user who has received a license key can activate it from the dashboard, with required email verification. The flow is available in the dashboard for a user who is not yet in an organization: Enter the license key and confirm the previewed organization and tier. Submit, then enter the single-use, time-limited code emailed for verification. The activated user lands as the owner of the newly created organization. Activation completes only after the emailed code is confirmed — verification is required, not optional. The activation lookup is non-oracular (it never confirms whether an arbitrary key exists) and the flow is rate-limited. Note that activation creates a new organization from the license; it does not attach a license to an existing organization. Invalid-key and bad/expired-code states are handled inline, and the exact-match-email path completes without a separate code round-trip. This gives Enterprise customers a direct, self-service path to stand up a licensed organization without manual back-office steps.

sections.heading: Ownership transfer
sections.text: Every organization has exactly one owner. The owner can transfer ownership to an existing admin directly from the dashboard members surface, through a two-step flow: The current owner initiates a transfer to a target admin. The target sees an Accept / Decline banner; the initiator sees a pending banner with Cancel. Each shows the transfer's expiry. On accept, the target becomes the new owner. The owner role is shown in the members list, and the owner row is protected from demotion or removal. Both parties' standing is re-validated at accept time, and a pending transfer expires if it is not accepted. Last-owner safety is enforced throughout: an org can never be left without an owner, so removing or deactivating the last owner is blocked until ownership is transferred, and admins have a force-transfer path with a full audit trail. (This is organization ownership transfer, distinct from project transfers.)

sections.heading: Org personas: activity and history (v0.23.0)
sections.text: Clicking an org persona opens a panel with its recent sessions, open tickets, latest knowledge entry and latest agent run, limited to the projects you can see. Org admins also see who has represented the persona over time. Your account page lists the org personas you represent, each linking to its organization. GET /api/v1/projects/{id}/personas/{name}/rollup GET /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/personas/{name}/rollup GET /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/personas/{name}/represent-history

sections.heading: Weekly activity digest (v0.23.0)
sections.text: Owners and admins of Team and Enterprise orgs get a weekly email covering the previous week (Monday to Sunday, UTC): sessions, tickets, agent runs, knowledge claims, handoffs and admin actions, each linking to the matching view in the dashboard. Each owner or admin can turn it off for themselves under Organization → Policies → Notifications, or with PUT /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/members/me/digest ({"opt_out": true}). On self-hosted servers the digest is sent by a scheduled sweep; see Self-Hosted.

sections.heading: Session helper AI key (Enterprise, v0.23.0)
sections.text: Owners and admins can set one provider, model, API key and optional base URL that the session helper uses for members without a key of their own: Organization → Policies → AI key for the session helper, or GET/PUT/DELETE /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/llm-settings. The key is encrypted at rest and never shown again after saving (only its last four characters). It can be switched off without deleting it, and a custom base URL passes the same address checks as other user-supplied LLM endpoints. A member's own key always takes precedence. Since v0.28.0, Fetch models lists the models the key can use, as on the personal form, and you can still type a model id when the provider can't list them.

sections.heading: Jira Cloud (Enterprise, v0.23.0)
sections.text: Owners and admins connect the org to Jira Cloud from the Integrations tab (or sfs org jira connect), map projects to Jira projects and check the integration's health. Members then promote tickets to Jira issues from the ticket panel. Since v0.26.0, status changes and comments can sync both ways and admins can define custom story templates. Since v0.27.0, a ticket can also be linked to an issue that already exists in Jira. Since v0.28.0, a publish can place the issue in a sprint, set its parent from the ticket's parent and carry the due date and estimate; admins review the detected sprint and epic-link fields under Connection → Agile fields. See Jira Cloud.

sections.heading: Confluence Cloud (Enterprise, v0.26.0)
sections.text: Owners and admins connect the org to Confluence Cloud from the Integrations tab (or sfs org confluence connect) and map projects to a space and parent page. Project wiki pages and the compiled context can then be published there. See Confluence Cloud.

sections.heading: Project groups (Team+, v0.26.0)
sections.text: Owners and admins can group the org's projects, grant members reader, editor or admin access to a whole group, and turn on restricted project visibility so members see only the projects they own, created, or reach through a group. See Project Groups.

Project context is one part of the Living Knowledge Base. Entries accumulate from sessions, get compiled into this document, and generate wiki pages. See Living Knowledge Base for the full loop. Share a single source-of-truth document with every AI agent working on your codebase. Any teammate, on any device, using any AI tool with the SessionFS MCP server, gets the same project context. As of v0.9.7, the context document is auto-compiled from knowledge entries — not just manually edited. You can still edit it directly, but the recommended workflow is to let entries accumulate from sessions and compile them into the document periodically.

sections.heading: Quick Start
sections.text: # From inside your git repo sfs project init sfs project edit # Opens in $EDITOR # Other teammates can now see it sfs project show

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.text: One document per repository — matched by git remote URL. Every spelling of the same remote (HTTPS, ssh://, git://, scp style such as git@github.com:org/repo, with or without .git or a trailing slash) maps to the same project Shared across the team — anyone with sessions in the repo can read it and add to it; the owner and the project's org members can change it (see Who can change a project) Accessible via MCP — AI agents call get_project_context to read the document and add_knowledge to contribute back Auto-compiled from entries — knowledge entries from sessions are merged into the document during compilation Free-form markdown — you can still edit directly; compiled content and manual edits coexist

sections.heading: The Compile Workflow
sections.text: Sessions sync → entries extracted → entries accumulate (pending) ↓ sfs project compile ↓ context document updated + wiki pages generated Knowledge entries build up as pending until you run sfs project compile. Compilation merges them into the context document and generates wiki section pages. You control the cadence — compile after a sprint, weekly, or whenever sfs project health tells you entries are piling up.

sections.heading: Who can change a project
sections.text: Anyone who can see a project can read it and add to it. Changing it is limited to its owner and its organization. | Who | Read | Add (knowledge entries, tickets, comments, agent runs, feedback) | Change (settings, rules, wiki pages, context document, knowledge curation, personas, work queues) | | Project owner | Yes | Yes | Yes | | Member of the project's organization (any role) | Yes | Yes | Yes | | Anyone else who synced a session from the same repository | Yes | Yes | No | What people in the last row add waits for the owner or an org member: Their knowledge entries stay notes (confidence at most 0.7), are never promoted or allowed to supersede other entries automatically at compile time, and so don't reach the context document or compiled rules files until an owner or org member promotes them. Bulk promote leaves their notes out unless include_reader_notes is set. An add_knowledge call with upsert=true (which retires the other entries in its slot) needs change rights. Their tickets start as *suggested*. The assignee isn't notified and autonomous work queues don't pick the ticket up until an owner or org member approves it. They can keep editing tickets they created. Editing one after it was approved sends it back to *suggested* for approval again. Once work has started, or a work queue has picked the ticket up, they can only change its reference lists (context refs, file refs, related sessions). A work queue doesn't hand out a ticket that is back in *suggested* (or cancelled) until an owner or org member approves it again. Their comments are visible to people in the dashboard, API and MCP tools, but aren't passed to automated agents: work queues leave them out of the comments they send to agents, and they don't start a reviewer's turn. On tickets they can dismiss, reopen or accept tickets they created (but not accept work they resolved themselves), and start, complete, block or unblock tickets they created or resolved. Approving a suggested ticket needs change rights. They can cancel or complete agent runs they triggered, but not anyone else's. A rules compile they run returns the compiled files without adding a version to the rules history. Project-scope skill install requests need change rights; personal (user or device) requests don't. A change they try gets 403 project_edit_forbidden, and the dashboard hides the controls they can't use (the project response carries can_edit). Renaming, linking repositories, merging, transferring and deleting still need project-admin standing (the owner, or an org owner or admin). Service keys keep their own boundary: the key's organization and project allowlist.

sections.heading: sfs project init
sections.text: Create a project context for the current repository. Detects the git remote automatically. cd ~/code/my-project sfs project init # Project created for myorg/my-project # Run 'sfs project edit' to add context.

sections.heading: sfs project edit
sections.text: Open the context document in your editor. Changes are uploaded on save. sfs project edit # Opens in $EDITOR (default: nano) Set your preferred editor: export EDITOR=vim # or export EDITOR="code --wait"

sections.heading: sfs project show
sections.text: Display the current project context with metadata. sfs project show # Project: my-project # Remote: myorg/my-project # Updated: 2026-03-26 # # # Architecture # ...

sections.heading: sfs project set-context
sections.text: Set the context from a file (useful for CI or scripting). sfs project set-context ./PROJECT_INSTRUCTIONS.md # Project context updated (2.4 KB).

sections.heading: sfs project get-context
sections.text: Output raw markdown to stdout (useful for piping). sfs project get-context > local-copy.md

sections.heading: sfs project compile
sections.text: Compile pending knowledge entries into the context document and generate wiki pages. Uses deterministic merging by default; pass an LLM API key for smarter deduplication and reorganization. sfs project compile # Compiling pending entries... # Project context updated. 12 entries compiled.

sections.heading: sfs project compile-schedule
sections.text: Compile the project's knowledge on a schedule instead of by hand: nightly, weekly or off, optionally with a waiting-claims threshold (v0.23.0). The same setting is under the project's Settings → Scheduled KB compile. Scheduled compiles use the deterministic compiler, never an LLM. sfs project compile-schedule weekly --after-claims 20 sfs project compile-schedule off --no-after-claims New projects start at nightly when their plan includes project context; existing projects start at off. The project Overview shows when the context was last compiled and how many claims are waiting, with a one-click compile when it is out of date. On a self-hosted server the schedule only takes effect once the operator runs the compile sweep.

sections.heading: sfs project health
sections.text: Check the health of your project's knowledge base — pending entry count, staleness, document size, and an overall score. sfs project health # Project Health: my-project # # ✓ Context document exists (1200 words, 8 sections) # ✓ 45 knowledge entries (38 compiled, 2 dismissed) # ⚠ 5 entries pending compilation # ✓ Last compiled: 2026-04-01 # # Health Score: 90%

sections.heading: Auto-Narrative
sections.text: Enable auto-narrative to have session summaries extracted as knowledge entries automatically on sync. This is the lowest-effort way to keep the context document current — just use your AI tools normally and let entries accumulate. sfs project set --auto-narrative When enabled, each synced session is analyzed for decisions, patterns, bugs, and other notable facts. Extracted entries are stored as pending until compilation. Requires an LLM API key (client-side — SessionFS never stores your key).

sections.heading: MCP Integration
sections.text: The SessionFS MCP server exposes 115 tools, including several for project context, knowledge, rules, personas (Pro+), tickets (Team+), CI agent runs (Team+), agent feedback (Team+), handoffs (Pro+ for direct, Team+ for team handoffs), autonomous work queues, project groups (Team+), and the skills marketplace. When connected, AI agents can read the shared document, contribute knowledge entries, update wiki pages, fetch canonical rules, manage personas, run a ticket through its full FSM, record AgentRun outcomes, create + claim coordination handoffs with provenance carry-through, service a work queue of tickets unattended, and search, preview, and request installs of skill packages. This works with any MCP-aware tool (Claude Code, Cursor, etc.). | Tool | Description | | get_project_context | Read the compiled context document | | add_knowledge(content, type) | Contribute a knowledge entry | | update_wiki_page(slug, content) | Create or update a wiki page | | list_wiki_pages() | List all wiki pages | | search_project_knowledge(query) | Search entries by content | | ask_project(question) | Research a question across context, entries, and sessions | The tools auto-detect the git remote from the current working directory; you can also pass it explicitly as an argument.

sections.heading: What to Include
sections.text: The default template provides a starting structure: # Project Context ## Overview What is this project? One paragraph. ## Architecture Tech stack, infrastructure, key services. ## Conventions Coding standards, branch strategy, PR process. ## API Contracts Key endpoints, request/response formats. ## Key Decisions Important decisions that are locked and shouldn't be revisited. ## Team Who works on what. Write whatever is useful for your team. Some ideas: Database schema overview Deployment process Testing conventions Security requirements Third-party service credentials (names only, not values) Links to external documentation

sections.heading: Access Control
sections.text: Read: Any authenticated user with sessions in the repository Write: Same as read (team trust model) Owner: The user who ran sfs project init

sections.heading: API Endpoints
sections.text: | Method | Path | Description | | POST | /api/v1/projects/ | Create a project context | | GET | /api/v1/projects/{remote} | Get project context by git remote | | PUT | /api/v1/projects/{remote}/context | Update the context document | | GET | /api/v1/projects/{id}/compile-status | Last compile, claims waiting, and whether a compile is recommended (v0.23.0) |

Project groups are flat, org-scoped collections of projects. They let a Team or Enterprise organization grant a member read or edit access to a subset of its projects, and — when combined with restricted project visibility — narrow who can see and change each project from "every org member" to a chosen few. Project groups are available on the Team and Enterprise tiers.

sections.heading: What is a project group?
sections.text: A group is always scoped to one organization (org_id is immutable) and can only ever contain projects from that same org. A project can belong to many groups. Each member of a group holds a role: | Role | Meaning | | reader | Can read the group's projects (read tier). | | editor | Can change the group's projects (edit tier: settings, rules, wiki, knowledge curation, context document, personas, work queues). | | admin | Everything an editor can do, plus manage the group itself (rename, grant/revoke members, add/remove projects). | No group role grants project-admin standing (rename, link, merge, transfer, delete). That stays with the project owner or an org admin/owner. Org admins and owners have admin standing on every group in their org.

sections.heading: Restricted project visibility
sections.text: By default an organization keeps today's behavior: every member can read and edit every org project. An org can opt into restricted project visibility, which narrows standing per project: | Action | Unrestricted (default) | Restricted | | Read | Owner, any org member, captured-session reader | Owner, org admin/owner, group grant (reader/editor/admin) | | Edit | Owner, any org member | Owner, org admin/owner, group grant (editor/admin) | In a restricted org, syncing a session from a project's repository no longer gives anyone access to that project, and a pushed session is linked to the project only if the person pushing it already has read access; otherwise it stays an unlinked session that belongs to them. Turning it on is an org-wide access change, so it is recorded in the org audit trail. It requires the project_groups feature (Team+); if the org's plan later drops that feature, the restriction stays on (fail closed) until an admin clears it. If an org's stored settings can't be read, the org is treated as restricted. GET /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/settings # read (includes restrict_project_visibility) PUT /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/settings # {"restrict_project_visibility": true}

sections.heading: REST API
sections.text: Group CRUD is org-scoped: GET /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/groups — list (org admins see all; members see groups they're granted on) POST /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/groups — create (org admin) GET /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/groups/{group_id} — detail (org admin or a member granted on the group) PATCH /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/groups/{group_id} — rename/re-slug/re-describe, compile_enabled (group admin) DELETE /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/groups/{group_id} — soft delete (org admin) Membership grants (group admin): PUT /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/groups/{group_id}/members/{user_id} {"role": "reader" | "editor" | "admin"} DELETE /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/groups/{group_id}/members/{user_id} Non-members of the org get 404 on every group route. Grantees must be active members of the group's org; granting a non-member returns 422 not_org_member. Removing a member from the org, or deactivating their account, deletes their group grants in the same transaction. Project placement (group admin): PUT /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/groups/{group_id}/projects/{project_id} DELETE /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/groups/{group_id}/projects/{project_id} Only projects whose org_id matches the group's org can join (422 project_not_in_org otherwise). A group admin who is not an org admin can only add projects they can already edit; a project they can't read returns 404. A project leaving an org (transfer) leaves all of its groups; merging a project moves its group memberships to the target, deduplicated. Creating a group, granting a member and adding a project need the project_groups feature. Reading, renaming, revoking, removing a project and deleting a group keep working after a downgrade so admins can clean up. Reads from the project and caller side: GET /api/v1/projects/{project_id}/groups — the groups a project belongs to (project reader who is an org member) GET /api/v1/me/groups — the caller's groups across orgs

sections.heading: Group knowledge
sections.text: A group can surface the knowledge of its member projects as one shared picture, without widening who can see each individual project. Every group-knowledge read respects the caller's per-project access: a claim, page or context document is only visible to a caller who can read its source project, so a group grant never leaks a project's knowledge to someone who couldn't read it anyway. GET /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/groups/{slug}/knowledge/search?q=&entry_type=&limit= — active KB claims across readable member projects GET /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/groups/{slug}/pages?limit= — wiki pages across readable member projects, newest first POST /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/groups/{slug}/compile — compile the deterministic overview (opt-in) GET /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/groups/{slug}/context — the stored overview document knowledge/search returns active claims (not dismissed, superseded, or stale) with each hit carrying its source project id/name, entry id, type, confidence, freshness and content. q is an optional case-insensitive substring of 3–200 characters (% and _ match literally). entry_type is one of decision, pattern, discovery, convention, bug, dependency; limit caps at 100. pages returns up to limit pages (default 200, max 500). Every group-knowledge route needs standing on the group, exactly like the group detail: org admins/owners, or a member holding a grant on it. Any other caller — including an org member without a grant, in a restricted org or not — gets 404.

sections.heading: Compiled context
sections.text: compile builds a deterministic overview from the group's active claims — no LLM. It is opt-in: the group's compile_enabled flag defaults to false, so existing groups keep their current behavior until a group admin or org admin/owner turns it on: PATCH /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/groups/{group_id} {"compile_enabled": true} sfs project group set SLUG --compile Turning it on needs the project_groups feature (Team+); turning it off never does. The change is recorded in the org audit trail. Once it is on, a group editor/admin or org admin can run compile. The compile is attributed to, and scoped by, the person who runs it: only member projects they can read contribute. For each, the overview quotes the start of the project's compiled context and lists its highest-value active claims (at most 50 per project, highest confidence first, then most recently relevant) grouped by type, each citing [project/claim #id]. The document is capped at 20,000 words; when it would overflow, the budget is split fairly across projects (a large project can't crowd out the others), a note says how many claims were left out, and the footer counts the claims actually included. It stores who compiled it and which projects contributed. The scheduled platform sweep (POST /api/v1/admin/sweeps/kb-compile) also recompiles opted-in groups that were never compiled or whose member projects compiled since the group last did — however the project compile happened — up to the sweep's limit groups per run. A scheduled recompile is attributed to the group's creator and is skipped (with a log line) if the creator is deactivated, no longer an org admin or group admin, or the org's plan no longer includes project groups. Each attempt is stamped on the group, so a group that keeps being skipped or failing waits ten minutes and then queues behind healthy groups, and two overlapping sweeps never compile the same group. A group reader (or org admin) can view the stored document with context. The stored document is returned only to a caller who can still read *every* contributing project; if a source project has since been deleted, removed from the group, or restricted away from the caller, context returns `403 group_context_partial` rather than leaking a partial picture.

sections.heading: CLI and MCP
sections.text: The CLI ships sfs project group (list/create/show/set/delete/add/remove/ members/grant/revoke/access/search/context/compile) and `sfs project list --group SLUG`. The MCP server exposes the same surface as fifteen tools (list_project_groups, get_project_group, create_project_group, update_project_group, delete_project_group, add_project_to_group, remove_project_from_group, list_group_members, grant_group_access, revoke_group_access, list_group_access, search_group_knowledge, get_group_context, compile_group_knowledge, and ask_group). Both address groups by org-scoped slug and resolve the org from --org/org_id else the default org (list_group_access / sfs project group access need no org). sfs project group create NAME [--slug SLUG] [--description TEXT] [--org ORG_ID] sfs project group set SLUG [--name NAME] [--slug NEW_SLUG] [--description TEXT] [--compile|--no-compile] sfs project group add SLUG PROJECT_ID... sfs project group grant SLUG EMAIL_OR_USER_ID --role reader|editor|admin sfs project group revoke SLUG EMAIL_OR_USER_ID sfs project group search SLUG [QUERY] [--entry-type TYPE] [--limit N] sfs project group compile SLUG sfs project group context SLUG

sections.heading: Ask the session helper about a group
sections.text: On the Enterprise plan, the session helper can answer a question across a whole group (v0.28.0): pick the group in the drawer's scope menu, run sfs helper ask --group SLUG "...", or pass group_id to the ask_session_helper MCP tool. The answer only draws on the group's member projects you can read. When the group has a compiled overview and you can read every project behind it, that overview goes into the prompt too, redacted with your DLP policy.

sections.heading: Meetings in a group
sections.text: A group can hold its own meeting transcripts (v0.29.0). Open Meetings on the group page to upload, search and read them; action items are promoted into a ticket in one of the group's projects that you can edit.

sections.heading: Lifecycle
sections.text: Soft delete frees a group's slug for reuse but keeps the row for audit continuity. Soft-deleted groups grant nothing. Transfer-out removes a project from all of its groups when it leaves the org. Merge moves the source project's group memberships to the target project, dropping duplicates. Account merge moves a user's grants to the surviving account, keeping the higher role.

sections.heading: Audit
sections.text: Group create/update/delete (including turning the knowledge compile on or off), group compiles, member grant/revoke, project add/remove (including removals and moves caused by transfers, merges, member removal and account deactivation), and restricted-visibility toggles all write org audit events, so access changes are reconstructable from the org audit trail.
Time: Under 2 minutes. Prerequisites: Python 3.10+ on macOS or Linux (Windows support is planned)

sections.heading: 1. Install
sections.text: pipx install sessionfs This installs two commands: sfs (CLI) and sfsd (daemon). See Installation for alternative methods (curl, pip).

sections.heading: 2. Run the Setup Wizard
sections.text: sfs init The wizard auto-detects which AI coding tools you have installed and asks which ones to track. It then starts the daemon, installs the MCP server for your tools, and — if you have existing sessions — captures your most recent one on the spot: ✓ Captured your most recent session: "Debug auth middleware" (claude-code, 47 messages) Then it prints the payoff: Now ask your agent: "what did we do last session?" Because MCP was installed in the same wizard step, you can ask that question immediately — your agent reads the captured session and picks up right where you left off. If you have no existing sessions yet, the wizard prints a graceful fallback and your first session will be captured automatically when you use your AI tool next. The daemon watches your AI tools in the background using filesystem events (not polling). Negligible CPU overhead. It automatically detects and captures sessions from all ten supported tools: Claude Code Codex CLI Gemini CLI Copilot CLI Cursor IDE Amp Cline Roo Code Kilo Code Antigravity (desktop app, agy CLI, IDE)

sections.heading: 3. Ask Your Agent
sections.text: Open Claude Code (or whichever tool you use) and ask: "what did we do last session?" Your agent reads the captured session via MCP and catches up without you re-explaining anything.

sections.heading: 4. Use Your Tools Normally
sections.text: No behavior change required. Just use your AI coding tools the way you always do. SessionFS captures sessions silently in the background.

sections.heading: 5. Browse Your Sessions
sections.text: sfs list Sessions (12) ┌──────────────┬─────────────┬────────┬──────────┬───────────────────────┐ │ ID │ Tool │ Model │ Messages │ Title │ ├──────────────┼─────────────┼────────┼──────────┼───────────────────────┤ │ ses_a1b2c3d4 │ claude-code │ opus-4 │ 47 │ Debug auth flow │ │ ses_e5f6a7b8 │ gemini-cli │ gem-2 │ 23 │ Add rate limiting │ │ ses_c9d0e1f2 │ codex-cli │ codex │ 31 │ Refactor DB schema │ │ ses_g3h4i5j6 │ cursor │ son4.5 │ 8 │ Fix CI pipeline │ └──────────────┴─────────────┴────────┴──────────┴───────────────────────┘ Filter and sort: sfs list --since 24h sfs list --tool claude-code --sort tokens

sections.heading: 6. Resume a Session
sections.text: Resume in the same tool or a different one: # Resume in Claude Code (default) sfs resume ses_a1b2c3d4 # Resume a Cursor session in Codex sfs resume ses_g3h4i5j6 --in codex # Resume any session in Gemini CLI sfs resume ses_e5f6a7b8 --in gemini Four tools support resume: Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, and Copilot CLI. Sessions from capture-only tools (Cursor, Amp, Cline, Roo Code, Kilo Code, Antigravity) can be resumed in any of the four bidirectional tools. See Installation for details on supported tools.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Run the health check first: sfs doctor This runs 9 diagnostic checks — including capture health, which detects when a tool's format change breaks capture — and auto-repairs common issues (broken indexes, stale locks, permission problems). "No sessions found" after sfs list Make sure the daemon is running and at least one AI tool has been used: sfs daemon status If the daemon shows 0 sessions, try importing existing sessions: sfs import --from claude-code Daemon won't start Check the logs: sfs daemon logs Common causes: Another sfsd process is already running (ps aux | grep sfsd) The ~/.sessionfs/ directory doesn't exist or isn't writable Daemon is running but not detecting sessions sfs daemon status If a watcher shows degraded or broken, check sfs daemon logs --lines 100.

sections.heading: What's Next
sections.text: Once you're capturing sessions, explore these features: # Search across all sessions sfs search "rate limiting" # Get a quick summary of any session sfs summary ses_abc # Audit a session for hallucinations sfs audit ses_abc --model gpt-4o # Set up project knowledge base and wiki sfs project init sfs project edit # Install MCP server (115 tools) so AI agents # can search sessions, query the knowledge base, and read wiki pages sfs mcp install --for claude-code # Enable automatic cloud sync sfs auth login sfs sync auto --mode all # Hand off a session to a teammate sfs handoff ses_abc --to colleague@company.com See the full CLI Reference for all commands and options.

The worker review loop is a way to build a change with several coding agents without letting any of them grade their own work. Workers write code from a written brief, one branch each, in their own git worktree. A separate reviewer reads the code, not the worker's summary, and posts a verdict. The worker's fix pass goes back to the same reviewer, and nothing merges until that reviewer says it is clean. SessionFS holds the state of the loop, so it works with any coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI and others) and anyone on the project can see where each piece of work stands. The worker-review-loop skill in the launch catalog teaches an agent to run it. For wrapping agents you launch yourself in agent runs, see also External Agent Orchestration. | Piece of the loop | SessionFS primitive | | Brief | A ticket with acceptance criteria | | Each worker or reviewer launch | An agent run | | Review loop | A work queue in review_until_clean mode | | Reviewer | A registered trusted reviewer posting verdicts | | Worker that runs out of turns | A continuation run or a handoff | | Discoveries | Knowledge base entries (add_knowledge) | Tickets and agent runs are available on Team and Enterprise. Registering a trusted reviewer needs an org owner or admin on Team or Enterprise.

sections.heading: 1. Write the brief as a ticket
sections.text: The brief is the worker's only context: anything not in the ticket, the worker does not know. Create one ticket per branch with the create_ticket MCP tool or sfs ticket create, and put each testable outcome in its acceptance criteria. A good brief names: the goal, in one sentence; the spec, with the parts that matter quoted; the files to read first, in order; the scope: which paths may change, which may not, and whether new dependencies are allowed; the vendor documentation for every external API the change calls; the required tests and the command that must pass, plus a migration run on a real database if the change has migrations; what "done" means, including a status line the worker prints at the end (for example WORKER-STATUS: DONE). sfs ticket create --title "Add retry to the export client" \ --description "$(cat brief.md)" \ --criteria "Retries 429 and 503 responses with backoff, up to 3 attempts" \ --criteria "tests/test_export_client.py covers both status codes" \ --file src/export/client.py --output-id Tickets an agent files start as suggested. Approve them (sfs ticket approve or approve_ticket) before a work queue will pick them up.

sections.heading: 2. One worker per branch, one worktree per worker
sections.text: git worktree add ../wt-export-retry -b export-retry main Workers never share a worktree or a branch, so they cannot see or overwrite each other's files.

sections.heading: 3. Launch workers as agent runs
sections.text: Record each launch as an agent run, then start your coding agent inside the worktree with the brief: sfs persona create implementer --role "Implements ticket briefs" \ --content "Work the ticket's brief in this worktree, commit, and report." RUN_ID=$(sfs agent run implementer --ticket <ticket_id> --output-id) The worker calls start_ticket first, which loads the ticket, the persona and related knowledge, and records what it learns with add_knowledge as it goes.
