When several workers run at once in different worktrees, give each its own run id in SFS_AGENT_RUN_ID: each worker then keeps its own active ticket, a copy for the worktree is kept under ~/.sessionfs/workspaces/ (never inside the repository), and captured sessions are tagged with a ticket only when the ticket's repository matches the session's. Keep the full output in a log file. A fast, inexpensive model often works well as a worker when a stronger model reviews, but that split is optional.

sections.heading: 4. Detect how the worker exited
sections.text: A worker's own summary is not evidence that it finished. Check the log and the branch: Search the whole log for the status line. Do not anchor the check to the start of a line. Tools wrap, indent or prefix their final message, and an anchored check has missed real out-of-turns exits. Confirm with git that the worktree is clean and the branch has the commits. Look for your tool's turn-limit message or exit status to tell running out of turns apart from a crash. | Exit | Signs | Next step | | Finished | Status line present, tree clean, commits on the branch | sfs agent complete $RUN_ID --summary "...", then, on the first pass only, sfs ticket complete <ticket_id> --notes "..." --file <path> so the ticket moves to review (fix-pass workers skip this: the ticket is already in review), then one ticket comment with the branch, commit and test command. | | Out of turns | Turn-limit message, no status line | Commit what exists as work in progress, complete the run with --status errored, and start a continuation. | | Crashed | Non-zero exit, no turn-limit message | Complete the run with --status errored, fix the cause, relaunch the same brief in the same worktree. | A continuation is a short new brief: continue this ticket, the spec is the ticket, the previous worker stopped at commit <sha> (read its diff first), and these criteria are still open. Create it with sfs agent replay <run_id> --prompt-file continuation.md --context-ref <sha> (MCP: replay_agent_run) so the new run links to the one that stopped, and start it with sfs agent run --run-id <new_run_id>. The ticket is already in progress, so a continuation worker skips start_ticket. If a person should take over instead, push the session and send a handoff that carries the ticket.

sections.heading: 5. Register the reviewer and create the queue
sections.text: Give the reviewer an identity nothing else uses, usually an org service key, and register it as a trusted reviewer: sfs admin service-keys create --org <org_id> --name reviewer \ --scope tickets:read --scope tickets:write \ --scope work_queues:read --scope work_queues:write \ --scope agent_runs:write --scope knowledge:read \ --project <project_id> --output-key sfs persona create reviewer --role "Reviews branches read-only" \ --content "Review the code, not the worker's report. Post one verdict per round." sfs admin trusted-reviewers add --org <org_id> \ --service-key-id <key_id> --persona reviewer Then create a work queue with the create_work_queue MCP tool: { "name": "export-retry review", "mode": "review_until_clean", "selector": {"ticket_ids": ["<ticket_id>"]}, "assigned_persona": "reviewer" } Run the reviewer under that key only, for example as its own auth profile (sfs auth login --profile reviewer --key <key>, then SESSIONFS_PROFILE=reviewer in the reviewer's shell), never under a worker's identity. knowledge:read lets the reviewer read the project context and wiki pages (v0.29.1) in addition to the ticket and queue — useful when the brief points at a spec page or a compiled context section to judge against. Keep it read-only: this key has no knowledge:write, so the reviewer cannot alter the knowledge base or wiki it is judging. assigned_persona must match the persona the reviewer is registered for. The server counts a verdict only when the caller's identity is registered for exactly that persona, and it ignores any persona name a client sends.

sections.heading: 6. Independent, read-only review
sections.text: The reviewer runs in its own checkout, may not edit files, and never commits. On each wake it calls run_work_queue_step (no more often than the queue's cadence, which is at least 120 seconds). A post_review directive means a worker posted new work; it carries the review_round number and the findings still open from earlier rounds. Brief the reviewer with the branch, the commit, the base and the ticket, not with the worker's conclusion. Ask it to read the diff against the acceptance criteria, run the tests, check every external request against the vendor's documentation rather than the test mocks, confirm migrations ran on a real database, and re-check every open finding. The reviewer delivers its verdict through complete_work_queue_step, passing the directive's ids, outcome: "posted_review" and the verdict as verdict_content. The server writes the verdict comment itself, with the queue's persona and its server-stamped trusted provenance. Post the verdict through the queue rather than add_ticket_comment, so the round and directive stay linked and the loop can close. The server reads this format, with the reviewer's own name in place of <Reviewer> whichever tool reviews and <review_round> taken from the directive: <Reviewer> R<review_round> review on <ticket_id>: CHANGES_REQUESTED Findings: - HIGH — src/export/client.py:88 retries POST without an idempotency key - LOW — tests/test_export_client.py does not cover the 503 path <Reviewer> must start with a letter and contain only letters, digits, ., _ or - (at most 32 characters). A verdict_content whose header does not parse is rejected with verdict_header_unparseable before anything is written. The reviewer may also pass reviewed_commit — the full commit id (40 or 64 lowercase hex characters) of the head commit it actually read — so the verdict is bound to the code it reviewed. A merge gate later requires the clean verdict to be bound to the current head, so a verdict on a SHA that has since moved no longer marks the branch ready. The reviewer also records its own agent run, with the severity and findings, so the review shows up next to the worker runs. Findings on a run can carry round, severity, class, harm and stage keys (see complete_agent_run), so mistakes can later be counted by kind and by whether they were caught in design or in code.

sections.heading: 7. Fix pass and re-review
sections.text: Read the open findings with get_ticket_review_state or sfs ticket review-state <ticket_id>. Launch a fix worker in the same worktree with a brief listing those findings. Handle its exit as in step 4, except that the ticket is already in review: the fix worker calls neither start_ticket nor sfs ticket complete. The fix worker commits and posts one ticket comment with the new commit. Any comment that is not a trusted verdict hands the turn back to the reviewer, so post one comment per pass. The same reviewer re-reviews. The loop for that ticket ends only on a trusted <Reviewer> R<N> review on <ticket_id>: VERIFIED-CLEAN with no open findings. APPROVED and similar wording is displayed as clean but never ends the loop.

sections.heading: 8. Merge
sections.text: Merge when the ticket is ready at the head commit you are about to merge. check_merge_readiness (or sfs loop ready <ticket_id> --sha <head>) returns ready: true only when all of these hold: a trusted strict VERIFIED-CLEAN verdict exists; its reviewed_commit equals the requested head exactly (a prefix match is not accepted); the reviewer's identity differs from every implementer identity recorded for the ticket, so no one grades their own work (a service key counts as the person who created it, so two keys minted by the same person are one identity); no open finding is harmful. A finding's harm is read from a harm: <tag> marker in its line (data-exposed, money-spent, wrong-actor, crash, other or none). harm: none marks a finding as checked and harmless; an untagged finding of medium severity or higher counts as harmful. If no implementer identity was recorded for the ticket, the answer is not ready. get_ticket_review_state still shows the raw state (sfs ticket review-state prints Strict VERIFIED-CLEAN: yes), but readiness is the merge gate: it also enforces the commit binding and the reviewer-identity check that review state alone does not. Run the full test suite on the merged result, then resolve the ticket (resolve_ticket or sfs ticket resolve) and remove the worktree. The work queue never changes a ticket's status on its own.

sections.heading: Start a loop and set limits (v0.29.2)
sections.text: Instead of wiring the queue by hand you can start a loop in one call: sfs loop start (MCP: start_review_loop, API: POST /api/v1/projects/{id}/loops). Pass an existing issue to adopt it as the loop parent, or a title to create one. Each brief becomes a child task, and SessionFS creates the reviewer's review_until_clean queue. sfs loop start "Billing fixes" --reviewer-persona reviewer \ --ticket "Fix proration::Round to the cent" --token-budget 400000 --max-review-rounds 4 sfs loop status # every loop, or pass a loop id for its children A loop can carry three limits: a token budget, a dollar budget (set only by org owners and admins) and a cap on review rounds. There is no default round cap. When a limit is reached the item stops and is handed back to a person as needing a human instead of continuing to spend. A person can raise a limit with sfs loop update (MCP: update_review_loop) or Raise limit in the dashboard, or settle the item with sfs loop close-item or Close item. Closing items is for people only; service keys cannot do it, and the ticket keeps its own status. The review checklist is a per-project list of traps that every brief carries. Seed it with the generic starters (sfs loop checklist seed), propose items by hand, and accept or retire them; new kinds of finding from reviews are proposed automatically. sfs loop report <ticket_id> shows each review round's findings by harm, how many were known classes versus new, and what the round cost; sfs loop insights rolls that up over a date range. In the dashboard, the project's Work section shows runs, a story of each ticket, and the Checklist panel.

sections.heading: Track spend
sections.text: Each run can record its model, role and token usage: pass --model, --provider and --role to sfs agent run, report usage while it runs with sfs agent usage (MCP: report_agent_run_usage), and send the final figures with sfs agent complete --input-tokens --output-tokens --cost-usd --cost-basis. sfs agent spend --ticket <ticket_id> (MCP: get_spend_summary) then shows what a ticket cost across workers, reviewers and review rounds. Token totals are visible to everyone who can read the project; dollar amounts only to org owners and admins, or the owner of a personal project.

sections.heading: Lessons
sections.text: The brief is the only context. Name the spec, the files to read first, the scope limits and the required tests. A self-report is not a gate. The trusted verdict is. Mocked tests can encode the wrong API. A branch can pass its tests while asserting the wrong request shapes for a vendor API. Check against the vendor's documentation, and prove migrations on a real database. Write down what you learn. Vendor quirks, dead ends and conventions go into the knowledge base as they are found, so the next worker starts with them.

Manage your project's AI instructions in one place. SessionFS keeps a canonical rules record per project and compiles it into the tool-specific files each AI agent reads — CLAUDE.md, codex.md, .cursorrules, .github/copilot-instructions.md, and GEMINI.md — so instructions stay consistent across every tool your team uses. Every captured session also records the rules and instruction artifacts that shaped it, so you can always answer: *what was the agent told when this session happened?*

sections.heading: The Problem
sections.text: AI-heavy teams maintain the same project conventions in five different places: | Tool | Instruction File | | Claude Code | CLAUDE.md | | Codex | codex.md | | Cursor | .cursorrules | | GitHub Copilot | .github/copilot-instructions.md | | Gemini CLI | GEMINI.md | Each format drifts. One file gets updated, the others don't. A developer who switches tools gets an agent that doesn't know the project's conventions, security rules, or architecture decisions. Sessions generated under different rule sets are impossible to compare after the fact.

sections.heading: Mental Model
sections.text: canonical project rules (SessionFS) + active knowledge claims + project context sections │ │ sfs rules compile ▼ CLAUDE.md · codex.md · .cursorrules · copilot-instructions.md · GEMINI.md │ ▼ agent sessions shaped by those rules │ ▼ sessions captured with rules_version + rules_hash + instruction_artifacts The canonical record is the source of truth. Compiled tool files are projections — they carry a SessionFS marker so future compiles know they are safe to overwrite.

sections.heading: Quick Start
sections.text: # From inside your git repo sfs rules init # pick tools, seed canonical rules sfs rules edit # edit static preferences in $EDITOR sfs rules compile # write CLAUDE.md / codex.md / etc. git add CLAUDE.md codex.md .cursorrules .github/copilot-instructions.md GEMINI.md git commit -m "Add project rules" Teammates who clone the repo see the compiled files immediately. Even developers who don't run SessionFS still get consistent agent behavior — the compiled rule files are just text, readable by every tool that natively supports them.

sections.heading: Shared vs Local-Only
sections.text: Compiled rule files are committed by default. Opt into local-only mode with sfs rules init --local-only when the canonical rules contain team-internal conventions you don't want in the shared repo. Committing compiled files is deliberate: Fresh clones get consistent agent behavior with zero setup Developers who don't run SessionFS still see the project contract Teammates can review rule changes in normal code review Compiled files embed a SessionFS marker so future sfs rules compile knows they're safe to regenerate Local-only mode adds the compiled paths to .gitignore. The canonical record is still shared via sfs rules push / sfs rules pull. You can switch between modes later by editing .gitignore by hand.

sections.heading: sfs rules init
sections.text: Seeds canonical rules for the current project. sfs rules init [--local-only] At init time, SessionFS preselects enabled tools using this precedence: Existing repo rule files — if CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules, etc. are already present, the corresponding tools are preselected with reason file present. Recent captured tool usage — tools with sessions captured in the last 90 days are preselected with reason recent usage. User picker — if neither signal is present, SessionFS prompts you to pick tools interactively. Only the five supported tools are considered in v0.9.9: claude-code, codex, cursor, copilot, gemini. The picker shows a reason for each preselection so you can override. If exactly one unmanaged recognized rule file exists (for example, a hand-written CLAUDE.md), sfs rules init offers to import it as the canonical seed. Multiple unmanaged files are never auto-merged — you must pick one source explicitly.

sections.heading: sfs rules edit
sections.text: Opens the canonical static_rules document in $EDITOR. sfs rules edit This is the primary surface for editing project conventions. Save, exit, then run sfs rules compile to regenerate tool files.

sections.heading: sfs rules show
sections.text: sfs rules show Shows current canonical version, enabled tools, knowledge injection config, context injection config, and whether compiled outputs are in sync.

sections.heading: sfs rules compile
sections.text: Compiles canonical rules into the tool-specific files. sfs rules compile [--tool TOOL] [--dry-run] [--force] | Option | Description | | --tool TOOL | Compile for a single tool only (claude-code, codex, cursor, copilot, gemini) | | --dry-run | Show what would be written without touching disk | | --force | Overwrite unmanaged files (dangerous — see below) | Compilation is deterministic — the same inputs always produce the same outputs. A new rules_versions row is only created when at least one compiled output changes by hash. Recompiling with no input changes is a no-op. --force overwrites files not managed by SessionFS. Use it only when you are certain the destination file should be replaced.

sections.heading: Managed-File Safety
sections.text: SessionFS will only overwrite a rule file it considers managed. A file is managed if: it was created by sfs rules compile, or it contains the SessionFS managed marker, or it was explicitly imported via sfs rules init If a target path already exists and is not managed, compilation refuses to overwrite it: $ sfs rules compile ERROR CLAUDE.md exists and is not managed by SessionFS. Run 'sfs rules init' to import it, or re-run with --force.

sections.heading: Managed Marker
sections.text: Every compiled file embeds a small marker that names SessionFS as the generator, records the canonical version, and stores the content hash: The marker is lightweight and tool-compatible. It is what allows future compiles to know the file is safe to overwrite.

sections.heading: sfs rules push
sections.text: Push the canonical record and latest compiled version to the SessionFS API. sfs rules push Uses optimistic concurrency. If the remote is ahead, the push fails with 409 Conflict and you must sfs rules pull and retry.

sections.heading: sfs rules pull
sections.text: Pull canonical rules from the SessionFS API into the local project. sfs rules pull Fetches the current canonical record and writes it into the local rules config. Run sfs rules compile afterwards to regenerate tool files from the pulled rules.

sections.heading: Compilation Model
sections.text: Compiled output is assembled from three inputs: Static rules — the canonical preferences you edit with sfs rules edit. Project knowledge claims — active, durable claims from your project's knowledge base. Project context sections — selected sections of the compiled project context document.

sections.heading: Knowledge Injection
sections.text: Enabled by default, knowledge claims are injected descriptively — as project facts, not as commands. | Default Types | Not Injected | | convention | bug | | decision | discovery | | | note | Only active, durable claims are injected. A claim is eligible when: claim_class = 'claim' (not a hypothesis or raw observation) not dismissed not superseded freshness is in an active state Good — descriptive: Project fact: API routes live in src/server/routes/. Bad — prescriptive: Always use src/server/routes/ because the knowledge base says so. Preferences in static_rules are prescriptive (those are your team's rules). Knowledge is descriptive (those are project facts the agent should *know*).

sections.heading: Context Injection
sections.text: Selected project-context sections are appended to the compiled output. Defaults: overview architecture Configure which sections to include by editing the canonical rules record.

sections.heading: Token Budgeting
sections.text: Each compiler knows its approximate token ceiling. Large-budget tools receive the full combined payload; smaller-budget tools get a progressively condensed form. Compilation remains deterministic — if the budget forces a trim, the trim is reproducible. No LLM is required for rules compilation in v0.9.9.

sections.heading: Enabled Tools, Not Default Tools
sections.text: sfs rules init does not enable every possible tool. Only explicitly selected or inferred tools are compiled. This avoids generating CLAUDE.md for a team that has never used Claude Code, or .cursorrules for a team that doesn't touch Cursor.

sections.heading: Hook-based injection (Claude Code)
sections.text: Claude Code only Hook-based injection requires native hook support in the AI tool. As of v0.10.1, Claude Code is the only supported tool with that capability. File-based compile remains the universal path for codex, cursor, copilot, and gemini. SessionFS can inject compiled rules through Claude Code's SessionStart hook instead of (or alongside) a CLAUDE.md file. Every time Claude Code starts a session, the hook runs sfs rules emit and pipes the latest compiled rules into the system prompt. | | File-based compile | Hook-based injection | | Tools | claude-code, codex, cursor, copilot, gemini | claude-code only | | Source of truth | CLAUDE.md on disk | local rule cache (sfs rules compile / sfs rules pull) | | Freshness | only as fresh as the last commit | refreshed every Claude Code startup | | File on disk | yes | no | | Commit required | yes (default) | no | The hook reads the local rule cache that sfs rules compile and sfs rules pull populate. It does not hit the network on Claude Code startup, so there is no latency cost and no offline failure mode. If the cache is empty, the hook emits an empty payload and exits cleanly — Claude Code starts normally.

sections.heading: Install
sections.text: sfs hooks install --for claude-code By default the hook is written to ~/.claude/settings.json (--user scope) and applies to every Claude Code session on this machine. To install a project-scoped hook that ships with the repo, use --project: sfs hooks install --for claude-code --project That writes to .claude/settings.json in the current repo root, where it can be committed and shared with teammates. Project-scope hooks layer on top of user-scope hooks. Install is idempotent — running it twice does not duplicate the entry. The SessionFS-managed hook block carries an "sfs:managed": true sentinel so uninstall can find and remove it without touching other user-defined hooks.

sections.heading: Verify
sections.text: sfs hooks status Lists which scopes have the hook installed across all supported tools. Tools without native hook support are listed as N/A.

sections.heading: Uninstall
sections.text: sfs hooks uninstall --for claude-code Removes the SessionFS-managed entry from settings.json and leaves any other user-defined hooks untouched. Add --project to remove the project-scope hook, --force to skip the confirmation prompt.

sections.heading: Coexistence with CLAUDE.md
sections.text: Hook is additive, not exclusive If both a managed CLAUDE.md and the hook are present, both inject the same rules and Claude Code sees them twice. sfs hooks install warns when it detects this. Pick one mode unless you have a specific reason to layer them. Two reasonable workflows: Hook only. Delete the committed CLAUDE.md (or never compile one) and rely on the hook. Each developer's machine pulls rules with sfs rules pull and re-emits on every startup. No file management, no commits, always fresh — but only works for Claude Code users. File only. Skip the hook entirely. Compile to CLAUDE.md / codex.md / .cursorrules / copilot-instructions.md / GEMINI.md, commit them, and let every tool read its native file. Works for every supported tool and every developer, regardless of whether they have SessionFS installed. A hybrid (committed CLAUDE.md for team baseline + the hook for personal freshness) is supported but produces duplicated context inside Claude Code.

sections.heading: What sfs rules emit prints
sections.text: sfs rules emit --tool claude-code --format hook prints JSON in Claude Code's hook output spec: { "hookSpecificOutput": { "hookEventName": "SessionStart", "additionalContext": "<the compiled rules content>" } } --format file prints the plain compiled body — the same text that would land in CLAUDE.md. Use --format file when you want to pipe the compiled content into another tool or inspect it from the shell. The hook is offline by design. Run sfs rules pull (or sfs rules compile) when you want to refresh the cache.

sections.heading: Resume-Time Rules Sync
sections.text: sfs resume preflights the target tool's project rules file from the current canonical SessionFS rules before launching the tool. The session transfer carries the conversation; resume-time sync makes sure the resumed agent reads the same project contract the rest of the team is using.

sections.heading: Resume Targets
sections.text: Rules sync runs for these four resume-capable tools: claude-code — writes CLAUDE.md codex — writes codex.md copilot — writes .github/copilot-instructions.md gemini — writes GEMINI.md Cursor, Cline, Roo Code, Kilo Code, Antigravity, and Amp are capture-only — they are not resume targets, so resume-time sync does not apply.

sections.heading: Default Flow
sections.text: sfs resume ses_abc123 --in codex Resolve the source session and target project path. Read the source session's rules provenance from manifest["instruction_provenance"] (if present). Resolve the current project and its canonical rules. Compile only the target tool from current canonical rules and write the file (subject to the managed-file safety cases below). Launch the target tool's resume. Typical stderr output: Source session used rules v3 (sessionfs). Current project rules are v5. Synced codex.md from SessionFS rules v5. The default is always the project's current canonical rules, not the source session's historical version. Source session provenance is displayed on stderr for awareness, but it is never used as the runtime default. If you need to know what shaped the original session, check the provenance fields in the session manifest or the dashboard session detail view. Historical replay (--rules-from-session and --rules-version N) is deferred to v0.9.10. The underlying provenance data is persisted starting in v0.9.9.

sections.heading: Write-Policy Cases
sections.text: | Case | State | Behavior | | A | Target file missing | Compile and write | | B | Target file exists, SessionFS-managed | Overwrite (refresh) | | C | Target file exists, unmanaged | Do not overwrite; warn on stderr; resume continues | | D | Target file exists, unmanaged, --force-rules passed | Overwrite with SessionFS-managed content | A file is managed if it carries the SessionFS managed marker, was created by sfs rules compile, or was explicitly imported via sfs rules init. This is the same ownership model used by sfs rules compile — resume does not implement a second policy.

sections.heading: Flags
sections.text: | Flag | Description | | --no-rules-sync | Skip the preflight entirely for this invocation. Per-invocation only — not persisted. | | --force-rules | Allow Case D: overwrite an unmanaged target-tool rules file with SessionFS-managed content. Applies only to the target tool file for this resume. | --force-rules takes ownership This is a one-time permission, not a temporary override. Once SessionFS writes managed content over an unmanaged file, the file is SessionFS-managed going forward — the managed marker is embedded, and the next sfs resume without --force-rules will refresh it (Case B), not refuse (Case C). That is intended: passing --force-rules opts the file into SessionFS ownership. If you want to stop SessionFS from refreshing the file later, delete the managed marker, remove the file, or skip preflight with --no-rules-sync.

sections.heading: Source Session Provenance Display
sections.text: When the source session's manifest includes instruction_provenance, resume prints a short summary: Source session used rules v3 (sessionfs). Source session used manual rules (hash only). Source session used mixed rule sources. Source session had no recorded rules provenance. When the manifest has no provenance entry (older captures, or the source tool never ran with a rules file), the output shows Source session had no recorded rules provenance. Provenance display is informational only — it does not change what gets written.

sections.heading: When Preflight Is Skipped
sections.text: Rules sync is skipped silently when: the target tool is not one of the four resume targets above --no-rules-sync was passed the target path does not resolve to a git-backed project SessionFS can map to a project record Rules sync is skipped with a short info message when canonical rules are not meaningfully initialized — enabled_tools is empty, static_rules is empty, and tool_overrides is empty: No initialized SessionFS project rules found for this repo. Continuing resume without rules sync. Launching gemini --resume latest ...

sections.heading: Target Tool Not in enabled_tools
sections.text: Resume-time sync compiles the target tool even if it is not listed in the canonical enabled_tools set. Rationale: the user explicitly chose to resume in that tool, and rules portability should carry behavior across tool switches without requiring pre-enabling every possible tool. The compile used by resume is partial and non-versioning: it writes only the target tool's file it does not create a new rules_versions history row it does not mutate canonical enabled_tools If you want the tool added to enabled_tools permanently, run sfs rules init or edit the canonical record directly.

sections.heading: Failure Semantics
sections.text: Rules sync during resume is best-effort and non-fatal. If project lookup, compile, or file write fails, SessionFS prints a warning on stderr and continues the resume. sfs resume always exits 0 for rules-sync failures — the session transfer is more important than rules sync, and a rules preflight issue must not block cross-tool resume.

sections.heading: Preview
sections.text: There is no --dry-run flag on sfs resume. For a preview of what a target tool's file would look like under current canonical rules, use: sfs rules compile --tool codex --dry-run That command shows the exact content resume would write, without touching disk.

sections.heading: Session Instruction Provenance
sections.text: Every captured session records what guided the agent at the time. Four fields are persisted on the session row: | Field | Value | | rules_version | Canonical version ID when SessionFS-managed, else null | | rules_hash | SHA-256 of the tool's rule file at capture time | | rules_source | sessionfs, manual, mixed, or none | | instruction_artifacts | List of artifact objects (see below) | rules_source = mixed means both SessionFS-managed and manual/global artifacts shaped the session (for example, a project CLAUDE.md managed by SessionFS alongside a hand-written global ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md).

sections.heading: Provenance Capture Summary
sections.text: Not all artifact types are equally reconstructable. SessionFS captures full content for managed rules only; everything else is recorded by hash for identity/change verification. | Artifact type | What's captured | Reconstructable? | | SessionFS-managed project rules | version + hash; full text in rules_versions | Yes — any historical version | | Unmanaged project rules (e.g. hand-written CLAUDE.md) | path + hash + source + scope | No — hash only, no content stored | | Global rules/settings (e.g. ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) | path + hash (when SFS_CAPTURE_GLOBAL_RULES=on) | No — hash only | | Nested project agents/skills (.agents/, .claude/commands/, .claude/skills/, etc.) | path + hash per file (up to 30 per directory root) | No — hash only | What is NOT reconstructable SessionFS cannot reconstruct the exact text of unmanaged project rules, global rules, or nested agent/skill files. You can verify whether a file has changed since a session by comparing hashes, but you cannot display a text diff for these artifact types.

sections.heading: Instruction Artifacts
sections.text: Each artifact is a small JSON object: { "artifact_type": "rules_file", "path": "CLAUDE.md", "scope": "project", "source": "sessionfs", "hash": "sha256:9a1c…" } | Field | Values | | artifact_type | rules_file, agent, skill, settings | | scope | project, global | | source | sessionfs, manual, tool |

sections.heading: What Gets Captured
sections.text: Scope differs by artifact type: Managed compiled rule files (source: sessionfs) — version + hash. Full text is stored immutably in rules_versions, so any historical version can be reconstructed. Unmanaged project artifacts (e.g. a hand-written CLAUDE.md) — path + hash + source + scope only. Content is not stored. You can verify identity or detect changes by hash, but cannot reconstruct the original text. Global artifacts (user home directory rules, global agent files) — hash only, discovered best-effort. Content is never stored. Suppressed entirely when SFS_CAPTURE_GLOBAL_RULES=off. Nested skills/agents — project-local files under .agents/, .claude/commands/, .claude/skills/, and similar directories are discovered recursively. Capture is bounded at 30 files per directory root and uses deterministic sorted order. Only path + hash are recorded; content is not stored. Capture is best-effort and non-fatal. If SessionFS cannot classify an artifact, it records what it can and moves on. Session capture never fails because of missing or malformed rule files.

sections.heading: Privacy: SFS_CAPTURE_GLOBAL_RULES
sections.text: Global rule files can leak personal conventions from a developer's home directory into shared session records. To suppress all global instruction artifact capture: export SFS_CAPTURE_GLOBAL_RULES=off When set, SessionFS skips hashing any artifact with scope: global. Project-scope artifacts continue to be captured normally. Default is on. The sfs rules diff <session_id> subcommand — showing current canonical rules vs the rules a specific session used — is deferred to v0.9.10. The underlying data (rules_version + rules_hash + instruction_artifacts) is persisted starting in v0.9.9, so the history is already there when the subcommand lands.

sections.heading: API Reference
sections.text: All endpoints require authentication.

sections.heading: GET /api/v1/projects/{id}/rules
sections.text: Returns the canonical rules record. { "id": "rls_a1b2", "project_id": "prj_xyz", "version": 4, "static_rules": "…markdown…", "include_knowledge": true, "knowledge_types": ["convention", "decision"], "knowledge_max_tokens": 2000, "include_context": true, "context_sections": ["overview", "architecture"], "context_max_tokens": 2000, "enabled_tools": ["claude-code", "codex", "cursor"], "tool_overrides": {}, "updated_at": "2026-04-13T12:00:00Z" }

sections.heading: PUT /api/v1/projects/{id}/rules
sections.text: Update the canonical rules record. Uses optimistic concurrency — send the current version you read, and the server will reject stale writes with 409 Conflict. { "version": 4, "static_rules": "…new markdown…", "enabled_tools": ["claude-code", "codex", "cursor", "gemini"] } Responses: 200 OK — update accepted, returns new record with incremented version 409 Conflict — your version is stale; fetch, merge, retry The server never does last-write-wins.

sections.heading: POST /api/v1/projects/{id}/rules/compile
sections.text: Trigger a server-side compile. Returns the compiled outputs and (if any output hash changed) creates a new rules_versions row. { "version": 5, "changed": true, "compiled_outputs": { "claude-code": { "path": "CLAUDE.md", "content_hash": "sha256:…" }, "codex": { "path": "codex.md", "content_hash": "sha256:…" } } } If nothing changed, changed: false and no new version is created.

sections.heading: GET /api/v1/projects/{id}/rules/versions
sections.text: List the immutable compile history.

sections.heading: GET /api/v1/projects/{id}/rules/versions/{version}
sections.text: Fetch a specific compiled version, including compiled_outputs, knowledge_snapshot, context_snapshot, and content_hash.

sections.heading: MCP Tools
sections.text: When the SessionFS MCP server is connected, AI agents can read the canonical rules and their compiled projection directly. | Tool | Description | | get_rules | Returns the canonical rules record and compilation config for the current repo | | get_compiled_rules | Returns the compiled rule text for a requested tool, or for the current tool if safely inferable | Neither tool allows the agent to modify rules. Agent rule suggestions and auto-accept are explicitly deferred; humans control the canonical record in v0.9.9.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
sections.text: sfs rules compile refuses to overwrite my existing CLAUDE.md That file predates SessionFS and has no managed marker. Either run sfs rules init to import it as the canonical seed, or rerun with --force if you're sure you want to overwrite. I ran sfs rules compile but the compiled file didn't change Compilation is deterministic and idempotent. If no input changed (static rules, knowledge claims, context sections), the output won't change and no new version is created. This is by design. sfs rules push returned 409 Conflict Someone else updated the canonical rules on the server. Run sfs rules pull, re-apply your local changes, and push again. Sessions aren't capturing rules_hash Session capture is best-effort. Check sfs daemon logs for warnings. If the project has no recognized rule file for the active tool, rules_hash will be null and rules_source will be none — that's expected. I don't want my global ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md hashed into session records export SFS_CAPTURE_GLOBAL_RULES=off Project-scope artifacts continue to be captured.

sections.text: Project Context — the content injected into compiled rules Environment Variables — SFS_CAPTURE_GLOBAL_RULES CLI Reference — full syntax for every subcommand
Deploy SessionFS on your own Kubernetes cluster.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.text: SessionFS can be deployed to any Kubernetes cluster using the official Helm chart. The deployment includes: API Server -- FastAPI application handling session CRUD, sync, and authentication MCP Server -- Model Context Protocol bridge (optional, experimental: remote MCP for web clients is not yet supported, so you can leave it disabled with mcp.enabled=false; desktop tools use the local sfs mcp serve) Web Dashboard -- React management interface (optional) PostgreSQL -- Built-in or external database Blob Storage -- Local PVC, Amazon S3, or Google Cloud Storage

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.text: Kubernetes 1.26 or later Helm 3.12 or later kubectl configured for your cluster A PersistentVolume provisioner (most managed clusters include one)

sections.heading: Security Posture
sections.text: SessionFS ships with a hardened default security posture — no action required on your part. The Helm chart and container images meet CIS Kubernetes benchmark and Pod Security Standard restricted profile.

sections.heading: Container images
sections.text: Both sessionfs-api and sessionfs-mcp Docker images: Run as non-root user (UID 10001, dedicated sessionfs system user) Ship with no shell or package manager for the runtime user Are scanned on every release via trivy (CRITICAL/HIGH findings block the pipeline)

sections.heading: Kubernetes SecurityContext
sections.text: Every pod declared by the chart — API, MCP, dashboard, PostgreSQL, and the helm test hook — runs with: | Setting | Value | | runAsNonRoot | true | | runAsUser | 10001 (or 999 for PostgreSQL, matching upstream convention) | | readOnlyRootFilesystem | true | | allowPrivilegeEscalation | false | | capabilities.drop | [ALL] | | seccompProfile.type | RuntimeDefault | The PostgreSQL container mounts emptyDir volumes at /tmp and /var/run/postgresql so it can write its socket directory and temp files even with a read-only root filesystem. The persistent data volume (/var/lib/postgresql/data) uses a standard PVC.

sections.heading: Network policies
sections.text: The chart does not ship NetworkPolicies by default so the chart works on clusters without a CNI that supports them. To apply restrictive NetworkPolicies: # values.yaml security: networkPolicies: enabled: true The API policy allows egress to PostgreSQL, DNS and public addresses on 443 only. If you poll an internal Git server (see Git Registry Polling), the ranges you list in api.registryPolling.allowedPrivateCidrs are added to it.

sections.heading: Secrets
sections.text: All secrets (database credentials, verification secret, encryption key, SMTP credentials, Resend API key) live in Kubernetes Secret objects, never in ConfigMaps. See Secrets Management below.

sections.heading: Verification
sections.text: You can verify the security posture of a rendered chart with trivy: helm template sessionfs sessionfs/sessionfs \ --namespace sessionfs \ > /tmp/rendered.yaml trivy config /tmp/rendered.yaml --severity CRITICAL,HIGH A clean scan should report zero CRITICAL or HIGH misconfigurations.

sections.heading: 1. Add the Helm Repository
sections.text: helm repo add sessionfs https://charts.sessionfs.dev helm repo update

sections.heading: 2. Create a Namespace
sections.text: kubectl create namespace sessionfs

sections.heading: 3. Choose Your Configuration
sections.text: Minimal (development / evaluation) Single replica, built-in PostgreSQL, no ingress: helm install sessionfs sessionfs/sessionfs \ --set mcp.enabled=false \ -f values.minimal.yaml \ --namespace sessionfs Access via port-forward: kubectl port-forward svc/sessionfs-api 8000:8000 -n sessionfs Standard Two API replicas, built-in PostgreSQL, ingress enabled: helm install sessionfs sessionfs/sessionfs \ --set mcp.enabled=false \ --namespace sessionfs \ --set ingress.hosts[0].host=sessionfs.yourdomain.com Production External database, cloud storage, autoscaling, network policies: helm install sessionfs sessionfs/sessionfs \ -f values.production.yaml \ --namespace sessionfs \ --set postgresql.enabled=false \ --set externalDatabase.existingSecret=sessionfs-db \ --set security.existingSecret=sessionfs-secrets \ --set storage.type=s3 \ --set storage.s3.bucket=my-sessionfs-bucket \ --set ingress.enabled=true \ --set ingress.className=nginx \ --set ingress.hosts[0].host=sessionfs.yourdomain.com \ --set ingress.hosts[0].paths.api=/api \ --set ingress.hosts[0].paths.dashboard=/ \ --set mcp.enabled=false

sections.heading: Secrets Management
sections.text: SessionFS requires several secrets for operation. You can either provide them inline in values.yaml (not recommended for production) or reference pre-existing Kubernetes secrets.

sections.heading: Create Secrets Manually
sections.text: # Application secrets kubectl create secret generic sessionfs-secrets \ --namespace sessionfs \ --from-literal=verification-secret="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" \ --from-literal=encryption-key="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" \ --from-literal=resend-api-key="re_your_key_here" # External database (if not using built-in PostgreSQL) kubectl create secret generic sessionfs-db \ --namespace sessionfs \ --from-literal=database-url="postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@host:5432/sessionfs" Then reference them in your Helm values: security: existingSecret: sessionfs-secrets externalDatabase: existingSecret: sessionfs-db

sections.heading: Local (default)
sections.text: Uses a PersistentVolumeClaim. Suitable for single-node clusters or evaluation. storage: type: local local: persistence: enabled: true size: 10Gi

sections.heading: Amazon S3
sections.text: storage: type: s3 s3: bucket: my-sessionfs-bucket # Bucket name only — no slashes region: us-east-1 prefix: "" # Optional key prefix (e.g. "sessionfs/") Using IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts): If your EKS nodes use IRSA, no additional credentials are needed. Attach this IAM policy to the service account role: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject", "s3:DeleteObject", "s3:ListBucket" ], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::my-sessionfs-bucket", "arn:aws:s3:::my-sessionfs-bucket/*" ] } ] } Annotate the service account in your Helm values: serviceAccount: create: true annotations: eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/sessionfs-s3-role Using static credentials: kubectl create secret generic aws-creds \ --namespace sessionfs \ --from-literal=aws-access-key-id=AKIA... \ --from-literal=aws-secret-access-key=... storage: s3: existingSecret: aws-creds

sections.heading: Google Cloud Storage
sections.text: storage: type: gcs gcs: bucket: my-sessionfs-bucket If using Workload Identity, no additional credentials are needed. Otherwise: kubectl create secret generic gcs-creds \ --namespace sessionfs \ --from-file=gcs-credentials-json=./sa-key.json storage: gcs: existingSecret: gcs-creds

sections.heading: Built-in PostgreSQL (default)
sections.text: The chart deploys a single-replica PostgreSQL StatefulSet. Suitable for small deployments. postgresql: enabled: true auth: username: sessionfs database: sessionfs persistence: size: 10Gi

sections.heading: External Database
sections.text: For production, use a managed PostgreSQL service (AWS RDS, GCP Cloud SQL, Azure Database for PostgreSQL). postgresql: enabled: false externalDatabase: host: your-db-host.region.rds.amazonaws.com port: 5432 username: sessionfs database: sessionfs existingSecret: sessionfs-db Important: Do NOT add sslMode or ?sslmode=require to the connection URL. SessionFS handles SSL negotiation automatically via asyncpg. For RDS and Cloud SQL, SSL is negotiated transparently for non-localhost connections.

sections.heading: TLS / HTTPS
sections.text: Configure TLS through your ingress controller. Example with cert-manager: ingress: enabled: true className: nginx annotations: cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod hosts: - host: sessionfs.yourdomain.com paths: api: /api dashboard: / tls: - secretName: sessionfs-tls hosts: - sessionfs.yourdomain.com

sections.heading: Monitoring
sections.text: Enable Prometheus ServiceMonitor (requires prometheus-operator): monitoring: serviceMonitor: enabled: true interval: 30s labels: release: prometheus

sections.heading: Operator metrics
sections.text: The API serves Prometheus metrics at GET /api/v1/admin/metrics: request latency by route, push outcomes and sizes, pulls, handoffs, DLP findings, authentication failures, active users, session count and database pool use. Labels never contain ids or raw paths. The endpoint isn't anonymous: scrape it with a platform admin key or a service key with the admin_metrics:read scope, supplied as a Bearer token in your scrape config. Set api.metrics.scrapeAnnotations: true to add prometheus.io/* scrape annotations to the API pods. A ready-made Grafana dashboard ships in the repository at docs/observability/sessionfs-ops.json.

sections.heading: Upgrading
sections.text: helm repo update helm upgrade sessionfs sessionfs/sessionfs \ --namespace sessionfs \ --reuse-values Database migrations run automatically as a Helm pre-upgrade hook. Upgrading to v0.23.0 runs migrations 084–092 (org helper keys, agent run replay columns, the org digest ledger, transfer proposals, resumable uploads, compile schedules, helper audit rows without a project, Jira tables and helper conversations). All are additive except 090, whose downgrade deletes helper audit rows that have no project. Existing projects keep compile scheduling off until someone turns it on. The scheduled compile, org digest and helper retention only run once something calls their sweeps; see Scheduled sweeps. Upgrading to v0.24.0 runs migration 093 (ticket followers, notifications and per-persona cursors; additive). Also: Helm generated secrets now persist across upgrades. Charts before 0.24.0 generated a new verification-secret and encryption-key on every helm upgrade, which broke stored LLM keys and GitLab/Jira tokens. From 0.24.0 the chart reuses the existing values. If stored keys stopped working after an earlier upgrade, re-enter them once. GitOps flows that render with helm template can't read the cluster: set both values explicitly or use security.existingSecret. Set SFS_VERIFICATION_SECRET to a real secret. Stored LLM keys and integration tokens are encrypted with a key derived from it (existing values still decrypt). With an unset or placeholder value, routes that store or read encrypted secrets return 503 encryption_unavailable outside development. Schedule the ticket digest if you want ticket emails; see Scheduled sweeps. Upgrading to v0.25.0 runs migrations 094 (helper actions) and 095 (helper settings and the token-usage ledger); both are additive. Also: Project editing is limited to the owner and org members. People who only synced a session from a project's repository can still read it and add knowledge entries, tickets, comments and agent runs, but changing the project returns 403 project_edit_forbidden. See Project Context. Review collaborator contributions. Tickets and knowledge notes created by people outside your org now wait for an owner or org member to approve or promote them, and work queues with auto-adopt skip open tickets from non-members until they are approved. Upgrading to v0.26.0 runs migrations 096–100 (project groups, custom Jira templates, group context, Confluence, and two-way Jira sync); all are additive. Also: Schedule the Jira sync and Confluence publish sweeps if you use them, so outbound Jira changes are retried and opted-in Confluence pages stay current; see Scheduled sweeps. Restricted project visibility is off by default. Turning it on for an org limits members to projects they own, created, or reach through a project group. Upgrading to v0.27.0 runs migration 101 (direct-to-person ticket assignment; additive). Existing tickets keep their persona assignments. Work-queue completions whose verdict header can't be parsed are now refused with 422 verdict_header_unparseable; verdict headers may name any reviewer. Upgrading to v0.28.0 runs migrations 102 (ticket due dates, estimates and the ticket change history) and 103 (Jira sprint and parent fields); both are additive. Also: Detect the Jira agile fields once. An existing Jira connection has no sprint or epic-link field until an org admin opens Organization → Integrations → Jira → Connection → Agile fields, runs Detect fields and saves. Until then the publish dialog offers no sprint. See Jira Cloud. Check your sweep keys. A platform_sweeps:run key only works while the admin who minted it and the user it runs as are still platform admins. sfs admin service-keys list now shows a key that has stopped working as inactive, with the reason. See Scheduled sweeps. Optional sweep CronJobs. The chart can now schedule every sweep for you; see Scheduled sweeps. Upgrading to v0.29.0 runs migrations 104 and 105 (meeting transcripts, participants and action items); both are additive. Also: Optional meeting retention sweep. Stored meetings are deleted after the org's retention window (180 days by default); schedule the sweep if you use meetings. See Scheduled sweeps and Meetings. Upgrading to v0.29.1 runs migrations 106 (agent run usage, cost, model, role and loop fields), 107 (service-key attribution on wiki revisions), 108 (the reviewed commit on review verdicts) and 109 (service-key attribution on retrieval audit contexts); all are additive. Existing runs carry no usage, and existing verdicts carry no reviewed commit, so merge readiness reports them as not ready until a reviewer posts a verdict bound to the head commit. Upgrading to v0.29.2 runs migrations 110 (review loop settings on the parent issue and service-key attribution on work queues), 111 (the needs_human work-queue item status) and 112 (the review checklist); all are additive. API keys gain the loops:read and loops:write scopes. No new settings are needed.

sections.heading: Check pod status
sections.text: kubectl get pods -n sessionfs kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n sessionfs

sections.heading: View API logs
sections.text: kubectl logs -n sessionfs -l app.kubernetes.io/component=api --tail=100

sections.heading: Check migration job
sections.text: kubectl get jobs -n sessionfs -l app.kubernetes.io/component=migration kubectl logs -n sessionfs job/sessionfs-migrate-<revision>

sections.heading: Run Helm tests
sections.text: helm test sessionfs --namespace sessionfs

sections.heading: Common Issues
sections.text: Pods stuck in Pending: Check that your cluster has a PersistentVolume provisioner and sufficient resources. Database connection errors: Verify the database URL and credentials. For external databases, ensure network connectivity (security groups, VPC peering). Ingress not working: Confirm your ingress controller is installed and the ingress class name matches. Security context errors (runAsNonRoot): SessionFS images currently run as root. Set security contexts in values.yaml: api: podSecurityContext: runAsNonRoot: false asyncpg SSL errors: Do not add ?sslmode=require to the database URL — SessionFS handles SSL parameter translation internally. For RDS/Cloud SQL, asyncpg negotiates SSL automatically for non-localhost connections.

sections.heading: API Documentation
sections.text: After deployment, the API is documented via OpenAPI: Swagger UI: https://your-domain/api/docs ReDoc: https://your-domain/api/redoc OpenAPI JSON: https://your-domain/api/openapi.json Key endpoints: | Endpoint | Description | | POST /api/v1/auth/signup | Create account | | GET /api/v1/auth/me | Current user profile | | GET /api/v1/sessions | List sessions | | POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/audit | Run LLM Judge | | GET /health | Health check |

sections.heading: Git Registry Polling
sections.text: Organization marketplace registries on https:// can be polled by the API, which publishes each new matching tag through the normal publish checks (see Skills Marketplace). Polling only runs when the poller endpoint is called, never in user requests. Schedule it. Mint a service key with only the skills_registry:poll scope (a platform admin must mint it), store it in a Secret, and enable the CronJob: sfs admin service-keys create --org <ORG_ID> --name registry-poller --scope skills_registry:poll --output-key > key.txt kubectl create secret generic sessionfs-registry-poll --from-file=registry-poll-api-key=key.txt -n sessionfs api: registryPolling: enabled: true cronJob: enabled: true schedule: "*/5 * * * *" existingSecret: sessionfs-registry-poll The CronJob only sends one request to the API service; the fetch happens in the API pods. Overlapping runs are safe (each registry is leased while it is polled, and the lease is renewed as it works). Timing: each registry gets a 300 s fetch budget (timeoutSeconds) plus 300 s for publishing; a run stops claiming registries once that would overrun runBudgetSeconds (1200 s), and the CronJob's curl and job deadlines are 1320 s and 1380 s. If you raise the budget, keep your own cron's timeout above budget + 120 s. maxPerOrg (10) caps polling-enabled registries per organization and maxPerOrgPerRun (2) keeps one organization from starving the others. Without the CronJob, run sfs admin registries poll from any cron with SESSIONFS_API_KEY set to that key. Network egress. The API pods need outbound HTTPS to your Git hosts. By default only globally routable addresses are fetched; private ranges, loopback, link-local and cloud metadata addresses are refused, every resolved address is checked, Git is pinned to the checked address (no DNS rebinding) and redirects are not followed. To poll an internal GitLab, opt in explicitly with its range (loopback, link-local and metadata stay refused): api: registryPolling: allowedPrivateCidrs: - 10.20.0.0/16 This sets SFS_REGISTRY_POLL_ALLOWED_PRIVATE_CIDRS and, with security.networkPolicies.enabled, opens API egress to that range on 443. Outbound proxies are not used by the poller (its Git environment is replaced to keep the address pin effective). Credentials for private repositories. Create one Secret per credential with a token, the org id allowed to use it and the hosts it may be sent to (all three required), and optionally a username (GitLab deploy tokens need theirs), and list it: kubectl create secret generic acme-gitlab -n sessionfs \ --from-literal=token=<deploy-token> --from-literal=org=<ORG_ID> \ --from-literal=username=gitlab+deploy-token-12 --from-literal=hosts=gitlab.internal.example api: registryPolling: credentialSecrets: - acme-gitlab The org's admin then sets credential_secret_ref to k8s:acme-gitlab. Alternatively expose a credential as SFS_REGISTRY_CRED_<NAME> with SFS_REGISTRY_CRED_<NAME>_ORG and SFS_REGISTRY_CRED_<NAME>_HOSTS (via api.env from a Secret) and reference it as env:SFS_REGISTRY_CRED_<NAME>. A credential bound to another organization or host, or missing either binding, is refused; the organization only sees a generic message and the API log records the reason. The token reaches Git only as an HTTP header for that registry's origin; it is never put in a URL, an argument list, a response or a log. The API image includes git (2.44 or newer is required). Clones go to a /tmp emptyDir (api.registryPolling.tmpSizeLimit, default 1 GiB) because the root filesystem is read-only. Set api.registryPolling.enabled: false to turn polling off entirely.

sections.heading: Email Configuration
sections.text: SessionFS supports three email providers: Resend (SaaS), SMTP (enterprise), or none (air-gapped).

sections.heading: Resend (default for cloud)
sections.text: helm install sessionfs sessionfs/sessionfs \ --set mcp.enabled=false \ --set email.provider=resend \ --set email.resend.apiKey=$RESEND_KEY

sections.heading: SMTP (enterprise / internal)
sections.text: helm install sessionfs sessionfs/sessionfs \ --set mcp.enabled=false \ --set email.provider=smtp \ --set email.smtp.host=smtp.company.internal \ --set email.smtp.port=587 \ --set email.smtp.username=sessionfs \ --set email.smtp.password=$SMTP_PASS \ --set email.fromAddress=sessionfs@company.com For implicit SSL (port 465): --set email.smtp.port=465 \ --set email.smtp.ssl=true \ --set email.smtp.tls=false

sections.heading: No email (air-gapped)
sections.text: helm install sessionfs sessionfs/sessionfs \ --set mcp.enabled=false \ --set email.provider=none \ --set api.env.SFS_REQUIRE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION=false Users will be auto-verified on signup. Email notifications (handoff, retention) will be logged but not sent.

sections.heading: SMTP with Kubernetes Secrets
sections.text: kubectl create secret generic smtp-creds \ --namespace sessionfs \ --from-literal=username=sessionfs \ --from-literal=password=$SMTP_PASS helm install sessionfs sessionfs/sessionfs \ --set mcp.enabled=false \ --set email.provider=smtp \ --set email.smtp.host=smtp.company.internal \ --set email.smtp.existingSecret=smtp-creds

sections.heading: Automatic (Helm)
sections.text: Migrations run automatically on helm install and helm upgrade. On upgrades the migration job is a pre-upgrade hook that finishes before new API pods start (hook weight -5). On a fresh install the job is created alongside the database and its credentials and retries until the database is ready; API pods report ready only once the schema is migrated, so new code never serves against an old schema.

sections.heading: ArgoCD
sections.text: If you deploy SessionFS with ArgoCD (through its Helm source, or by rendering the chart with helm template), the chart orders the rollout with ArgoCD sync waves: the database and its credentials come up first, then the migration job runs, then (in local license mode) the license is seeded, and only after those succeed do the API and MCP deployments roll to the new version. Nothing to configure: the annotations ship in the chart. As a safety net, API pods only report ready (/health/ready) once the database schema has been migrated for their version, so they never take traffic against an old schema, and the API logs a clear error at startup if the schema does not match. /health/ready returns 200 {"status":"ready","schema":"current"} (or "ahead" after an image rollback) and 503 {"status":"not_ready","schema":"behind"} (or "missing", or "unknown" while a new pod cannot reach the database). It is served on the API pod and, through the chart's ingress, at https://<your-host>/health/ready; /health on the ingress host is the dashboard's own liveness check. If you ever run alembic upgrade head by hand, restart the API deployment afterwards (kubectl rollout restart deployment/sessionfs-api) so its database connections pick up the new schema.

sections.heading: Manual
sections.text: kubectl exec -it deploy/sessionfs-api -- alembic upgrade head

sections.heading: Troubleshooting Migrations
sections.text: If the migration job fails, check logs: kubectl logs job/sessionfs-migrate-<revision> -n sessionfs If the schema does not match the running code (for example, a migration was skipped), the API logs a clear error at startup naming both revisions and the fix. Check the API logs if authenticated routes start failing with "column ... does not exist".

sections.heading: Auditing Operator Overrides
sections.text: Operators sometimes need to act without the normal consent flows: move a user's personal project into the organization while the owner is unavailable, merge a duplicate account, or change a tier. Every platform-admin action the API performs writes a row to the admin_actions table with the admin, the time, an optional reason and, for overrides, the state before and after the change. Use the paved paths below so the audit trail answers "who changed this, when, and why" without reconstructing terminal history. Move a project into an organization (the owner does not need to initiate or accept): sfs admin override project-transfer proj_abc123 --to-org org_xyz --expect-from personal \ --reason "Owner on leave; care team needs access (ticket OPS-412)" The move, an accepted transfer record, the audit entry and organization audit events commit in one transaction. Merged projects are refused, open work assigned to org personas the destination lacks is refused unless --force, and any pending transfer for the project is cancelled. The owner of an organization project must be a member of that organization: if the current owner is not (for example, they have left), add --new-owner <user-id> with an active member, and ownership changes in the same transaction. --expect-from makes a retried command safe: it refuses if the project is no longer where you expected it. Merge a duplicate account. For a duplicate signup (for example a typo in the email), preview and then apply the merge instead of reassigning rows by hand: sfs admin override user-merge <duplicate-id> <kept-id> --reason "Typo in email domain (ticket OPS-77)" # dry run sfs admin override user-merge <duplicate-id> <kept-id> --reason "Typo in email domain (ticket OPS-77)" --apply This calls POST /api/v1/admin/users/{source_id}/merge-into/{target_id}. The dry run lists the rows that would move; --apply reassigns them, deduplicates org memberships (higher role wins), revokes the duplicate's API keys, deactivates it and writes one user_merge audit entry, all in one transaction. It refuses when both accounts hold an active plan or the duplicate owns marketplace assets or has billing attached; resolve those first. See sfs admin override user-merge. Merge duplicate projects. When the same repository ended up as two projects, the owner can run sfs project merge. When the two projects belong to different users, merge them as an operator: sfs admin override project-merge <duplicate-project-id> <kept-project-id> --reason "Duplicate from an ssh:// remote (OPS-81)" # dry run sfs admin override project-merge <duplicate-project-id> <kept-project-id> --reason "Duplicate from an ssh:// remote (OPS-81)" --apply Everything moves to the kept project and the duplicate becomes a redirect to it, with one project_merge audit entry. Since v0.22.0 the server stores one canonical remote for every URL form of a repository (ssh://, git://, scp remotes with any user, trailing slashes), so new duplicates of this kind no longer appear. Upgrading runs migration 083, which rewrites stored remotes to the canonical form and prints any project it left alone because its canonical remote already belongs to another project: those are the pairs to merge. See sfs admin override project-merge. Record a change made by hand. When you have to change data directly in the database, record it afterwards: sfs admin override record --action user_merge --target-type user --target-id <kept-user-id> \ --reason "Duplicate signup with a typo in the email domain; 62 rows reassigned" \ --before-file before.json --after-file after.json Recorded entries are stored with source operator_record: the server attests who recorded them and when, not that the described change happened. Review the log: sfs admin audit-log --target-type project --target-id proj_abc123 sfs admin audit-log --source operator_record --json PUT /api/v1/admin/users/{id}/tier, PUT /api/v1/admin/orgs/{id}/tier and POST /api/v1/admin/orgs/{id}/force-transfer-owner also accept an optional reason in their request body and record the before and after values. The audit log does not protect against someone with direct database access; restrict who holds database credentials, and use database-level logging if you need that guarantee.

sections.heading: Scheduled Sweeps
sections.text: SessionFS has no scheduler of its own. These features run only when a scheduled job calls their sweep endpoint. Authenticate with a platform admin key or, better for cron, a platform_sweeps:run service key: it works only while the platform admin who minted it and the user it runs as are both still active platform admins. Since v0.28.0 this is visible up front: minting or rotating such a key returns a minter_tier_coupling warning, sfs admin service-keys list shows a key that has stopped working as inactive with the reason (coupling_ok and coupling_reason in the API), and a request with that key gets a 403 naming the cause and the fix. Making someone a platform admin just long enough to mint a key doesn't work: the key stops as soon as they're demoted. Mint sweep keys as a user who stays a platform admin. See API keys. | Sweep | Endpoint | What it does | | KB compile | POST /api/v1/admin/sweeps/kb-compile | Compiles every project whose schedule (nightly / weekly) has elapsed or whose waiting-claims threshold is reached. Deterministic compiler only, one transaction per project; body {"limit": N} (default 100, max 1000) | | Org digest | POST /api/v1/admin/sweeps/org-digest | Sends the weekly activity digest to owners and admins of Team and Enterprise orgs. Sends once per org per week however often it runs, and always covers the last completed week, so run it daily | | Helper retention | POST /api/v1/admin/sweeps/helper-retention | Deletes session helper messages older than the org's helper_retention_days (default 90), then removes empty threads | | Ticket digest | POST /api/v1/admin/sweeps/ticket-notifications | Emails each user one digest of their pending ticket notifications, following their preference (off, your_turn by default, or all). Access is re-checked before anything is sent (v0.24.0) | | Jira sync | POST /api/v1/admin/sweeps/jira-sync | Delivers queued outbound Jira changes (status moves, comments, completion evidence) with retry and backoff, and expires old ones. Body {"limit": N, "budget_seconds": S} (defaults 100 and 50 s) (v0.26.0). See Jira Cloud | | Meeting retention | POST /api/v1/admin/sweeps/meeting-retention | Deletes stored meeting transcripts older than the org's meeting_retention_days (default 180) and meetings deleted more than 30 days ago, together with their participants and action items (v0.29.0). See Meetings | | Confluence publish | POST /api/v1/admin/sweeps/confluence-publish | Republishes opted-in wiki pages and, where the mapping allows it, the context document; unchanged pages are skipped and pages edited in Confluence are never overwritten (v0.26.0). See Confluence Cloud | Suggested schedules: KB compile every 15 minutes, org digest, helper retention and meeting retention daily, ticket digest every 10 minutes, Jira sync every minute (its first retry is due one minute after a failed delivery; without the job a failed change never reaches Jira) and Confluence publish every 15 minutes. Every sweep is safe to run repeatedly and returns immediately when there is nothing to do. Example CronJob for the KB compile sweep, every 15 minutes: apiVersion: batch/v1 kind: CronJob metadata: name: sessionfs-kb-compile namespace: sessionfs spec: schedule: "*/15 * * * *" jobTemplate: spec: template: spec: restartPolicy: OnFailure containers: - name: sweep image: curlimages/curl:latest args: ["-s", "-X", "POST", "https://your-api/api/v1/admin/sweeps/kb-compile", "-H", "Authorization: Bearer $(SWEEP_KEY)", "-H", "Content-Type: application/json", "-d", '{"limit": 100}'] env: - name: SWEEP_KEY valueFrom: secretKeyRef: name: sessionfs-sweep-key key: token The chart can create the CronJob for each sweep. They are all off by default and each needs a Secret holding a platform_sweeps:run service key (existingSecret is required when enabled): api: ticketNotifications: enabled: true cronJob: schedule: "*/10 * * * *" # every 10 minutes existingSecret: sessionfs-sweep-key secretKey: ticket-notifications-api-key orgDigest: enabled: true cronJob: schedule: "0 4 * * *" # daily existingSecret: sessionfs-sweep-key secretKey: org-digest-api-key kbCompile: enabled: true cronJob: schedule: "*/15 * * * *" # every 15 minutes existingSecret: sessionfs-sweep-key secretKey: kb-compile-api-key helperRetention: enabled: true cronJob: schedule: "0 3 * * *" # daily existingSecret: sessionfs-sweep-key secretKey: helper-retention-api-key jiraSync: enabled: true cronJob: schedule: "* * * * *" # every minute existingSecret: sessionfs-sweep-key secretKey: jira-sync-api-key confluencePublish: enabled: true cronJob: schedule: "*/15 * * * *" # every 15 minutes existingSecret: sessionfs-sweep-key secretKey: confluence-publish-api-key meetingRetention: enabled: true cronJob: schedule: "30 3 * * *" # daily existingSecret: sessionfs-sweep-key secretKey: meeting-retention-api-key Each CronJob pod sends one authenticated request to the API sweep endpoint and exits; the work itself runs in the API pods. The key is read from the Secret into an environment variable and never printed, and the pods don't mount a Kubernetes service account token. When network policies are enabled, the chart adds an ingress rule so each enabled CronJob can reach the API, and an egress policy that lets the CronJob pods reach only DNS and the API, so the key can't be sent anywhere else. With email.provider=none the digest sweep sends nothing but still records each org's run. Digest links use SFS_DASHBOARD_URL, falling back to an explicitly set SFS_APP_URL, and are left out when neither is set.

sections.heading: Rate Limiting
sections.text: Rate limiting is per API key, defaulting to 120 requests per minute. api: rateLimitPerMinute: 120 # Requests per minute per API key # Set to 0 to disable rate limiting (recommended for internal deployments) Or via environment variable: api: env: SFS_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE: "0" # Disable for internal deployments

sections.heading: Architecture
sections.text: SessionFS uses a reverse proxy architecture. All external traffic routes through the dashboard nginx, which proxies /api/ and /mcp/ to internal ClusterIP services: Internet -> Ingress -> Dashboard Nginx -> API Service (ClusterIP) -> MCP Service (ClusterIP) -> Static Files The ingress template routes everything to the dashboard service. Do NOT create separate ingress rules for /api or /mcp — this causes ALB target groups to stay in "unused" state.

sections.heading: Upload size limit
sections.text: The dashboard nginx has client_max_body_size configured (default 100MB). Override in values.yaml: dashboard: clientMaxBodySize: "200m"

sections.heading: Upload time limit
sections.text: Pushing a large session waits for the server to DLP-scan and store it. The dashboard nginx waits up to apiProxyTimeout (default 300s) for the API, and the CLI and daemon wait up to SFS_UPLOAD_TIMEOUT seconds (default 300). If very large sessions time out, raise both together and keep any load balancer idle timeout in front of the chart at least as long: dashboard: apiProxyTimeout: "600s" export SFS_UPLOAD_TIMEOUT=600 # or upload_timeout = 600 under [sync] in ~/.sessionfs/config.toml The chart's Ingress passes matching timeout and body-size annotations to ingress-nginx by default; anything you set under ingress.annotations takes precedence. Other ingress controllers need their own timeout set. Sessions over 8 MiB are uploaded in resumable parts (8 MiB by default), each retried on its own; an interrupted push resends only the missing parts, and unfinished uploads expire after 24 hours. Older servers get the single-request push automatically.

sections.heading: Session helper streaming
sections.text: The session helper streams answers as Server-Sent Events from POST /api/v1/helper/turns. The chart's dashboard nginx passes that route through unbuffered with a 600-second timeout. If you put another proxy or load balancer in front of the chart, turn off response buffering for that path and allow long-lived responses (the API sends a keep-alive comment every 15 seconds).

sections.heading: GitLab Integration
sections.text: SessionFS supports GitLab merge request comments (cloud and self-hosted instances).

sections.heading: Setup
sections.text: Create a GitLab personal or project access token with api scope Add a webhook to your GitLab project: URL: https://your-sessionfs-domain/webhooks/gitlab Secret token: the per-user secret you save in step 3, or a server-wide secret set in your Helm values (SFS_GITLAB_WEBHOOK_SECRET) Events: "Merge request events" Save your instance URL, access token and webhook secret in the dashboard under Settings → Integrations → GitLab (or with PUT /api/v1/settings/gitlab). The token and secret are write-only: neither the dashboard nor GET /api/v1/settings/gitlab shows them again. To accept one server-wide secret instead, set it via Helm: api: env: SFS_GITLAB_WEBHOOK_SECRET: "your-webhook-secret" Self-hosted installs usually point at an internal GitLab, so the chart allows private, loopback and plain-http instance URLs by default (SFS_GITLAB_ALLOW_PRIVATE_HOSTS=true). Link-local and cloud-metadata addresses stay blocked either way, and the host is re-checked before every request. To restrict the integration to public https GitLab hosts, set: api: gitlab: allowPrivateHosts: false The same applies to custom LLM endpoints (the base_url users can set for the LLM judge and narrative summaries): the chart allows private, loopback and plain-http endpoints by default (SFS_LLM_ALLOW_PRIVATE_HOSTS=true) so an in-cluster Ollama, vLLM or LiteLLM works, and link-local and cloud-metadata addresses stay blocked. To allow only public https endpoints: api: llm: allowPrivateHosts: false GitLab MR comments include the same AI session context as GitHub PR comments, including audit findings when available.

sections.heading: Environment Variables
sections.text: See Environment Variables Reference for the complete list of SFS_* configuration options.

sections.heading: Further Troubleshooting
sections.text: See Troubleshooting Guide for common errors, sync debugging, and Kubernetes-specific issues.

The session helper answers questions over the sessions and project knowledge you can already read: "find the session where we fixed the SSO redirect", "what did we decide about Redis and why?", "summarize these three sessions". It searches sessions, reads summaries and excerpts, searches project knowledge and finds sessions that touched a file, then answers with citations back to the sessions and messages it used. It sees exactly what you can see: your own sessions, the projects you can access, and your org memberships. An org admin doesn't get a wider view through it. For questions about SessionFS itself — how to set up Jira, what Auto Narrative does, which commands and settings exist — it searches the official docs instead of guessing. Those answers cite the docs pages and sections they drew from alongside the session citations, and each link opens the page in a new tab. Available on the Enterprise plan. Added in v0.23.0.

sections.heading: Requirements
sections.text: Enterprise plan. A project-scoped question uses the plan of the project's org, and a group-scoped question the plan of the group's org; otherwise your own plan. Other plans get upgrade_required. A model key you supply. SessionFS never supplies one. For each question the helper uses, in order: your own key, from Settings → Data protection → Security review model; your org's helper key, when an org owner or admin has set one and switched it on; otherwise the request returns 409 helper_key_required. Answers and audit rows record which of the two was used (user or org), never the key.

sections.heading: Supported providers
sections.text: The same provider list powers the security review, the helper, summaries and Jira drafting (v0.24.0): Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini, OpenRouter, DeepSeek, Kimi (Moonshot), xAI (Grok), Mistral, Z.ai (GLM), Qwen (Alibaba Cloud), MiniMax, Groq, Together AI and Fireworks AI. Pick the provider, paste your key and choose a model: Fetch models lists the models your key can use, and any model id can be typed in. A custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint URL (LiteLLM, vLLM, Ollama, or a regional endpoint) replaces the provider default. A saved key is only ever sent to the provider or endpoint it was saved with; changing either requires entering the key again. Gateways that reject temperature, top_p or reasoning settings for a reasoning model are handled automatically: the request is retried once without them, and that is remembered for the endpoint and model.

sections.heading: Where to use it
sections.text: Dashboard. Ask the helper in the sidebar or the Cmd+K palette opens a drawer. The same button on a project or session page scopes the question to it, and the drawer's scope menu also lists the project groups you can see. The drawer remembers the scope you last picked for the rest of the browser tab, so a new conversation starts where you left off. The memory belongs to the account you're signed in with: signing in as someone else in the same tab starts from All my sessions. Answers stream in with citations; a citation opens the session at the exact message and highlights it (/sessions/<id>?msg=<n>). The composer stays pinned at the bottom, and earlier threads and New are always at hand. Retrying a failed answer doesn't save your question twice. Ticket and wiki citations become links as soon as the answer finishes, without reloading the conversation. Ids in an answer are clickable. A ticket id (tk_…) opens a preview right over the conversation, with its status, priority, assignee, project, description and latest comments, plus Open ticket for the full view. Project (proj_…) and session (ses_…) ids open their pages, and when the scoped project has a single GitHub-verified repo, PR #123 and commit SHAs link to GitHub. Ids inside code blocks stay as text. CLI. sfs helper ask "Where did we fix the SSO redirect?" streams the answer to the terminal; --project, --group (a group id pg_… or slug) or --session scope it. sfs helper conversations list|show|delete manages threads, and sfs helper status shows whether the helper is available and which key it would use. See the CLI reference. MCP. The ask_session_helper tool returns the whole answer with its citations, so an agent can ask without shelling out. It takes project, group_id or session_ids to scope the question. See MCP Server.

sections.heading: Scope a question to a project group
sections.text: A question can cover a whole project group instead of one project (v0.28.0). Pick the group in the drawer's scope menu, run sfs helper ask --group SLUG "...", or pass group_id to ask_session_helper. A question takes one scope: a project, a group or a list of sessions. Only what you can read. The helper searches sessions, knowledge, tickets and wiki pages from the group's member projects that you can read, and nothing else.
