With restricted project visibility, a member project you can't read stays out. The group's overview. When the group has a compiled overview and you can read every project that went into it, that overview is added to the prompt, redacted with your DLP policy like everything else sent to the model. If you can't read one of those projects, the overview is left out rather than sent in part. Plans. Project groups need the Team plan or above on the group's org, and the helper needs Enterprise. Not found. A group that doesn't exist and a group you can't see both return 404 group_not_found.

sections.heading: Actions
sections.text: Besides answering, the helper can propose these changes for you: Turn Auto Narrative on or off for one or more projects. Move sessions to Trash, for example to clean up old scratch sessions or "every session that used DeepSeek". Create a ticket with a title, description, acceptance criteria, priority and optional assignee. When you ask for it, the same confirmation also publishes the new ticket to Jira (Enterprise, with a Jira mapping for the project). You can name a different Jira project (one mapped to a SessionFS project you can edit), a story template (pinned to its current version until you confirm) and an active or future sprint (v0.28.0). Assign a ticket to a persona or directly to a teammate. You can name a persona, a teammate's email, or a display name; a display name goes to the persona that represents that person when there is one, otherwise to the person. Comment on a ticket with a plain user comment, optionally sent to the linked Jira issue too when the org forwards comments to Jira. Link a ticket to an existing Jira issue by its key (v0.27.0). Overwrite one side of a linked ticket and Jira issue: replace the Jira issue's summary and description with the ticket's, or the ticket's title and description with the issue's. See Link an existing issue. Jira proposals are refused up front when they can't work, for example when the ticket has no Jira link, you can't edit it, or the org doesn't forward comments to Jira. Every Jira condition is checked again when you confirm. The helper never makes a change itself. Each proposal appears in the answer as a card listing every target and what will happen to it: *will change*, *unchanged*, or *skipped* with the reason. Nothing changes until you press Confirm (or Move to Trash); Cancel drops it. Proposals expire after 15 minutes. Confirming applies exactly the targets on the card, with your own permissions. Access is checked again for each target when you confirm, and the card shows which targets applied and which failed. Turning Auto Narrative on or off needs change rights on the project (its owner or a member of its organization); a project you can only view is skipped as *You can view but not edit this project*. Ticket cards are editable before you confirm: the create form's title, description, acceptance criteria, priority and assignee are pre-filled from the helper's draft and can be changed, and the comment form's body can be edited the same way. Confirm creates the ticket or comment under your own name and links the new ticket from the card. A ticket a captured-session reader creates starts *suggested* so a project editor can approve it; a helper comment is always a plain comment, never a trusted review verdict. To trash sessions by model, provider, project, tool or date range, the helper hands those filters to the server, which picks the matching sessions itself — it never trashes sessions just because their text mentions a model. One proposal covers at most 100 sessions, the most recently active first. When more match, the helper says how many are left; confirm, then ask again for the next batch. Cleanup is reversible: sessions go to Trash. Restore them from Sessions → Trash within 30 days; after that they can be purged for good.

sections.heading: Sessions by model
sections.text: Each session records the AI model it ran on, as reported by the tool that captured it. Ask "which models do my sessions use?" or "show my sessions that used DeepSeek" and the helper: lists the models across your sessions with list_session_models: session counts, the capturing tools, and first and last dates; filters the session tools (search_sessions, list_recent_sessions, sessions_touching_path) by model or provider. Matching ignores case and catches a whole family, so deepseek finds both deepseek-v4-pro and deepseek-flash. Several values match any of them, and unknown finds sessions with no recorded model. These sessions are grouped the same way as in the dashboard's model filter; narrows by date with days, since or until (last activity, in UTC). search_sessions doesn't need a keyword when a filter is given. Every session line shows its model, for example [claude-code] model: deepseek-v4-pro. A Claude Code session can show a DeepSeek model when Claude Code was pointed at DeepSeek. Long lists come in pages (up to 100 sessions, or 20 for a keyword search) that start with "Showing 1–100 of 240"; the helper pages through with offset. In a conversation scoped to one project, the helper can't reach another project's sessions: it tells you to start an unscoped conversation instead.

sections.heading: Who is asking (v0.29.0)
sections.text: The helper knows who you are, so "my tickets" and "what is assigned to me" work. A name is looked up as a person, a persona or a project group (by name, slug or abbreviation), and tickets assigned to either a persona or a person are found. It still reads only what you can already see.

sections.heading: Project work items
sections.text: Beyond sessions and project knowledge, the helper reads the project's own work items and people — still only what you can already see: Tickets — list_tickets / get_ticket. Work items (ids like tk_…), with status, priority, assignee, project, acceptance criteria, dependencies and the last 10 comments. Wiki pages — list_wiki_pages / get_wiki_page. A project's knowledge pages, with the body capped at 20k characters. Agent runs — list_agent_runs / get_agent_run. CI review runs, with persona, status, severity and findings. Personas — list_personas. The project's own personas and the org personas visible from it, with role and active state. Jira issues — get_jira_issue. The Jira issue linked to a ticket: summary, status, assignee, priority, labels, components, last update and the latest comments, read through the org's Jira connection. It takes a ticket id, never a free-form Jira key, so it can only read an issue a ticket you can see already points at. Comments that came from Jira are marked as such on get_ticket. Meetings — search_meetings, list_recent_meetings, get_meeting, list_my_meeting_actions. Stored meeting transcripts: search titles and text, list the newest, read one as numbered lines (L12| …, at most 400 lines per call, with a range to read on) together with its participants and extracted action items and decisions, and list the pending action items owned by you or by a persona that represents you. Scope is a hard filter: a project-scoped question reads that project's meetings only; a group-scoped question reads the group's own meetings plus the meetings of its member projects you can read; a session-scoped question reads the meetings of the sessions' projects; an unscoped question reads every meeting you can read. Group meetings also need standing on the group and a plan with project groups. Transcript text is untrusted data: it is already DLP-redacted when stored, and the helper treats instructions inside it as text. These tools follow the same plan gates as the matching pages: tickets and agent runs need the project's plan to include them, and personas need it to include personas. On a project whose plan doesn't, the helper says they aren't available instead of reading them. Long fields are capped with a visible "…[truncated]" (ticket descriptions, each acceptance criterion, run summaries and finding messages), and one tool result is capped at 40,000 characters. In a conversation scoped to a project, nothing from any other project comes back. A session counts as the project's when it is attributed to it, or when it has no project and sits on one of the project's repositories. A session attributed to another project stays out, even on a shared repository. The helper may cite a ticket or wiki page only after one of its tools returned it in that question, and only when it belongs to a project you can read inside the conversation's scope; any other [ticket:…] or [wiki:…] marker is removed from the answer. A meeting passage is cited as [meeting:<id> L<first>-<last>]. The marker is kept only when a tool returned that meeting earlier in this conversation (this question or a previous one in the same thread), you can still read it in the conversation's scope, and the line range lies inside the transcript (1 <= first <= last <= line count); anything else is removed from the answer. In the API a kept citation is {"kind": "meeting", "meeting_id", "line_start", "line_end", "title", "project_id", "group_id", "at"}, and a streaming turn sends it as a meeting_citation event. Every line a tool returns carries a source date as YYYY-MM-DD (Nd ago). When the newest source for a claim is more than 7 days old, the helper says so with "As of \<date\>, ..." so you can see the information may be stale.

sections.heading: Org AI key
sections.text: Enterprise org owners and admins can set one provider, model, API key and optional base URL for members who don't have a key of their own: Organization → Policies → AI key for the session helper, or GET/PUT/DELETE /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/llm-settings. The key is encrypted at rest and never shown again after saving; only its last four characters are displayed. It can be switched off without deleting it. A custom base URL goes through the same address checks as other user-supplied LLM endpoints. Fetch models lists the models the key can use, the same way as the personal key form (v0.28.0). When the provider can't list them, type the model id yourself. Model lookups are rate-limited per user (429 models_rate_limited). POST /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/llm-settings/models does the same. Test connection sends one tiny chat request with the form's values (the stored key only when the provider and base URL are unchanged) and shows the endpoint, model and latency, or why it failed. POST /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/llm-settings/test does the same. Leave the base URL empty to use the provider's own API. It must be an API address, not a console: https://platform.deepseek.com is refused with "use https://api.deepseek.com". Saving a new base URL runs the test first; a timeout or rate limit still saves, with a warning.

sections.heading: Configure the assistant
sections.text: Model settings live at two scopes — your own (GET/PUT /api/v1/settings/helper) and the org's (GET/PUT /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/helper-settings; owners/admins write, members read the effective values) — and every turn resolves an effective set from them. Each field is optional; anything unset falls back to the default. | Setting | Range | Default | | max_output_tokens | 256–32000 (integer) | 4096 | | temperature | 0–2, or null for the provider default | 0 | | top_p | 0–1 | unset (not sent) | | max_tool_steps | 1–20 (integer) | 8 | | reasoning_effort | off · low · medium · high | unset | | answer_style | concise · detailed | concise | max_tool_steps counts tool rounds: after its last allowed round the model always gets one more step to answer. On Anthropic, setting top_p drops temperature, since the API refuses both together. Settings are stored apart from the LLM keys: saving them never creates a key, and deleting or rotating a key never touches the settings, instructions or budget. Plan. The personal routes need the helper on your plan (403 upgrade_required otherwise); the org PUT needs the org's Enterprise plan. The org GET works on any plan and reports plan_includes_helper. Updating. PUT merges: a field you leave out keeps its value and an explicit null clears it, and inside settings each key merges the same way. {"monthly_token_budget": 2000} changes only the budget; {"instructions": "…"} leaves the budget and settings alone. For temperature, top_p, reasoning_effort and the ceilings, null is itself the value (provider default, not sent, no ceiling). Precedence. A turn using your own key uses your personal settings, with defaults for anything unset. A turn using the org key uses the org's settings, which the org can additionally cap with two ceilings (ceiling_max_output_tokens, ceiling_max_tool_steps). Ceilings only apply on the org-key path; a personal-key turn is governed solely by your own settings. The range bounds above are absolute caps on every path, and GET /api/v1/helper/status reports the effective settings for the key a turn would use. Custom instructions. Org instructions allow up to 4000 characters, personal instructions up to 2000. Org instructions apply when the turn uses that org's key, and when the conversation is scoped to that org's project (or its projects' sessions), whichever key is used. Instructions from an org you are not an active member of never apply. Your personal instructions always apply, after the org block. Instructions are not secret: any member can ask the helper to repeat them, and when a member uses their own key the org's instructions go to that member's provider. Never put credentials or confidential information in them. The prompt always starts with the helper's fixed rules; each instruction block follows between <org-instructions> / <personal-instructions> tags, under a header stating it cannot override those rules (access, scope, citations, treating tool output as data, confirming before acting). Saving text that contains those tags fails with 422 instructions_invalid. The text is control-stripped and DLP-redacted before it is stored, the length limit applies after redaction (422 instructions_too_long), and a failed DLP scan is refused with 422 instructions_redaction_failed. Each turn redacts the stored text again under that turn's DLP policy. Usage and budget. Usage is recorded in an append-only ledger, one row per turn that used any tokens — including turns that end in a disconnect, a provider error, the deadline or the step limit. Budgets and usage figures read only this ledger, so deleting a conversation or the retention sweep never changes them; ledger rows are kept 13 months. An org admin can set monthly_token_budget and read a per-member summary for the current UTC calendar month; members see only their own usage. Only turns using the org's key count against its budget, and once it is reached the next turn fails with 429 helper_budget_exceeded. The budget is checked before each turn, so turns running at the same time can each overshoot it by up to about one turn's maximum tokens. GET /api/v1/settings/helper reports your own month's usage. Every settings change writes an audit row carrying the instruction text's length and sha256 only, never the text.

sections.heading: API
sections.text: User API keys only; service keys get service_key_not_allowed. Each user can run 2 questions at a time per server process (409 helper_busy). | Method | Path | Purpose | | POST | /api/v1/helper/turns | Ask a question. Server-Sent Events by default; one JSON document with "stream": false | | GET | /api/v1/helper/conversations | Your threads, newest first | | GET | /api/v1/helper/conversations/{id} | One thread with its messages | | DELETE | /api/v1/helper/conversations/{id} | Delete a thread and its messages | | GET | /api/v1/helper/actions/{id} | A proposed change with its targets and state | | POST | /api/v1/helper/actions/{id}/confirm | Apply a proposed change (access re-checked per target) | | POST | /api/v1/helper/actions/{id}/cancel | Drop a proposed change | | GET | /api/v1/helper/status | Whether the helper is enabled for you, which key source, provider and model it would use, the effective settings, and whether org/personal instructions are set (never their text) | Request body for POST /api/v1/helper/turns: { "conversation_id": "hc_…", "message": "What did we decide about Redis and why?", "scope": { "project_id": "proj_…" }, "stream": true } conversation_id and scope are optional. scope takes at most one of project_id, group_id (v0.28.0) or session_ids (up to 100 ids). Set "retry": true when re-asking after a failed answer: if the thread's last question is still unanswered and identical, it is reused instead of being stored twice. When streaming, the events are conversation (always first), text, tool_call, tool_result, citation, doc_citation, ticket_citation, wiki_citation, action_proposed, done and error. Every citation carries kind (session, doc, ticket or wiki); session, ticket and wiki citations also carry at, the source's last update as an ISO timestamp. A keep-alive comment is sent every 15 seconds. If the client disconnects, the model call is cancelled and the partial answer is kept. With "stream": false the response is: { "conversation_id": "hc_…", "answer": "…", "citations": [ { "kind": "session", "session_id": "ses_…", "message_index": 0, "title": "…", "at": "2026-10-20T09:12:00+00:00" }, { "kind": "ticket", "ticket_id": "tk_…", "project_id": "proj_…", "title": "…", "at": "…" } ], "tool_calls": [{ "id": "…", "name": "…", "args": {} }], "usage": { "input_tokens": 0, "output_tokens": 0 }, "stop_reason": "stop", "key_source": "user" } Provider failures return 502 provider_error with a sanitized message. When the failure has a known cause, reason names it (for example endpoint_not_api when the base URL is a provider's console, not its API, and the message names the right address).

sections.heading: Retention
sections.text: Threads are private to the user who started them. Helper messages are deleted 90 days after they were written by default. An org can set 1–3650 days with helper_retention_days on PUT /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/settings; an explicit null returns it to the default. Threads without an org use the 90-day default. The token-usage ledger is kept 13 months: the same sweep deletes ledger rows older than 400 days, whatever the org's message window. Deletion runs from the sweep POST /api/v1/admin/sweeps/helper-retention (a platform admin or a platform_sweeps:run service key). On self-hosted servers the Helm chart can schedule it; see Self-Hosted.

sections.heading: Data protection
sections.text: Every excerpt, summary and knowledge text sent to the model is redacted with your org's DLP policy (the default policy for personal scope). When several orgs are involved, the strictest policy applies. The helper's tools check your access on every call, and a thread bound to an org re-checks your membership on every turn. Messages are stored redacted. Each question writes one retrieval-audit context and, per tool call, one event for each project the call read from, so every project's audit trail shows what the helper took from it. A call that returned nothing from a project writes no event for that project, and repeating an identical call in the same question writes nothing new. That way an org can answer "what did the helper send to the model?" Logs record ids, token counts and timings, never prompts, excerpts or keys.

sections.heading: Proxies
sections.text: Answers stream as they are written. The Helm chart's dashboard nginx already passes /api/v1/helper/turns through unbuffered with a 600-second timeout. If you run another proxy in front of SessionFS, turn off response buffering for that path.

Sessions are stored as .sfs directories containing: manifest.json — identity, provenance, model info, stats messages.jsonl — conversation history with content blocks workspace.json — git state, files, environment tools.json — tool definitions and shell context All file paths within are relative to workspace root. Sessions are append-only — conflict resolution appends both sides rather than merging.

sections.heading: manifest.json
sections.text: { "sfs_version": "0.1.0", "session_id": "ses_a1b2c3d4e5f6a1b2", "title": "Debug auth middleware", "tags": ["auth", "jwt"], "created_at": "2026-03-20T14:30:00Z", "updated_at": "2026-03-20T16:45:00Z", "source": { "tool": "claude-code", "tool_version": "2.1.59", "original_session_id": "abc123-def456" }, "model": { "provider": "anthropic", "model_id": "claude-opus-4-6" }, "stats": { "message_count": 47, "turn_count": 12, "tool_use_count": 28, "total_input_tokens": 34200, "total_output_tokens": 12800 } }

sections.heading: messages.jsonl
sections.text: Each line is a JSON object with role, content, and optional metadata: {"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Fix the auth bug"}]} {"role": "assistant", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "I'll read the middleware."}]} {"role": "assistant", "content": [{"type": "tool_use", "id": "t1", "name": "Read", "input": {"file_path": "src/auth.py"}}]} {"role": "tool", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "t1", "content": "import jwt\n..."}]} Content block types: text, tool_use, tool_result, thinking, image.

sections.heading: workspace.json
sections.text: { "root_path": "/Users/dev/project", "git": { "remote_url": "https://github.com/org/repo.git", "branch": "feature/auth-fix", "commit_sha": "a1b2c3d4e5f6" } }

SessionFS treats reusable agent capability as a governed package. A team can inspect one immutable Agent Skill or Agent Plugin, see what changes across tools, then consume the same package through local installation, an authenticated feed, MCP instruction loading, or an organization assignment. The canonical authoring formats remain Agent Skills and Agent Plugins 1.0. SessionFS adds source identity, content hashes, DLP scanning, compatibility plans, consent, policy, and session provenance; it does not introduce a competing skill language.

sections.heading: Before You Trust a Package
sections.text: Every Marketplace detail response and dashboard dossier includes: Immutable version_id and SHA-256 content hash Source type, locator, subdirectory, and pinned commit when supplied Public, personal, or organization visibility Verification state and declared license Per-tool instruction count and deliberate omissions Risk flags for scripts, MCP declarations, and executable extensions Previewed instructions are untrusted text. Previewing does not install, approve, or execute anything.

sections.heading: Install Disclosure
sections.text: Before anything is installed, every surface shows the same disclosure card, computed from the package bytes (never from what the package claims about itself): Per tool: the exact files that land on disk (for example .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md or ~/.codex/skills/... for user scope), and what is not installed for that tool. What can run: scripts (with their interpreter), SKILL.md frontmatter hooks (event and matcher), executable extensions, and MCP servers (local command or remote origin, plus the environment variable names they read). Tool pre-approvals: allowed-tools grants the skill gives itself. Network endpoints referenced anywhere in the package. Shell commands the instructions tell the agent to run (from fenced shell blocks), with file and line. Scanner findings, and hidden or bidirectional Unicode and control characters, shown visibly as ⟦U+202E⟧ with file, line and column. The card appears in sfs skill inspect and sfs skill add, in the dashboard package view and on the project Skills tab next to every pending approval, in MCP get_marketplace_package (display only; MCP never grants consent), and at GET /api/v1/marketplace/versions/{id}/disclosure?tools=codex,claude-code&scope=project. A local install of a package that contains the hidden-character classes the publish gate refuses (bidirectional overrides or zero-width characters in SKILL.md or scripts, Unicode tag characters, raw control characters) needs --allow-hidden-unicode.

sections.heading: Updates and Re-Consent
sections.text: Each version has a capability digest: two versions with the same digest grant the same access. An update is classified by comparing the version you consented to with the new one: | Update | What changed | Personal sfs skill update | Org assignment / daemon | | Text | Instructions or assets only | One confirmation (--yes works); the consent you gave carries forward | Applied by the daemon | | Code | Script, hook, MCP-config or executable-extension bytes, with no new access | The changed capability's flag again (--allow-scripts / --allow-hooks / ...); --yes alone is refused | Held until approved | | Widening | Any new access: a new capability, hook event or matcher, MCP server or changed MCP command, remote origin, allowed-tools grant, network endpoint, environment variable, persistence target, or a lost publisher verification | Always stops: --approve-widening (or an interactive yes to the widening prompt), plus the capability flags; --yes never approves it | Never auto-applied | sfs skill rollback and sfs skill sync --locked apply the same rules to the version they replace (and a locked sync is all-or-nothing). Any change to MCP configuration counts as widening. sfs skill diff <name> and GET /api/v1/marketplace/versions/{from}/diff/{to} show the files added, removed and changed (with bounded text diffs), the capability changes, new scanner and hidden-character findings, and the update class. Devices never apply a widening or code update on their own: sfs skill pull and the daemon keep the installed version and report the update as held. A held org update is applied once an organization admin approves it: POST /api/v1/orgs/{org}/skills/assignments/{id}/advance with approve_widening (or approve_code_change) records the approved capability digest on the assignment, and devices apply only a version whose digest matches. GET /api/v1/orgs/{org}/skills/assignments/updates lists every assignment with a newer version and its update class (paginated: pass the returned next_cursor as cursor). Assigning another version of a package to a target that already has one is refused with 409 use_advance (the server keeps one active assignment per package and target), and approving a project install request for a newer version of a package already approved in that project is refused with 409 reapproval_required unless the request explicitly approves the widening or code change. Approvals bind the approved capability digest to the install request (or assignment) at approval time; approvals made before this release never count as approving a specific digest, and an update from such a grant is treated as widening. A grant is refused with 503 while the package's manifest cannot be computed. A device applies a widening update only for the tools of the grant that bound that exact digest. Re-approving a text update in the dashboard carries the capabilities confirmed for the previous version forward; a code update asks only for the changed capability. Advancing an assignment keeps the old one as superseded history. Consent receipts record the capability digest and the access that was consented to. When consent carries forward to a text update, the new receipt names the receipt it was carried from, so the audit trail shows which bytes a person actually reviewed. An Enterprise exception, letting an org auto-apply code updates from a publisher whose signed release workflow it trusts, is reserved for verified publishers and trusted publishing and is not active yet.

sections.heading: 1. Local Device Installation
sections.text: Use sfs skill when an engineer or CI runner controls the filesystem: sfs skill inspect https://github.com/acme/agent-capabilities.git --pin <40-char-sha> sfs skill add https://github.com/acme/agent-capabilities.git \ --pin <40-char-sha> \ --for claude-code \ --for codex The client computes a deterministic plan, checks collisions and path safety, writes through a transaction journal, and records the actual output hashes. SessionFS refuses unmanaged-file clobbering. Consent is an inert allowlist, not a denylist: any skill asset that is not plain documentation or data (.md, .txt, .json, .yaml, images, LICENSE, ...) needs --allow-scripts; SKILL.md frontmatter hooks: or allowed-tools: needs --allow-hooks; a hooks.json or hooks/ directory inside a skill needs --allow-executable-extensions. --yes alone is refused for any of these, with the message naming the hook or tool grant. Local MCP activation is not silently enabled.

sections.heading: 2. Authenticated Target Feed
sections.text: GET /api/v1/marketplace/feeds/{tool} returns a target-aware portability plan with the immutable download path, target install roots, and omitted components. This feed is a SessionFS authenticated download-and-translate feed, used by sfs skill. The response says so explicitly, and for tools with a native catalog it also links it: { "projection_type": "sessionfs-portability-plan", "native_marketplace_install": false, "delivery": "authenticated-download-and-translate", "native_catalog_url": "https://api.sessionfs.dev/api/v1/git/public/sessionfs.git" }

sections.heading: Native Tool Catalogs
sections.text: SessionFS also publishes approved packages as native plugin catalogs: read-only git repositories that each tool's own plugin command can add. Publish once, and the package installs with Claude Code's /plugin install, Copilot CLI's copilot plugin install, the Codex Plugins Directory, a Cursor team marketplace or gemini extensions install. sfs catalog add --for claude-code # prints: /plugin marketplace add <clone-url> sfs catalog add --for copilot --org <org> # an org catalog (Team+) | Catalog | Who | Contains | | Public (sessionfs) | Every signed-in user | Moderated public listings from verified publishers with no open high or critical scan findings | | Personal (sessionfs-user-…) | Starter and above | Versions you consented to install | | Organization (sessionfs-org-…) | Team and above | Org-wide assignments and approved install requests | A native install skips SessionFS's own consent prompt (the tool performs it), so a catalog only ever holds versions its scope already approved, and the tool's own trust prompt still applies. A block, yank or quarantine removes the entry the next time the catalog is fetched. Tools do not uninstall plugins that leave a catalog; sfs skill pull and device reconcile still remove blocked packages where sfs runs. Each catalog repository carries .claude-plugin/marketplace.json (Claude Code), .github/plugin/marketplace.json (Copilot CLI), .agents/plugins/marketplace.json (Codex) and .cursor-plugin/marketplace.json (Cursor), one plugins/<namespace>--<name>/ directory per package, and SESSIONFS-CATALOG.json, which binds every plugin to its version id, content hash and projection hash. Commits are deterministic: the same approved set always produces the same commit. Authentication: git sends your API key through the sfs catalog credential helper, which sfs catalog add configures for the SessionFS API host only, ahead of an empty entry that keeps other credential helpers (such as a keychain or store helper) from receiving the key. Keys never appear in URLs. One package never breaks a catalog: a package that cannot be projected safely, or that does not fit the catalog's size budget, is left out and listed with the reason in SESSIONFS-CATALOG.json, and if a rebuild fails the catalog keeps serving its last good commit, unless that commit still carries a version that has since been blocked, yanked, quarantined or had its grant revoked, in which case the catalog answers 503 until a rebuild succeeds. Cursor team marketplaces import from GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or Azure DevOps, so mirror an org catalog to a repository you own with sfs catalog export --to <remote>. Gemini CLI installs one extension per repository and lists public GitHub repositories, so it gets per-plugin repositories from the public catalog only. Antigravity only lists its official marketplace: clone the catalog and run agy plugin install <clone>/plugins/<plugin>.

sections.heading: Works In
sections.text: Every listing shows a per-tool works in matrix (sfs skill works-in <id>, GET /api/v1/marketplace/versions/{id}/works-in, and MCP get_marketplace_package): | Badge | Meaning | | verified | The tool's own installer accepted the package in the SessionFS verification harness (L1), with the tool version and date | | format-valid | The generated catalog entry matches the tool's documented format (L0, checked in-process) | | regressed | It verified on an earlier tool version and fails on the newest one | | expected | Computed by SessionFS's adapters; not yet verified | The harness runs each tool's installer in an isolated, short-lived sandbox with no secrets, as a separate unprivileged user from the harness process; it never runs a skill (that would need a model key, and SessionFS holds none). Works-in checks on private (org or personal) packages are a Team feature, with a daily per-organization quota.

sections.heading: 3. MCP Runtime Instructions
sections.text: Agents can search and preview packages over MCP. To load instruction text into a live agent context: Call request_skill_install with the exact version_id, content_hash, project, target tool, and scope. A project owner/admin approves the exact hash from the project Skills tab in the dashboard (or POST .../skill-install-requests/{id}/approve with approved_capabilities), confirming each elevated capability, or an organization admin creates a matching assignment. Approval is not available over MCP. If the approver is the same principal that filed the request, the server also requires a single-use confirmation code emailed to that account (POST .../skill-install-requests/{id}/challenge, 10-minute lifetime). Call load_marketplace_skill for that project and tool. The load response is instruction-only. It explicitly reports executable_components_included: false and untrusted: true with a fixed preamble marking the text as third-party data. MCP cannot write device paths or activate scripts, hooks, executable extensions, or local MCP servers.

sections.heading: 4. Organization Assignments
sections.text: Team and Enterprise organizations can manage multiple registry references and assign exact package versions to the entire organization, one member, or one member's device. Device assignments bind both the user and device identifier; another organization member cannot claim a guessed device ID. Assignments are desired state. Clients still perform local preflight and installation. Enterprise policy may make an assignment required, but it does not turn the server into a remote code-execution path.

sections.heading: Supported Tools
sections.text: sfs skill plans and installs packages for Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Amp, Cline, Kilo Code, and Roo Code. Roo Code support is legacy: its upstream repository was archived in May 2026, so the adapter keeps working but will not track future Roo changes.

sections.heading: Dashboard Workflow
sections.text: Open Marketplace in the dashboard to search everything visible to your identity. Search, the tool picker, sort and the category row stay on the page; the other filters sit behind Filters, and active filters show as removable chips. Each package card shows its version, installs and one capability label (Instructions only, or what else it includes). Opening a package shows what it can do, its source and where it was published from (Overview), the install disclosure card (Install details), the works-in and per-tool matrix (Compatibility) and the README. Choose Request for project to create an instruction-only request. Install in your tool at the top of the page shows each tool's own commands for adding the SessionFS catalog. Project owners/admins decide pending requests from the project's Skills tab, which shows the disclosure for the requested tools and, when the request updates a version already approved there, the changes to approve. Organization members also see registry policy, each registry's poll status (last and next poll, failures and the error summary) and effective assignments; owners and admins can Poll now. Organization owners and admins also get Updates to review: every assigned package with a newer version, its update diff and the full disclosure of the new version, with an acknowledgement (bound to the disclosure shown) and an Advance button. Private packages remain hidden from users outside the owning organization; unauthorized detail and download requests return 404 rather than disclosing existence.

sections.heading: Discovery and Freshness
sections.text: Browse by category (code review, testing, debugging, refactoring, documentation, security, frontend, backend and APIs, data, infrastructure, deployment, workflow, integrations, AI and ML, productivity) and narrow results by publisher, verified publisher, trusted-publishing provenance, declared license, worst open scan finding, capability (instruction-only, scripts, MCP servers, hooks, executable extensions, pre-approved tools), the tool a package is verified to work in, and how recently it was updated. The same filters are in the dashboard Filters menu, sfs skill search, the API (GET /api/v1/marketplace/packages) and the read-only MCP search_skill_marketplace tool. Every filter runs on the server before a page is cut. The default ranking is fixed and documented, with no stars or reviews: packages that are not deprecated come first, then the text match (exact name, name prefix, name contains, description), then verified publishers, then how many tools the package is verified to work in, then a log-scale bucket of 30-day installs, then the newest version. README: the package's README.md (or the first SKILL.md body) is shown on the listing. It is rendered without raw HTML, links are limited to http(s) and mailto and carry rel="nofollow", remote images are never loaded (no tracking pixels), and images inside the package load only through the authenticated asset endpoint (PNG, JPEG, GIF and WebP checked by content; never SVG). Hidden and bidirectional characters are shown as ⟦U+XXXX⟧ and listed with their line and column. Install counts by tool: installs over the last 30 days, per target tool. Counts under 10 show as <10. The server keeps daily totals only (one count per account per version, tool and day) and service-key installs are counted separately. The CLI and daemon send these counts best effort; SFS_SKILL_USAGE_REPORTING=0 or turning telemetry off stops them. Freshness: last updated and last verified per tool. A package is stale when it has had no new version for 180 days and either its works-in check regressed or (for a verified GitHub publisher) its source repository is archived. Deprecated is set by the publisher, with an optional successor from the same publisher, which search and installs point to. Unmaintained means the publisher's verification lapsed. A daily sweeper recomputes the flags. Publishers get an analytics view (dashboard Publishers → Analytics, sfs skill publisher stats): installs by tool, version and day, active installs, uninstall rate, translation failures, update adoption, works-in regressions, scan findings and open reports. Every count is floored at 10 and the organizations installs come from are never shown. Personal publisher analytics need Starter or above, organization publishers the Team plan. Organization owners and admins on Team can see what their own members use (dashboard Marketplace → Organization usage, sfs skill usage --org).

sections.heading: Publishing Boundary
sections.text: Publish with sfs skill publish, the authenticated API, or the publish dialog on the dashboard Marketplace page (for pre-built archives). Uploads are bounded, path-safe, DLP-scanned, instruction-scanned, normalized, and stored as immutable canonical archives. | Who can publish | Visibility | Requirement | | Any signed-in user on Starter or above | Personal (only you) | None beyond the upload checks | | Organization owners and admins on Team or Enterprise | Organization | The package's plugin.json must declare a license | | Verified publishers enabled for public publishing by SessionFS | Public | A declared license; a publisher's first public version, and any update that widens access, waits for review | Browsing, downloading, and loading approved instructions are available to every signed-in user, including the Free tier. Any declared license value is accepted for organization packages, including UNLICENSED or proprietary for internal work; packages without one are rejected with license_required. Hosted publishing limits: A package can be at most 48 MiB unpacked (about 58 MiB compressed); larger uploads are rejected with 413 package_too_large before the body is read. Local sfs skill imports keep their 128 MiB limit. Each API process accepts a small number of publishes at a time and one per user; beyond that it answers 503 publish_busy with a Retry-After header. An upload that stalls or takes longer than two minutes gets 408 publish_timeout. Personal packages count against your plan's storage (Starter 500 MB, Pro 2 GB, Team 1 GB per user, Enterprise unlimited). Organization packages count against the organization's storage, together with members' synced sessions. Every package keeps at most 100 stored versions, and personal packages share a limit of 50 stored versions per user across all of them. Delete an unreferenced version to free a slot. Uploads must be plain ustar/GNU tar.gz archives without PAX or GNU extended headers (no x/g/L/K records): member paths must fit the ustar name/prefix fields, and archives created with tar --format=ustar or Python's tarfile USTAR_FORMAT/GNU_FORMAT with short paths qualify. Extended-header archives are rejected outright because their metadata records are read with whatever size they declare.

sections.heading: Publishing from the CLI
sections.text: Validate a package before you publish it. sfs skill validate runs the server's publish checks locally: archive format, path safety, size caps, the plugin.json schema, SKILL.md frontmatter, MCP credential literals, and the secret/PHI scan. The server and the CLI share one validator, so they give the same answers: sfs skill validate ./review-helper # personal publishing sfs skill validate ./review-helper --visibility org # also requires a declared license Each problem shows the file and line (when known), why it fails, and how to fix it. Secret and PHI findings are listed by file and line, never by the matched text. Validation exits with code 1 on errors, so it can gate CI. On success it prints the content hash and the risk summary (scripts, hooks, allowed tools, MCP, executable extensions). sfs skill publish validates the same way, shows a summary (name, version, license, risk flags, size, target), asks for confirmation, then uploads: sfs skill publish ./review-helper # your personal library sfs skill publish ./review-helper --org org_123 --yes # an organization, no prompt A directory is packed into a deterministic ustar tar.gz, and .git and OS metadata files are left out. Those exact bytes are validated and uploaded, so the content hash shown before upload is the one the server stores. The upload is named after the package, so a new version lands under the same package. Some limits need server state, so only the server checks them: your plan, your org role, storage quota, version caps, concurrency (503 publish_busy), upload time (408 publish_timeout), and an organization's own DLP policy. When the server refuses an upload for one of these reasons, the CLI explains what happened and what to do next. Secret and PHI findings block a personal publish locally. When you publish to an organization, they appear as warnings instead, because the organization's DLP allowlist may permit the flagged values. The server applies that policy, and it rejects the upload if the policy does not allow them. Personal registry URLs are recorded as pinned references only; the server never fetches them. Organization registries can be polled by the server (next section).

sections.heading: Polling Git Registries
sections.text: An organization registry on https:// can publish itself: SessionFS polls it and every new Git tag that matches the registry's pattern becomes a new, immutable version in the organization's library. Nobody has to republish, and no CI pipeline needs a publishing key. Schedule. poll_interval_seconds defaults to 900 (15 minutes) for https:// registries; the minimum is 300, and 0 keeps the registry metadata-only (nothing is fetched). ssh:// registries are never polled. Registries created before polling existed stay metadata-only until an owner or admin turns polling on. An organization can poll at most 10 registries by default (409 poll_registry_limit), and each scheduler run polls at most two registries per organization so no organization starves the others. Which refs. tag_pattern defaults to semver (v?\d+\.\d+\.\d+, matched against the whole tag name). Patterns use a restricted syntax: literals, ., \d, \w, character classes and the quantifiers ? * + {n,m}; groups, alternation and backreferences are refused so a pattern can never be made slow. With branch_only_mode and a branch, the branch head is published instead; commits between two polls are not published individually. What gets published. A repository with a marketplace.json (.claude-plugin/, .codex-plugin/ or the root) publishes each plugin that lives in the repository; plugins that point at another repository are skipped (the server never follows URLs found inside a repository). A repository without a manifest is published as one package. Every package goes through exactly the checks of a manual organization publish: validation, the organization's DLP policy, instruction scanning, disclosure, quotas and moderation blocks. The organization owner or admin who last saved the polling settings is the publisher of record and must still hold that role; if they leave, any owner or admin re-saving the settings takes over. Immutability. Re-polling the same commit is a no-op. A tag that is force-moved to a different commit produces a new version with its own content hash; existing versions are never changed. A refused package (for example a DLP finding) is recorded against its tag and not retried until the tag moves. Private repositories. Set credential_secret_ref to a reference, never a token: env:SFS_REGISTRY_CRED_<NAME> or k8s:<secret-name>. The operator creates the credential and binds it to your organization and to the hosts it may be sent to; any problem with a reference shows one generic message (the operator's logs say why). Credentials never appear in the URL, in API responses, in poll errors or in logs. Status. The registry listing and the dashboard show last_poll_at, last_poll_status (ok, partial when some packages were refused, error), a sanitized last_poll_error_summary, consecutive_failures and next_poll_at. Failures back off exponentially (twice the interval, then four times, up to 24 hours). Network, TLS and server errors are retried; only a refusal of the content itself is recorded against a tag. Poll now in the dashboard (or POST /api/v1/orgs/{org_id}/skills/registries/{registry_id}/poll, at most once a minute) moves the registry to the front of the next run; GET .../poll-refs lists what each tag produced. curl -X PATCH "$API/api/v1/orgs/$ORG/skills/registries/$REGISTRY" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $SFS_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"poll_interval_seconds": 900, "tag_pattern": "v\\d+\\.\\d+\\.\\d+", "credential_secret_ref": "k8s:acme-gitlab"}' The fetch is hardened: https only, the host's addresses are checked (private, loopback, link-local and metadata addresses are refused; self-hosted operators can allow specific private ranges) and Git is pinned to them, redirects are not followed, hooks never run, nothing is checked out, and size, file-count and time limits apply. Polling never runs inside your API requests; the scheduler calls a dedicated endpoint. See Self-Hosted for operator setup.

sections.heading: Instruction Scanning
sections.text: Every published version is scanned for dangerous instructions and scripts: fetch-and-run, encoded execution, credential harvesting, exfiltration endpoints, permission bypass and hook auto-approval, persistence, concealment, defense evasion, and hidden or bidirectional Unicode. Critical findings refuse the publish; other findings are shown on the listing and in the install disclosure. Live versions are rescanned weekly and whenever the ruleset changes. A new critical finding quarantines the version: no new installs, downloads, approvals or MCP loads until a moderator blocks or restores it. Existing installs are warned, never removed by a quarantine alone.

sections.heading: Reports, Takedown and Revocations
sections.text: Anyone signed in can report a listing. SessionFS moderators, and an organization's owners and admins for their own listings, review reports in the dashboard moderation queue and can act on a version or a whole package with a required reason and an audit record: Yank keeps installed copies but refuses new installs. sfs skill list and sfs skill doctor show a warning. Block removes the package from every device. sfs skill pull and the daemon follow the revocations feed and move blocked packages into ~/.sessionfs/skills/quarantine/, keeping any local edits there. Blocked content is refused by content hash, so deleting and re-publishing the same bytes does not bring it back.

sections.heading: Verified Publishers
sections.text: A publisher owns a globally unique marketplace namespace, personal or organization-owned. Verification proves who the publisher is and shows as a badge on its listings, such as verified: acme.com or verified: github.com/acme. sfs skill publisher claim acme --org org_123 # claim a namespace sfs skill publisher verify pub_abc --dns acme.com # prints a TXT record to add sfs skill publisher verify pub_abc --github-org INSTALLATION_ID sfs skill publisher check pub_abc VERIFICATION_ID # re-check now DNS verification uses a sessionfs-verification=... TXT record; a domain your organization already verified for SSO is reused. GitHub verification goes through one of your own linked SessionFS GitHub App installations and needs a recent proof that you own or administer it. If a DNS record goes missing for seven days, the badge is dropped until it is back. Names that imitate a reserved brand or a verified publisher (lookalike letters from any script, digit swaps, typos, -official suffixes) are refused, and display names never carry a badge.

sections.heading: Trusted Publishing from GitHub Actions
sections.text: Trusted publishing lets a GitHub Actions workflow publish without a SessionFS API key stored in the repository. Allow a specific repository and workflow, ideally with a protected GitHub environment and a ref pattern: sfs skill publisher trust pub_abc --repo acme/review-helper \ --workflow publish.yml --environment release --ref-pattern 'refs/tags/v*' In the workflow, give the job permissions: id-token: write and run: sfs skill publish . --trusted-publishing --namespace acme The CLI exchanges the job's OIDC token for a single-use publish token that expires after 15 minutes. Pull-request events never publish. Each listing shows where the version was published from: repository, workflow, ref, environment and run. Remove a trust with sfs skill publisher untrust; tokens already issued under it stop working.

sections.heading: Trusted Publishing from GitLab CI
sections.text: GitLab CI jobs can publish the same way, using a GitLab CI ID token (the id_tokens: keyword; the removed CI_JOB_JWT variables are not supported). Allow a GitLab project by its numeric id (Settings > General), with a ref pattern and, ideally, an environment: sfs skill publisher trust pub_abc --gitlab-project 12345678 \ --gitlab-project-path acme/review-helper \ --ref-pattern 'refs/tags/v*' \ --environment production --require-protected-environment The command also pins the project's current namespace (group) id, read from the GitLab API (GET /api/v4/projects/<id>; public projects need no token, and GITLAB_TOKEN or CI_JOB_TOKEN is used when set). A project keeps its numeric id when it is transferred to another group, so without the pin that group's protected-ref pipelines would still match. If the lookup fails the command refuses: pass --gitlab-namespace ID to set the id yourself, or --no-namespace-pin to skip pinning (a warning is printed, the server flags the trust, and the dashboard shows "Namespace not pinned"). For self-managed GitLab add --gitlab-host https://gitlab.example.com; the server operator must list that instance in SFS_GITLAB_OIDC_ISSUERS (only https://gitlab.com is allowed by default), exactly as it appears in the token's iss (GitLab's external_url: lowercase host, no :443, no trailing slash). A job names its own environment, so --environment only adds security when that environment is protected in GitLab (a GitLab Premium feature). --require-protected-environment refuses tokens unless GitLab reports the environment as protected; leave it off on GitLab Free and rely on protected tags. Protect the tags or branches you publish from. SessionFS only accepts jobs running on a protected ref. In .gitlab-ci.yml, request an ID token for this server's audience (the audience from GET /api/v1/marketplace/trusted-publishing/config) and publish: publish-skill: environment: production id_tokens: SFS_ID_TOKEN: aud: https://api.sessionfs.dev rules: - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG =~ /^v/ && $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "push" script: # sessionfs==<version you tested>, hash-pinned; token kept out of pip. - env -u SFS_ID_TOKEN python -m pip install --require-hashes --only-binary=:all: -r requirements-publish.txt - sfs skill publish . --trusted-publishing --namespace acme The ID token is live for the whole job, so declare id_tokens: only on the publish job and install an exact, hash-pinned SessionFS release. The server checks the token's signature against the instance's published keys, the audience, the numeric project id, the protected ref and ref pattern, the environment, and the pipeline source: only push, web and api pipelines publish. Merge request, external pull request, child and downstream, trigger-token and scheduled pipelines never publish. GitLab mints the token when the job starts and SessionFS accepts it for 60 minutes, so keep publishing in its own short job. The token exchange returns the same single-use, 15-minute publish token, and each ID token can be exchanged once.

sections.heading: Launch Catalog
sections.text: The public catalog starts with sessionfs-workflows, an MIT-licensed package written by SessionFS. It contains four instruction-only skills with no scripts, hooks, or MCP servers: | Skill | What it does | | session-handoff | Hand a session to a teammate or another tool, or pick one up | | ticket-workflow | Work a SessionFS ticket from start to review | | project-knowledge | Load project context and record what you learn in the knowledge base | | worker-review-loop | Run brief-driven workers in isolated worktrees, gated by a trusted reviewer and a re-review before merge (see Worker Review Loop) | Find it under Marketplace in the dashboard. It reaches your tools the same way as any other package: request it for a project, load it through the target feed, or assign it to your organization. The source is also in the SessionFS repository under catalog/sessionfs-workflows, so you can also copy it into a project and run sfs skill add ./sessionfs-workflows.

sections.heading: Org Skills Policy (Enterprise)
sections.text: An Enterprise organization writes one skills policy and SessionFS applies it everywhere it can: On the server. Install requests, approvals, assignments, assignment updates and MCP instruction loads are refused when the org's current policy forbids the version. The refusal names the org and says to ask an org owner or admin. A policy change also applies to grants made earlier: the next reconcile withholds them. In each tool's own managed settings. The policy compiles into Claude Code and GitHub Copilot managed-settings.json, a VS Code device policy, the Gemini CLI system settings.json and the Codex requirements.toml. Cursor gets a checklist for its admin dashboard. For every field SessionFS shows whether the tool enforces it, whether only SessionFS checks it, or whether nothing checks it, so advisory controls are never presented as enforcement. The policy sets a mode (open, allowlist, library_only or disabled), allowed publishers and git sources (a git source matches only versions published from that repository through trusted publishing, never a repository an uploader merely declares), capability limits (hooks, scripts, local and remote MCP servers and their origins, hidden Unicode), a signature requirement and the highest scanner severity accepted. Every change is a new, immutable revision. Settings with side effects in a tool, such as stopping users' own hooks, must be acknowledged before a revision is published. Delivery starts in advisory mode: sfs skill pull and the daemon skip what the policy refuses and report each device's compliance, including whether IT deployed the compiled managed settings. A user can bypass advisory delivery on their own machine, so deploy the compiled files through your MDM for tool-level enforcement: sfs policy show # what applies to you, per tool sfs policy compile --tool claude-code > managed-settings.json sfs policy status # system or advisory, per tool sfs policy set --org org_123 --file policy.json # owners and admins If the organization later leaves Enterprise, its last policy stays enforced: owners and admins can still read it and can relax or disable it (sfs policy disable --org ORG), but not tighten it. Signed MDM bundles are planned. See the CLI reference for the full policy format.

sections.heading: Service Keys
sections.text: Automated clients should use the minimum required scopes: marketplace:read for search, inspect, preview, download, and feeds marketplace:write for package publishing skills:read for assignments, requests, and approved instruction loading skills:request to create/cancel requests skills:approve to approve project requests skills:admin for organization registries, packages, assignments and the skills policy devices:report to send skills-policy compliance reports (for example from CI runners) Service keys remain organization-bound. A key cannot cross its organization even if it knows another resource ID.
Every session automatically summarized — files changed, tests run, commands executed, packages installed. No more reading 2,000 messages to understand what the AI did.

sections.heading: Quick start
sections.text: sfs summary ses_abc Output: Debug auth middleware 2.3h | 327 msgs | 28 tool calls | Claude Code Branch: feature/auth-fix @ a1b2c3d Files modified (3): src/auth/middleware.py src/auth/tokens.py tests/test_auth.py Commands: 34 Tests: 6 runs (5 passed, 1 failed) Packages: pyjwt, redis

sections.text: sfs summary ses_abc --format md > session-summary.md

sections.heading: Today's sessions
sections.text: sfs summary --today Shows a table of all sessions captured today with key metrics.

sections.heading: Dashboard
sections.text: The Summary tab in the session detail page shows: Metric cards (duration, messages, tool calls, tests) Files modified and read (expandable) Activity section (commands, tests, packages, errors) Narrative section (if LLM-generated)
SessionFS collects anonymous usage telemetry to help us understand adoption and improve the product. This page is the full disclosure.

sections.heading: What is sent
sections.text: Six funnel events, each carrying four fields and nothing else: | Event | When | Fields | | install | First time SessionFS runs on a machine | install_id, version, os, event_ts | | init_completed | sfs init wizard finishes successfully | install_id, version, os, event_ts | | first_capture | First session ever captured (daemon or sfs recapture) | install_id, version, os, event_ts | | first_magic | First memory read (resume, MCP search/recall/ask) | install_id, version, os, event_ts | | heartbeat | Daemon is alive (at most once per 24h) | install_id, version, os, event_ts | | capture_degraded | Reserved — not yet emitted | install_id, version, os, event_ts, tool |

sections.heading: Fields
sections.text: | Field | Description | | install_id | Random UUID4 hex, generated once at ~/.sessionfs/install_id. Not derived from any identifying data. | | version | SessionFS version string (e.g. 0.29.2) | | os | darwin, linux, or windows | | event | One of the six event names above | | event_ts | ISO-8601 UTC timestamp of the event | | tool | Only sent with capture_degraded — the AI tool name (≤50 chars) | The payload is posted to https://api.sessionfs.dev/api/v1/telemetry with no authentication. The server records the event and returns {"status": "ok"}.

sections.heading: What is NEVER sent
sections.text: File paths, workspace paths, or project names Session content, messages, or tool calls Email addresses, user names, or hostnames API keys, tokens, or credentials Git remotes, branch names, or commit SHAs Environment variable values A server-side _contains_pii() guard rejects any payload that contains an email-like or IP-address-like string. The emitter never includes any of the above fields in the first place.

sections.heading: Where telemetry goes
sections.text: Payloads are POSTed to the configured API server. For the hosted product that is api.sessionfs.dev; if you set SESSIONFS_API_URL (self-hosted), telemetry goes to your own server, not to SessionFS. A long-running daemon picks up a config-file opt-out on its next config reload or within 24 hours (the daily heartbeat re-reads the config); `sfs daemon restart` applies it immediately. The env-var opt-out applies to any process started after it is set.

sections.heading: Opting out
sections.text: Two independent opt-outs, either of which disables all telemetry:

sections.heading: 1. Environment variable
sections.text: export SFS_NO_TELEMETRY=1 Any non-empty value disables telemetry. This takes precedence over the config file and is checked before any thread spawn or network attempt.

sections.heading: 2. Config file
sections.text: In ~/.sessionfs/config.toml: [telemetry] enabled = false Set enabled = true (or remove the block) to re-enable. Missing key defaults to enabled.

sections.heading: Marketplace install counts (signed-in only)
sections.text: Separate from the anonymous telemetry above: when you are signed in, the CLI and the daemon count installs of packages from the hosted SessionFS Marketplace, so publishers and organization admins see real usage. What is sent: POST /api/v1/marketplace/versions/{version_id}/events with your API key, carrying only the event (install from sfs skill add or a pull / daemon install, uninstall from sfs skill remove, active when sfs skill pull or the daemon's skill reconcile finds the package still installed, translation_failure when a package cannot be translated for a tool), the target tools, the source (download or reconcile), and optionally a project_id used only to pick the organization. No paths, session content or package files; local and git packages are never counted. Account and organization linkage: the server keeps a SHA-256 of your account (or service key) id for a 30-day de-duplication window (one count per account, version, tool, event and day), then deletes it, and otherwise stores daily totals only. Each total records the consuming organization: an org-private package counts toward its own organization, a personal package toward none, and a public package toward your project's (or default / only) organization. Only that organization's owners and admins see its totals. Publishers see aggregates only, with counts under 10 shown as <10, and never which organizations installs came from. Shown before anything is sent. Install counts have their own one-time notice (marker ~/.sessionfs/telemetry-markers/skill-usage-disclosure-shown, separate from the telemetry notice, so people who saw the telemetry notice before install counts existed are still told). The first interactive sfs skill command on a terminal that would send a count prints the notice first; the first-run telemetry notice and sfs init / sfs daemon start also show it. Until it has been shown, nothing is sent, including from the daemon and non-terminal runs, unless you set SFS_SKILL_USAGE_REPORTING=1 explicitly. The opt-outs below always win. The daemon: while signed in, its periodic skill reconcile sends install / active counts for assigned packages, at most one active per package and tool per day. Opting out: SFS_SKILL_USAGE_REPORTING=0 (or false, off, no) stops only these counts; either telemetry opt-out (SFS_NO_TELEMETRY or [telemetry] enabled = false) also stops them. A failed or disabled count never affects the command.

sections.heading: Data retention
sections.text: Telemetry events are stored server-side in the telemetry_events table. We retain them indefinitely for aggregate trend analysis. No personal data is linked to install IDs.

sections.heading: Questions
sections.text: Open an issue at github.com/sessionfs/sessionfs or email support@sessionfs.dev.

sections.heading: Common Error Responses
sections.text: | Status | Error | Cause | Fix | | 400 | Invalid session ID format | Session ID doesn't match ses_[hex]{8,40} | Check ID format — must be ses_ + 8-40 lowercase hex chars | | 400 | Payload too large | Sync payload exceeds server limit | Compact session first or check MAX_UPLOAD_SIZE | | 401 | Unauthorized | Missing or expired auth token | Run sfs auth login | | 403 | Email not verified | Account needs verification | Check email for verification link, or set SFS_REQUIRE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION=false | | 409 | ETag mismatch | Concurrent modification | Pull latest with sfs pull, then push again | | 413 | Request entity too large | Upload exceeds server limit | Check MAX_UPLOAD_SIZE setting | | 429 | Rate limited | Too many requests per minute | Wait, or increase SFS_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE. Set to 0 to disable |

sections.heading: Session ID Format
sections.text: SessionFS generates session IDs in the format: ses_ followed by 8-40 lowercase hex characters. Examples: ses_ae7652a4 (8 chars — short form) ses_346b4d7288214b0f (16 chars — standard) ses_a1b2c3d4e5f6a1b2c3d4e5f6a1b2c3d4e5f6a1b2 (40 chars — long form) All formats are valid for sync, push, pull, and handoff operations.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting Sync Failures
sections.text: Check daemon status: sfs daemon status sfs daemon logs Try a manual push (shows detailed errors): sfs push ses_abc12345 Check server logs: kubectl logs deploy/sessionfs-api -n sessionfs --tail=100 Verify authentication: sfs auth status Check local storage: sfs storage

sections.heading: A push is slow or times out
sections.text: Every PUT /api/v1/sessions/{id}/sync logs one INFO line on the API server with where its time went (milliseconds; no session content is logged): sync_push session=ses_abc12345 status=201 wait_ms=0 db_read_ms=8 read_ms=31 validate_ms=97 extract_ms=592 dlp_scan_ms=3933 dlp_redact_ms=4539 blob_upload_ms=180 blob_promote_ms=170 db_write_ms=12 bytes_in=7660919 dlp_mode=redact dlp_findings=77 bytes_stored=7660919 total_ms=9254 The same phases come back to the client in the response's Server-Timing header. | Phase | What it covers | | wait | Waiting for one of the user's 3 concurrent push slots | | db_read | Tier, session and ETag lookups | | read | Receiving the upload | | validate | Archive safety checks and per-file size limits | | extract | Manifest, search text and git metadata | | dlp_scan | Organization DLP scan (only when the org has DLP enabled) | | dlp_redact | Redacting and repacking (DLP redact mode with findings) | | blob_upload / blob_promote | Writing the archive to blob storage (S3/GCS/local) | | db_write | Updating the session row | A push whose If-Match ETag is out of date gets 409 etag_mismatch before the archive is processed, so a client retrying with a stale ETag no longer waits for a full DLP pass first. The INFO line needs SFS_LOG_LEVEL=INFO (the default). If your deployment supplies its own Python logging configuration, make sure the sessionfs.api logger is enabled at INFO.

sections.heading: MCP pods crash-looping
sections.text: Check that the MCP service port matches the container port (should be 8080): kubectl describe deploy sessionfs-mcp -n sessionfs Verify liveness/readiness probes target the correct port.

sections.heading: Dashboard returns 405 or shows malformed URLs
sections.text: The dashboard must proxy API requests through nginx, not call an external API URL directly. In the Helm chart, the dashboard nginx ConfigMap handles /api/ proxying automatically. If you see URLs like https://your-domain/https://api.sessionfs.dev, the dashboard image was built with a hardcoded API URL. Rebuild with: docker build --build-arg VITE_API_URL=/api -t sessionfs-dashboard .

sections.heading: S3 ParamValidationError: Invalid bucket name
sections.text: S3 bucket names cannot contain /. If you need a key prefix: storage: s3: bucket: "my-bucket" # Bucket name only, no slashes prefix: "sessionfs/" # Optional key prefix The code also handles bucket: "my-bucket/prefix" gracefully by splitting on the first /.

sections.heading: asyncpg SSL errors
sections.text: Do not add ?sslmode=require to the database URL. SessionFS handles SSL parameter translation internally. For RDS and Cloud SQL, asyncpg negotiates SSL automatically for non-localhost connections. # Correct — no sslmode externalDatabase: host: mydb.cluster-abc123.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com existingSecret: sessionfs-db # Wrong — do not add sslMode externalDatabase: host: mydb.cluster-abc123.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com sslMode: require # This will cause errors

sections.heading: Rate limiting returns 429 unexpectedly
sections.text: Rate limiting is per API key, not per IP. Check your configured limit: api: rateLimitPerMinute: 120 # Default: 120 requests/min per API key # Set to 0 to disable rate limiting entirely Or via environment variable: SFS_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE=0 # Disable SFS_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE=10000 # Effectively unlimited Changes require a pod restart to take effect.

sections.heading: Cursor sessions show 0 tool calls / audit returns 0 claims
sections.text: Cursor sessions captured before v0.9.4 may be missing tool calls. The Cursor converter now reads the agentKv:blob: layer which contains full tool call data. To fix existing sessions: Restart the daemon: sfs daemon restart The daemon re-scans and re-captures Cursor sessions with the updated converter Re-push affected sessions: sfs sync If the audit still returns 0 claims, the session may genuinely have no tool calls (e.g., a question-answer chat without code operations).

sections.heading: Codex resume fails
sections.text: If sfs resume --in codex fails with "Failed to resume session": Ensure you have Codex CLI installed: codex --version The resume command is codex resume <uuid> (a subcommand, not a flag) SessionFS auto-launches Codex after conversion If Codex shows the session picker but then errors, the rollout file format may be incompatible with your Codex version. Check ~/.codex/sessions/ for the generated .jsonl file.

sections.heading: Handoff recipient can't pull session
sections.text: The handoff claim now copies session data to the recipient's account. If the recipient gets "Session not found": Ensure the handoff was claimed: sfs pull-handoff hnd_xxx The correct command is sfs pull-handoff (not sfs pull --handoff) Check that the claim created a copy: the recipient should see the session in sfs list-remote

sections.heading: Resume fails with "path not found"
sections.text: When resuming a handoff session, the sender's working directory may not exist on the receiver's machine. SessionFS automatically falls back to the current working directory. Use --project to specify a different path: sfs resume ses_abc --in claude-code --project ~/my-project

sections.heading: SQLite "database locked" errors
sections.text: The daemon and CLI share a SQLite index. If you see "database is locked", it usually resolves within 5 seconds (busy_timeout is set to 5000ms). If persistent: Check if multiple daemon instances are running: ps aux | grep sfsd Stop all daemons: sfs daemon stop Restart: sfs daemon start

sections.heading: A session isn't syncing / keeps failing
sections.text: When pushes for a session keep failing (server errors, rate limits, network problems), the daemon backs off rather than retrying every cycle: after 1 minute, 5 minutes, 15 minutes, then hourly. After 12 failures over at least six hours it pauses that session until the session changes, the daemon restarts, or you retry it. See which sessions are backing off or paused, with their last error: sfs daemon status (or sfs doctor, under "Sync retries") Fix the underlying cause if the error points to one (for example sfs auth status for authentication problems) Retry now instead of waiting: sfs daemon retry-sync ses_abc12345 (a unique prefix of the ID works), or sfs daemon retry-sync with no ID to retry every backing-off or paused session. If you started the daemon with --config, pass the same --config PATH.

sections.heading: Autosync not working
sections.text: Check mode: sfs sync status Ensure authenticated: sfs auth status In selective mode, sessions must be watched: sfs sync watch ses_abc The daemon polls for settings changes every 60 seconds -- wait after changing mode in the dashboard Check daemon logs: sfs daemon logs

sections.heading: Deleted session keeps reappearing after sync
sections.text: This was a known bug before v0.9.9. The old behavior: deleting a session from the dashboard triggered a server soft-delete, but autosync would re-push the local copy and silently un-delete it. Fix (v0.9.9+): Deletes are now sync-aware. When you delete a session, the ID is added to ~/.sessionfs/deleted.json and autosync skips it in both directions. Upgrade to v0.9.9 or later and the problem goes away.

sections.heading: How to permanently delete a session
sections.text: Soft-deleted sessions are retained for 30 days. After that, an admin can purge them via POST /api/v1/admin/purge-deleted. This hard-deletes all expired sessions (blob + database row). Requires admin role.

sections.heading: Deleted session still counts against storage
sections.text: Soft-deleted sessions are excluded from storage quota calculations. If you see stale numbers after deleting sessions, the API may be serving a cached response. Wait a few minutes and check again, or run sfs sync status to get a fresh count.
